channel.title: KSL.com - Utah News
channel.description: Utah breaking news and local top stories from KSL.com

item.title: Salt Lake City said it's making progress on unruly parties. These residents disagree
item.description: Nearly two dozen Salt Lake City residents, including former Mayor Rocky Anderson, sent city leaders a 14-page letter disputing claims that last year's ordinance targeting unruly parties near the University of Utah is working. The city has issued 171 warnings to property owners but fined only 29 repeat offenders, and while police detective Marie Stewart called the warnings "incredibly effective," the residents describe late-night parties and officers who declined to step in, including after the Utah-Utah State game. The mayor's office says it is "actively working" on the issue, weighing changes to the ordinance and planning letters to rental property owners in the area.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Trump makes the Oval Office a national monument. But future presidents can still redecorate
item.description: President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room a national monument, his first official act since his party's midterm defeats, though the order explicitly preserves a president's authority to redecorate and can itself be reversed by a successor. Trump cast it in sweeping terms, saying the office "will not be allowed to be touched by anybody," and claimed major changes would need congressional review, a requirement the AP notes is not in the document's text. The order puts the Interior secretary in charge of the space, and it lands as Democrats such as Sen. Richard Blumenthal press donors to Trump's ballroom project for information.
item.dc:creator: Collin Binkley and Darlene Superville, Associated Press

item.title: Utah ski resorts ramp up for winter as eager skiers await opening day
item.description: Brighton Resort is targeting an opening in the third week of November, weather permitting, after months of equipment inspections and training for roughly 1,000 employees who are now "just waiting for that call," according to marketing vice president Jared Winkler. Meanwhile, college skiers drawn to Utah by its snow reputation, including Westminster student Jace McAdams, have been building small features on early-season patches to practice tricks.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Meet the woman whose mission is to beat loneliness, 1 step at a time
item.description: Lucy Rose, the 72-year-old founder of the Cost of Loneliness Project, is walking 51 days from Santa Monica to New York City through 17 states to gather people's stories and "put a face to this epidemic of loneliness". The walk ends Nov. 12 with a National Day of Connection, when Rose is asking everyone to spend at least 12 minutes at noon with someone they care about. The CDC says loneliness carries health risks comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day, and one survey found 42% of men and 37% of women are lonely.
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Stahl, KYW via CNN

item.title: Heading to the BYU-Utah game? What to know about traffic and transit
item.description: Ahead of Saturday's 10 a.m. BYU-Utah kickoff at Rice-Eccles Stadium, University of Utah police Lt. Ryan Speers expects the worst traffic on 500 South in the final 45 minutes, with Guardsman Way closed to through traffic from 7 a.m. and rolling closures on nearby roads such as Foothill Drive. Game tickets work as fare on UTA buses, TRAX and FrontRunner all day, and UTA is adding buses and TRAX cars, with special buses from Salt Lake Central and Courthouse stations starting at 8 a.m. UTA's Thomas Lee said riders should expect service to get "more crowded as we get closer to kickoff" and suggested tracking trains in the Transit app, while police recommend rideshare pickups on University Street.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: 'Pretty exhausted': Utah communities seek federal flood help after emergency declaration
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox's emergency declaration for flood-damaged San Juan and Washington counties followed calls from Bluff Mayor Josh Ewing for federal help, with Ewing saying residents are "pretty exhausted" and that repairs are "seven, eight-figure problems". The declaration lets Utah mobilize resources and request federal or interstate aid but guarantees no money for individual homeowners, and Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson conceded the state has few resources for individual flood victims while urging Utahns to donate supplies. State Route 163, a key route for emergency services and Monument Valley tourism, remains closed indefinitely, and Ewing also worries about damaged flood-control berms near Montezuma Creek.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Investigators found Utah senator likely engaged in workplace discrimination and harassment
item.description: An Oct. 26 report by the law firm Parsons Behle & Latimer, obtained by KSL through a public records request, found Democratic state Sen. Kathleen Riebe "more likely than not" violated state policies on workplace harassment and discrimination, including a pattern of conduct toward a female staffer tied to race, national origin or ethnicity. The staffer described racially charged comments and remarks about her clothing, body and pregnancy, and one witness said Riebe did not want "any gay interns". Riebe, already removed from the Senate Democratic caucus and urged to resign, has refused, tying the allegations to her leadership ambitions and her concerns about a staffer doing campaign work for Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, while saying in a statement that she takes workplace concerns seriously.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe's backlash spreads
item.description: Protesters broke into the construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam on Friday, climbing a crane, setting off flares and clashing with police, and Dutch police said they detained 150 to 200 people suspected of trespassing. The action coincided with two days of "Stop Dirty Data Centres" events in 15 European countries, including smaller Friday protests near Berlin and outside the Polish parliament, as organizers seek a moratorium on large developments over social and environmental concerns. Microsoft said it respects peaceful protest but does "not condone any actions that are unlawful", and PwC projects Europe will draw $5.6 trillion in data center capital spending from 2026 through 2050.
item.dc:creator: Mike Corder and Suman Naishadham, Associated Press

item.title: Trump administration holds up Utah as national example on this issue
item.description: HUD Secretary Scott Turner held up Utah this week as the national model for the Trump administration's move away from "housing first" toward treatment-focused homeless services, pointing to the state's drop in homelessness last year. "Housing First failed, Treatment First will succeed", Turner said, while HUD Assistant Secretary Ronald Kurtz said now-competitive Continuum of Care grants can fund outpatient care, job help and street outreach rather than only beds, making Utah a top contender. Tomco notes that lawsuits still constrain HUD's ability to cancel existing grants, and that the push toward institutionalizing homeless people, which Gov. Spencer Cox has cheered, has threatened a long-standing obligation to serve seriously disabled people in their own communities.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Feds investigate after damage found to 2 prehistoric petroglyphs near Moab
item.description: The Bureau of Land Management is asking for tips after someone carved names into two prehistoric petroglyph panels near Moab, one along state Route 279 west of town and the other in the Hell's Revenge area. Rock art in the area, some dating to 3500 B.C. according to AllMoab.com, is protected by the Archaeological Resources Protection Act, and officials said damaged panels "cannot be restored to their original condition". Penalties in recent cases have included fines, probation and temporary public-lands bans for a Colorado pair over a 2024 theft and disruption at a Canyonlands archaeological site, and nearly $15,000 in fines and restitution for a southern Utah woman who defaced petroglyphs near Lake Powell.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
item.description: President Donald Trump named Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff for policy and the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration agenda, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, days after Republicans lost control of Congress in Tuesday's midterms. AP reads the shuffle as Trump resisting a conciliatory approach, even though about 6 in 10 voters in the AP Voter Poll said immigration enforcement had gone too far, and incoming House Oversight Chairman Robert Garcia said Trump "is doubling down". Wiles, the first woman in the post and the longest-serving of Trump's chiefs of staff, resigned Thursday night, according to a person familiar with the events, and said serving had been "the honor of a lifetime."
item.dc:creator: Seung Min Kim, Associated Press

item.title: He nearly pulled off a Salt Lake City upset last year. Now he's headed to the Utah Legislature
item.description: Stephen Otterstrom, a west-side Salt Lake City Democrat and human resources consultant, ran unopposed for Utah House District 21 a year after losing a City Council race to Victoria Petro by 118 votes despite being outraised about five to one. Otterstrom got into politics through Nick Mitchell's 2022 congressional campaign and was pushed to run by opposition to the city's sales tax increase tied to Smith Entertainment Group's downtown project, and lists income tax reform, the Great Salt Lake, cooperative housing, education and maternal health among his priorities. With House Republicans possibly losing their supermajority, he expects a Legislature "more inclined to work toward progress than toward running a party line" and is weighing bills for what he hopes could be a "honeymoon session" in 2027.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Uruguay at start of South American tour less than a month after surgery
item.description: Pope Leo XIV, 71, landed in Montevideo on Friday to open a 12-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, the longest and farthest trip of his pontificate, less than a month after his Oct. 13 lung surgery, and Vatican communications chief María Montserrat Alvarado said "His stamina is fantastic." The AP sets the visit, the first to Uruguay by a pope since John Paul II in 1988, against the country's standing as Latin America's most secular, rooted in a weak colonial church and reflected in its early legalization of marijuana, abortion, same-sex marriage and assisted dying. Guzmán Carriquiry, former head of a Vatican commission for Latin America, expects Leo to try to revive Uruguay's Catholic roots, while Virginia Commonwealth University's Andrew Chesnut cautioned that the enthusiasm may not translate into "folks in the pews".
item.dc:creator: Nicole Winfield, Nayara Batschke and Isabel Debre, Associated Press

item.title: Cullimore concedes Utah Senate race to Democrat who wants new leadership in both parties
item.description: Utah Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore, R-Sandy, conceded the District 19 race to Democrat Shana Anderson, a stay-at-home mom and Army veteran leading by more than 3,600 votes, as Democrats and two unaffiliated candidates are on track to unseat 13 Republican incumbents and flip three other GOP seats. Cullimore blamed national "trickle-down" sentiment and said the public should engage more, while Anderson said she grew concerned about his support of the since-repealed union bill and a school voucher program and wants new leadership in both parties, including someone other than Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla. "He thought he was so powerful that he was untouchable," Anderson said.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: 'Here to help each other': UVU students launch clothing drive to help peers acquire business wear
item.description: Utah Valley University communications students are bringing the PowerSuit Project to campus Tuesday, letting students pick out donated professional clothing such as blazers, slacks, dresses, shoes and scrubs for free in the Clarke Building concourse. Junior Sydney Wilson, one of the organizers, said rising costs for gas, food and tuition leave students little room for work clothes, and the event will also offer headshots from a professional photographer and a resume-building table. Wilson said the goal is for students to feel valued, adding, "We're here to help each other."
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Unsealed indictment shows political motives behind alleged obstruction by local sheriffs
item.description: Newly unsealed, less-redacted indictments allege that Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby, now on paid leave, sent an anonymous letter attacking the credibility of Summit County detective Eric Mainord, an investigator in the Kouri Richins case who was running against Rigby for sheriff. Prosecutors say the letter's 13 paragraphs matched a records request for Mainord's personnel file signed by retired Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds, and that Rigby hoped to use the trial's publicity to push the detective out of the race; Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates told Rigby the effort "feels slimy." Rigby is also accused of sending a fake anonymous email urging Lt. Jeremy Hales not to run, and Hales went on to beat Rigby in the June primary and win this week's election.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft and Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Tesla set to wind down production of Cybertruck
item.description: Tesla will begin winding down Cybertruck production at its Austin, Texas, plant, the only one that makes the truck, "around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," CEO Elon Musk posted Friday on X. It wasn't clear whether the truck would be built elsewhere, though lead engineer Wes Morrill wrote that it "lives on through Cybercab". The vehicle fell well short of Musk's 2023 estimate of 500,000 a year, with Tesla reporting fewer than 37,000 sales of all models other than the Model 3 and Model Y this year, and the news followed a drop of more than 12% in both Tesla and SpaceX shares over the first two days of trading after the midterms.
item.dc:creator: Chris Isidore, CNN

item.title: Cox issues state of emergency over flooding in southern Utah
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox declared a state of emergency Friday for San Juan and Washington counties, freeing state resources and opening the door to federal or interstate aid after weeks of flooding that the governor said "damaged homes, disrupted access to drinking water and cut off important travel routes". The National Weather Service reported the San Juan River near the Four Corners crested at 21.3 feet Tuesday, nearly 7 feet above its old record, while Gould Wash flooding in Hurricane affected roughly 130 homes or RVs and the Comb Wash Bridge on U.S. 163 was closed. A Climate Prediction Center meteorologist tied the subtropical storms to a strong El Niño, which has helped lift parts of Utah out of drought but also caused flooding.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Midvale gold heist leaves store with heavy losses
item.description: Thieves backed a stolen truck through the glass entrance of Utah Gold Buyers in Midvale early Tuesday and took gold jewelry, coins and Cartier bracelets that owner Cole Cannon values at around $50,000, with repairs to his store and a neighboring business that he estimates could top $100,000. Cannon believes the break-in by at least three people was planned, though the ringleader who stayed longest went for a silver coin case instead of the gold jewelry: "He was basically stepping over gold to pick up silver." Unified police say the truck had been stolen about two hours earlier from a South Jordan home and was found abandoned in Sandy; no arrests have been announced.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Provo River Trail enters final phase of construction, expanding for safety and accessibility
item.description: Provo has started the last piece of a trail overhaul it began in 2018, widening a 0.8-mile stretch of the Provo River Trail between Columbia Lane and University Parkway from 6 feet to 14 feet and adding a pedestrian bridge east of State Street. The $5 million project, mostly covered by a $4.6 million Mountainland Association of Governments grant, aims to fix sightlines, grades and sharp turns and meet ADA rules, and parks planning and project manager John Bunderson says public input treats the segment as "the keystone part of the project" that people want finished. Runner Mary Ann Nielsen, whose child was hit by an electric scooter on this section, welcomes the extra width, though trail closures are expected through July and construction through summer 2027.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Panda fans flock to Zoo Atlanta for the debut of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang
item.description: Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, 6-year-old giant pandas on a 10-year loan from China, made their public debut Friday at Zoo Atlanta, whose enclosure had been empty since four pandas went back to China in 2024, ending a 25-year partnership amid strained relations. The AP notes China's long use of pandas in diplomacy, and Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng said the arrival "marks the renewal of a decade-long bond between China and Zoo Atlanta." Visitors included an 8-year-old from Sacramento who called seeing them "the best thing in my life" and a Georgia Tech student from the pandas' hometown of Chengdu, and Zoo Atlanta is now one of three U.S. zoos with the bears.
item.dc:creator: R.J. Rico and Emilie Megnien, Associated Press

item.title: USU partnership with local zoo is a win-win for exotic animals, future veterinarians
item.description: Utah State University veterinary students are getting hands-on practice with birds, reptiles, big cats and primates, from routine checkups to the occasional surgery, through a partnership with Logan's Zootah, formerly Willow Park Zoo. Dr. Mike McEntire, who teaches zoological medicine, says zoos struggle to find specialists, noting "There's only six of us in the whole state that have this kind of specialty," and that while a handful of vet schools partner with local zoos, to his knowledge none offer this early access. Zootah director Troy Cooper, who also teaches an exotic-animal elective, says the exposure could help the small zoo reach full accreditation.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: San Juan County man given 16 years for possessing child sex abuse material
item.description: Johnston Blackhorse, 43, of Aneth was sentenced Wednesday to 16 years in federal prison plus lifetime probation for receiving and possessing child sexual abuse material, years after calling himself "an untreatable pedophile" at a revocation hearing over obscene drawings of children. He was already on supervised release for a 2015 conviction when probation officers on a February 2025 home visit found a forensic wiping program that had been used that day on his computer, and a fuller examination recovered six images from deleted space. U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak said his pattern of behavior shows he "remains a dangerous offender with a significant likelihood of recidivism."
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah women raise awareness about heart health through personal stories, quilting
item.description: A group of local women has made more than 80 quilts to be auctioned at the Holiday Quilt Show, Nov. 10-12 at Thanksgiving Point, with proceeds going to Intermountain Health's Women's Heart and Vascular Program. Intermountain cardiac surgeon Dr. John Doty says medicine has historically focused on heart disease in men, and that women's warning signs can differ, with pain that may show up in the arm, neck or stomach. BYU nursing student Chloe Harmer, 21, who has had two open-heart surgeries, offers a simple message: "Don't take your health for granted and take care of your heart".
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Why does BYU-Utah rivalry game trigger such deep emotions? Sports psychology prof weighs in
item.description: A new Y2 Analytics poll of 786 Utahns found BYU narrowly ahead of Utah, 37% to 34%, as the team residents usually root for, though roughly 52% sided with the Utes when forced to choose, and 77% of BYU fans said they would likely cheer for Utah in a big out-of-state matchup compared with 47% of Utah fans returning the favor. University of Utah sports psychology professor Matt Moore traces the intensity to social identity, noting that rival fans share families, workplaces and church communities, which can make a loss or slight feel personal. Moore says social media amplifies a "loud minority" and urges fans to care deeply but remember "it is just a game."
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
item.description: Democrats who flipped governorships in states including Texas, Ohio and Georgia wove hard lines against data centers into their platforms, and Data Center Watch found 32 of 34 winning governor candidates back stronger regulation or restrictions, with 12 supporting bans or moratoriums. Morgan Stanley singled out Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Texas Gov. Greg Abbott as the "most important election result" for data center development, while Redbud Consulting counted restrictions approved in 44 of 45 completed local referendums and the AP Voter Poll found about three-quarters of voters oppose a new data center in their community. OpenAI asked policymakers for "clear rules for how the industry builds", and the Data Center Coalition's Dan Diorio warned that moratoriums would carry real-world consequences such as lost local tax revenue.
item.dc:creator: Marc Levy, Associated Press

item.title: Anthropic rapidly accelerating AI development amid slowdown calls, research group says
item.description: An analysis by the Berkeley nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research, which Anthropic gave "unprecedented access to internal data" and staff interviews over about 11 weeks, estimates the company is improving its models on "well specified tasks" around twice as fast as a year earlier. METR ruled out growth in training compute and guessed the speedup comes from using AI itself to improve AI, while cautioning that it could be overstating its findings and that Anthropic's redactions limited the detail it could share. Co-founder Sam McCandlish said many of the conclusions matched his own, and the report lands as CEO Dario Amodei urges the industry to slow down and the company prepares what could be the biggest IPO ever.
item.dc:creator: Kelvin Chan and Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press

item.title: Groundbreaking ceremony held in celebration of Davis County's replacement animal shelter
item.description: Davis County broke ground in Fruit Heights on a 27,223-square-foot animal shelter to replace the county's only shelter, an 11,000-square-foot building from 1985 that lacks room to quarantine sick animals and no longer meets the standard of care. The new building will hold 60 dogs in larger, angled kennels meant to cut stress and noise, up to 94 cats and some exotic animals, plus its own veterinary clinic, a community room and a fenced exercise area. Construction is set to begin in January with an expected opening in mid-2028, and Davis County Animal Care director Michelle Hicks said the community "has deserved better for a little while".
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch may have so much plastic, it's changing the color of the ocean
item.description: University of Bergen researchers, writing in Communications Earth & Environment, found that 20 years of satellite data show the Great Pacific Garbage Patch brightening in blue and green wavelengths relative to the surrounding ocean, likely shifting toward cyan, and their simulations pointed to microplastics rather than natural causes such as phytoplankton. Direct measurements at the patch are still needed to show the color "is directly and exclusively caused by plastics," said PhD candidate Shea Cheatham, but if confirmed, the approach could help track tiny particles that are otherwise laborious to quantify and that may help explain why so little of the plastic entering the ocean is found floating. Richard Thompson of the University of Plymouth, who was not involved, said remote detection from satellites would be faster and cheaper than counting debris piece by piece.
item.dc:creator: Laura Paddison, CNN

item.title: At 96, Utah woman continues making teddy bears for kids
item.description: Volunteers with the Teddy Bear Project, which 96-year-old Ruth Brasher has helped lead for 33 years, have sewn, stuffed and decorated more than 23,000 bears for children visiting the Utah County Children's Justice Center, a child-friendly setting for kids involved in abuse investigations. Brasher said the comfort reaches beyond the children themselves, asking, "what about the mothers, fathers who see their child having an opportunity to overcome a difficult experience in their life?" Springville volunteer Dana Sorenson, who joined after meeting Brasher about a year ago, called the work "a beautiful way to use my talent" to make something of worth for young kids.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Betting is high stakes among young gamblers — even in a state where gambling is illegal
item.description: Gambling is illegal in Utah, but phones make betting easy even for minors, and Caleb Silverman of the recovery app Bettrr said more than 2,200 Utahns called his gambling hotline last year, up 28%, while Common Sense Media found nearly half of boys have bet on sports by age 17. BYU professor Mark Johnson's research in states that legalized betting found investing fell as much as 20% among frequent bettors, with the biggest debt increases in the most vulnerable households, and he warns overconfident young bettors that "You're going to lose to the house 98% of the time." Required financial literacy classes, including one at Skyridge High School, now cover gambling, as Attorney General Derek Brown pursues criminal charges against prediction market company Kalshi and its executives, who have been ordered to appear in 3rd District Court next month.
item.dc:creator: Deanie Wimmer, KSL

item.title: 4 Ogden women among the wave of Democrats poised to flip seats in the Utah Legislature
item.description: Weber County, which sent no Democrats to the Utah House last year, is poised to send three, with Rosemary Lesser, Kim James and Angela Choberka all on track to win Republican-held seats while CJ Hernandez leads Jill Koford for the open District 5 Senate seat. Statewide, at least 13 Democrats were on track to unseat GOP House incumbents and two unaffiliated candidates to beat other Republicans, which would shift the chamber from 61-14 to 46 Republicans, 27 Democrats and two unaffiliated members, while House Speaker Mike Schultz said, "There are lessons from this election at every level". James said many lifelong Republicans told her while canvassing that they couldn't stand it anymore, often naming President Trump, and Hernandez and Lesser said voters raised corruption, data centers, rising costs and the Great Salt Lake.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Whitney Leavitt's life beyond 'Secret Lives' is coming to Hulu
item.description: Hulu has greenlit an untitled reality series about Whitney Leavitt, who announced her exit from The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives in May after five seasons; she will executive produce it with her husband, Connor, through Leavitt Media House, with Jeff Jenkins Productions also producing. Leavitt marked the news Wednesday with an Instagram video of fans' speculation and the caption "See you soon." The show adds to a busy stretch that has included a Dancing With the Stars semifinal finish and a record-setting Broadway run in Chicago, with a December return to Broadway in Just In Time and a film debut in Netflix's All For Christmas still ahead.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: Corrections department disputes claims of inadequate inmate care during month-long lockdown
item.description: Utah Corrections Watch founder Nadine Salyer says inmates told her of days without leaving their cells or showering, refunded commissary orders, missed medications and even "three different people swallowing razor blades" during the monthlong lockdown at the Salt Lake City and Gunnison prisons, but deputy corrections commissioner Mike Schoenfeld says those claims are false and that the department has "zero reports of that stuff." Schoenfeld acknowledged that visitation, programming and education were disrupted and that commissary was affected for about a week, but he said inmates still got an hour out of their cells each day. The lockdown followed a Sept. 24 attack at the Central Utah Correctional Facility that nearly killed a sergeant, which Schoenfeld called a coordinated effort by a group planning further attacks; officers now work in pairs, and the last tiers reopened Oct. 29.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Man gets probation for threatening family of man involved in Stratos data center project
item.description: Casey Hill, a spokesman for Kevin O'Leary on the Stratos data center project in Box Elder County, told a judge Thursday that "There is a fundamental difference between opposing a project and threatening the lives of the people that are involved," as Daniel Charles Kasimow, 56, was sentenced to two years of probation for misdemeanor stalking. Charges say Kasimow kept texting threats in late May, including that Hill and a business partner would be dead if the data center came to Utah, and that Hill spent thousands on security and relocated while his daughter was in hospice care. Under a plea deal, eight lesser counts were dismissed and Judge Adam Mow suspended a one-year jail term; Kasimow did not speak at sentencing but had written an apology letter, according to the charges.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Possible new dinosaur species discovered at dig site near Arches National Park
item.description: Fossils from the newly opened Ironstone Bonebed north of Arches National Park appear to belong to a previously unknown armored dinosaur species roughly 140 million years old, according to the Utah Geological Survey. State paleontologist Jim Kirkland, who leads the dig, hopes to name the species for assistant state paleontologist Don DeBlieux, his field partner of 25 years, who retires from the state at year's end. Because the site sits just above the Morrison Formation, it could help explain what followed the extinction event at the end of the Jurassic, and Kirkland expects "decades of work on this individual site".
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Wisconsin infant is third measles-related death this week in US
item.description: An infant has died in Wisconsin's largest measles outbreak in more than three decades, the state's first measles death in over 35 years and the third reported in the U.S. this week, after a child in New York's Lewis County and an unvaccinated resident of rural Pennsylvania. Wisconsin has logged 431 cases this year, compared with 36 in 2025, and with kindergarten MMR coverage at about 85%, well short of the roughly 95% needed, state epidemiologist Dr. Ryan Westergaard said the virus keeps "finding new hosts" among susceptible people. The state now recommends an early MMR dose for some at-risk infants ages 6 to 11 months, as the national count passes 4,800 cases, the most since 1991, ahead of an international review of U.S. elimination status next week.
item.dc:creator: Jen Christensen, CNN

item.title: Utahns vote to retain Supreme Court Justice Jill Pohlman, and other election updates
item.description: More than 77% of Utah voters chose to retain Associate Chief Justice Jill Pohlman, the Supreme Court's highest-ranking member, despite calls from Rep. Burgess Owens and Utah Republican Party Chairman Rob Axson to vote her out amid GOP frustration over the court's rulings on abortion and redistricting. The AP called the 2nd Congressional District for Rep. Blake Moore on Thursday, leaving Rep. Mike Kennedy's lead in the 4th District as the only uncalled race, while Democrats stayed on pace to flip legislative seats and Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore trailed Shana Anderson by more than 4,000 votes. Forward Party Sen. Emily Buss trailed Republican Brooks Benson by fewer than 200 votes as counting continued, with Salt Lake County planning more result releases Thursday night and possibly through Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: From Tonga to Utah's Capitol: Doug Fiefia celebrates historic Senate election
item.description: Republican Rep. Doug Fiefia, who led Democrat A. Dane Anderson with about 55% of the unofficial vote in Senate District 18, is poised to become the first Tongan-American in the Utah Senate, a result he tied to the sacrifices of parents who immigrated from Tonga in the 1970s. Crediting more than 100 volunteers, his wife, Jocelyn, and a relative who served in the Utah House decades ago, Fiefia said he is "standing on the shoulders of people who came before me," and hopes Polynesian kids and others are inspired to serve. Having reached the race by ousting Sen. Dan McCay in the June primary, Fiefia, who has worked in the tech industry, named affordability, parental rights and growth as priorities, with online child safety a particular focus, arguing that "Parents shouldn't have to fight billion-dollar companies alone to protect their children".
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera

item.title: Utah picks new mineral contractor for US Magnesium site, calls it a 'significant win'
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox called it a "significant win" that Texas-based Mariana Minerals will plan a phased restart of lithium and magnesium extraction at the former US Magnesium site on the Great Salt Lake, using low-water, non-evaporative methods in place of the site's large solar evaporation diversions. Utah bought the 4,500-acre property and its nearly 145,000 acre-feet of water rights for $30 million after the company's bankruptcy, and projects that royalties from the new operation could help pay for cleanup of what is also a Superfund site. Specific terms, including cleanup milestones, are still being finalized, and CEO Turner Caldwell said the aim is to transform the site into "a 21st-century operation that we can be proud of."
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: California Gov. Newsom says he will commute all death sentences in state to life without parole
item.description: Gov. Gavin Newsom said he will commute the sentences of all 548 people on California's death row to life without parole, though the state Supreme Court must approve 382 of them, roughly 70%, because those inmates were convicted of a felony more than once. Newsom, who imposed a moratorium on executions in 2019 and is leaving office while weighing a presidential run, wrote that "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values," a stance the ACLU applauded. Prosecutors and some victims' relatives condemned the move, with San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow calling it a "sickening abuse of power", while Polly Klaas' sister Jess Nichol, whose views changed over time, said execution distracts from what survivors actually need.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Austin, Jaimie Ding and Christopher Weber, Associated Press

item.title: Felony charges filed against Utah man following 3 1/2 hour standoff
item.description: A 46-year-old Saratoga Springs man, David Glenn Logsdon, faces felony charges including assault on a police officer, aggravated assault and domestic violence in the presence of a child after a Halloween-night standoff that lasted 3 1/2 hours. Charging documents say Logsdon repeatedly pointed a handgun at his wife and at himself during an argument after both had been drinking while their 1-year-old granddaughter slept in the basement; after the wife fled and called 911, an officer team went in and brought the baby out safely. From an upstairs window he threw a monitor, bottles and books at officers and claimed he had "plenty of ammunition" until chemical munitions brought him out, and police found two handguns but no spent casing proving he had fired.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump meets at the White House with Putin envoy after he appeared with Melania Trump
item.description: At a White House event honoring Melania Trump for brokering a six-day ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, where nearly 800 people evacuated and aid was delivered, both Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Ukrainian officials thanked the first lady, who said she hoped it would be "the modest spark that grows into a lasting flame of peace". President Trump later said he met privately with Dmitriev but not with the Ukrainians, and predicted "a big agreement" that would involve more than Ukraine, possibly all of Europe. The AP notes the truce was the most significant since Russia's full-scale invasion and part of a broader foreign-policy role for the first lady, who has also helped reunite nearly three dozen children with their families.
item.dc:creator: Darlene Superville, Associated Press

item.title: Bingo, Care Bears, Pokémon cards, playground slide make it into the Toy Hall of Fame
item.description: Care Bears got a boost from nearly 1 million social media followers, and Pokémon cards from anime and manga fans, on the way into the National Toy Hall of Fame, where they join bingo and the playground slide as this year's picks from 12 finalists. Curator Mirek Stolee noted that bingo, long associated with older players, has caught on with young adults in bars and nightclubs. Jeremy Saucier, vice president for collections, said people of all ages fondly remember "the simple, satisfying, and energizing experience of racing down a slide".
item.dc:creator: Mark Kennedy, Associated Press

item.title: Massive tech sell-off wipes $2.5T from the stock market
item.description: Fears that Democrats' midterm gains, notably Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's call for a temporary data center moratorium, could slow the AI buildout sent the Nasdaq down 5.52% into correction Thursday, erasing roughly $2.5 trillion in value, while the Dow gave back 1,833 points and all 11 S&P 500 sectors closed lower. Chip stocks led the rout, with Nvidia off 9.3% and a closely watched chipmaker index posting its worst day in about six and a half years, as the VIX jumped roughly 70% and the 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.84%. Truist's Keith Lerner, who viewed the swings as more knee-jerk than predictive, said "the risk-reward is improving for longer-term investors," while Ed Yardeni welcomed a slowdown, saying the buildout "was too frenzied and speculative".
item.dc:creator: Elisabeth Buchwald, John Towfighi and Matt Egan, CNN

item.title: A wipeout for AI stocks sends Wall Street reeling, and the S&P 500 tumbles more than 3%
item.description: Stocks tied to the AI data center buildout led a broad Wall Street sell-off Thursday that more than erased the previous day's rally, leaving the S&P 500 down 3.9% and on track for its worst drop since the April 2025 tariff shock, while the Nasdaq slid into correction territory, more than 10% below its October high. Nvidia fell 8.7% and AMD 15.5% amid worries about costly borrowing and the chance that Democratic midterm wins could lead governments to pause data center construction, though AppLovin jumped 28.5% on strong results. Easing Treasury yields hinted that investors were seeking safety, and in London the Bank of England raised rates for the first time in three years as Gov. Andrew Bailey said resolving "the conflict in the Middle East" was the best thing that could happen.
item.dc:creator: Stan Choe, Associated Press

item.title: Postal employee shot 2 coworkers at an Iowa post office before being captured, police say
item.description: Police in Des Moines say a 39-year-old postal worker opened fire Thursday in a nonpublic second-floor area of the city's main post office, wounding two female coworkers, while a male employee was hurt in a fall as he tried to escape; all three were in stable condition. Officers arrived within three minutes and detained the unnamed suspect without resistance on a nearby bike path, where a 9 mm handgun was recovered, and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service is investigating with local, state and federal agencies. Earlier postal shootings, including a 1986 rampage in Edmond, Oklahoma, helped prompt a study released in 2000 that concluded "going postal" was a myth.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press

item.title: Utah leaders discuss homelessness solutions at statewide summit
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox gave the keynote at the Central Utah Homeless Summit in Salt Lake City, the last of three regional gatherings, saying homelessness "touches every community in the state". Organizers reported a 2% drop in homelessness in Utah and a 9.7% decline in unsheltered homelessness, and State Homeless Coordinator Tyler Clancy said the Legislature fully funded Cox's top budget priority with about $17 million in ongoing money and about $25 million in one-time infrastructure funding. Switchpoint CEO Carol Hollowell urged statewide cooperation, warning that without it "we're going to be in a bigger crisis in the next go around".
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Russia and Ukraine trade airstrikes as reconstruction and security talks resume in Brussels
item.description: Talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction, 2027 funding and Western-backed security guarantees ran for a second day at NATO headquarters in Brussels, with the World Bank and BlackRock attending alongside U.S., European and NATO officials, days before planned Russia-Ukraine-U.S. negotiations in Abu Dhabi. Overnight, Russia said it downed 496 Ukrainian drones, Kremlin-installed officials said a Ukrainian strike on a bus killed five people in occupied Luhansk, and rescuers kept searching for more than 30 people believed trapped after Monday's guided-bomb attack in Komyshuvakha, where Zelenskyy said 43 have been confirmed dead. The European Commission also sent Ukraine $4.9 billion from a $101 billion EU loan, and Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF he hoped the Democrats' midterm win would help renew U.S.-European ties while adding that "I am also grateful to the Republicans".
item.dc:creator: Derek Gatopoulos, Associated Press

item.title: California resident is latest to be charged in Utah tap-to-pay scam
item.description: Prosecutors charged Liu Huan, 36, of Irvine, California, in 4th District Court with money laundering, theft by deception and other felonies, alleging tap-to-pay purchases since Oct. 1 in St. George, Orem, Sandy, Midvale, Salt Lake City and Draper. In these scams, phones loaded with stolen card numbers are tapped on self-checkout devices to buy gift cards or electronics, with gift card numbers sent to a handler who quickly moves the funds, and investigators believe a "criminal enterprise" of Chinese nationals headquartered in China, with U.S. bases in California and New York, is sending people to Utah. Police found dozens of gift cards and receipts plus boxed electronics in Huan's vehicle, and the charges say Huan admitted buying two gift cards for $980 and sending screenshots to a person in China for a promised $100.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Unemployment claims drop to 189,000, the fewest since mid-July
item.description: Weekly claims have stayed at or below 200,000 for eight weeks running, and the latest Labor Department count of 189,000 initial jobless claims is the lowest since mid-July, a sign that layoffs remain rare. Hiring is a weaker story: employers have added about 68,000 jobs a month this year and only 29,000 last month, though that still beats 2025's average of 9,700. Forecasters surveyed by FactSet expect Friday's October report to show 65,000 new jobs, with unemployment holding at 4.2%.
item.dc:creator: Paul Wiseman, Associated Press

item.title: 2 unaffiliated candidates poised to win seats in Utah Legislature
item.description: Utah could see its first independent general-election winners in modern history, as unaffiliated candidates Patrick Belmont and Sergio Sotelo lead races for Republican-held House seats: Belmont is ahead of Rep. Jason Thompson by more than 1,700 votes in Cache County, and Sotelo leads by nearly 1,100 in the open seat vacated by Rep. Cheryl Acton, where Republican Chris McConnehey has conceded. Belmont, a Utah State University professor who lost a 2024 bid, argued that "we have got to get away from party politics" and drop labels, while Sotelo, a longtime IBEW electrician, said his backers span parties and "vote with our pockets." Party records are spotty, but BYU's Adam Brown said no Utah legislator has lacked a party affiliation since at least 1934, and the Legislature's lone third-party member, appointed Forward Party Sen. Emily Buss, narrowly trails in her own race.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign
item.description: Wendy's board adopted a one-year "poison pill" plan, triggered when anyone holds 15% or more of its shares, after independent directors unanimously turned down a $1.4 billion offer from Nelson Peltz's investor group, which already holds 16.3% of the stock, saying the bid "substantially undervalues" the company. CEO Bob Wright, the chain's fourth chief executive since 2024, argued that his Dave's Way turnaround, from thicker bacon and creamier Frosties to a slimmer menu, is already working, and third-quarter revenue of $547 million beat analysts' forecast even as same-store sales fell 5.2%. Peltz, who chaired the Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024, had pitched his offer as the best path for shareholders amid high beef prices, aging stores and pressured consumers.
item.dc:creator: Dee-ann Durbin, Associated Press

item.title: State argues it alone should investigate leftover evidence after overturned 1985 murder conviction
item.description: Utah County prosecutors told the court this week that they intend to run forensic genealogy testing themselves on what remains of the evidence in the 1985 killing of Eva Olesen, opposing a request from Doug Carter's attorneys to do their own testing after DNA results found none of Carter's DNA and the knife carried only the victim's profile and an unknown man's. Prosecutor Christopher Ballard wrote that the investigation is ongoing and that the samples must be preserved for any future defendant, while the state still insists Carter is the killer, pointing to a confession the defense says was coerced and whose recording was destroyed. Defense attorney Neal Hamilton questioned why prosecutors waited until he sought a court order, saying "Their case has fallen apart" and that the state "stole 41 years of Doug's life" on death row.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson, KSL

item.title: The rivalry forecast: KSL Sports experts give their game-day predictions
item.description: Ahead of Saturday's 10 a.m. BYU-Utah kickoff in Salt Lake City, KSL Sports' Sam Farnsworth predicted BYU will turn Utah's 23-year streak of interceptions for touchdowns around by returning one itself in the second half, and said Byrd Ficklin could lead the Utes in rushing and even throw a touchdown pass. Jeremiah Jensen framed the game around quarterbacks, saying BYU's Bear Bachmeier must repeat his Notre Dame form while Utah's Devon Dampier gets a chance to make up for last year, and suggested the morning start could take some edge off a crowd that is loud and chaotic at night. The two agreed only that something unexpected is coming, or as Jensen put it, "Every year there is gonna be a crazy play."
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: El Niño has brought flooding. It's also slowly lifting Utah out of drought
item.description: Weeks of El Niño-driven rain have shrunk Utah's drought footprint from over 90% of the state to about two-thirds in one week, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor, with parts of the Uintas and southeast Utah out of any drought category for the first time since June 2025, and the share in severe or extreme drought falling to about 36%. Mountain soil moisture has climbed to nearly 78% saturation, above the typical spring peak, which Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton described as "uncharted territory," and Gunlock Reservoir went from 37% full to over 100% while Lake Powell rose 17 feet in a month. Still, the statewide reservoir system sits at just 50% of capacity after this year's record-low snowpack, and Clayton said it is too early to know how the soggy fall will shape conditions over the coming months.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Bob the poet, meet Bob the priest: Pope Leo XIV receives Bob Dylan at the Vatican
item.description: Pope Leo XIV, the Chicago-born pontiff born Robert Prevost, received Bob Dylan in a private audience at the Vatican's apostolic palace on Wednesday, a meeting the Vatican newspaper confirmed using Dylan's birth name, Robert Allen Zimmerman. Leo has already quoted an unpublished 1963 Dylan anti-nuclear protest song in the preface to a collection of his addresses, in keeping with the church's opposition to nuclear weapons that he has emphasized, and Dylan once performed for Pope John Paul II at a 1997 church event in Bologna. The Rev. Antonio Spadaro, the Vatican official who brokered the visit after arranging Leo's earlier meeting with Patti Smith, wrote that the encounter had "a real sense of history about it".
item.dc:creator: Christopher Lamb, CNN

item.title: Utah Food Bank faces growing challenges as holiday demand rises
item.description: As holiday demand rises, Utah Food Bank president and CEO Ginette Bott says monetary donations give the organization the most flexibility as costs climb, especially fuel for its fleet of about 70 delivery vehicles. Bott said flooding has created obstacles for the food bank's southern Utah pantries, and some communities are losing service from local pantries, adding strain to its distribution network. The food bank is also seeking nutritious food donations, and Bott urged shoppers to buy extra groceries because "Everything your family loves, another family will enjoy".
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Cache Valley Humanitarian Center turns volunteer hours into millions of dollars in aid
item.description: The Cache Valley Humanitarian Center, which opened in July 2021 with a $2,000 grant from two Logan Rotary Clubs, has produced more than $2 million worth of newborn kits, hygiene kits, sleeping mats, quilts and other items for people in need, according to co-founder and executive director Dwight Whittaker. Whittaker counts about 45,000 volunteer hours so far, and the center works with about 30 nonprofits and three school districts in an area stretching from Wellsville to Preston, Idaho. Volunteer Cloteel Liechty, 97, said the work "makes my day," and the center welcomes more individual volunteers and groups, especially youth groups.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: 'That was not discipline': Man accused of attempting to drown daughter sentenced
item.description: Andres Blas Hernandez, 46, who was accused of holding his daughter under the San Pitch River and pleaded guilty to two counts of child endangerment and a drug misdemeanor, had his prison terms suspended and was ordered to serve 270 days in jail and three years of probation with anger management, substance abuse and mental health requirements. His daughter told the court she wanted prison because "I could have died that day and he did not care," while Hernandez apologized and insisted he "intended to get the phone wet, and that was it." Sixth District Judge Robert Van Dyke said the conduct had built over time rather than being a single incident, pointing to Hernandez's earlier prison time and failed probation.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Cornell rape investigation will be led by a former prosecutor in the Sean 'Diddy' Combs case
item.description: New York Attorney General Letitia James named Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell alumna and former Manhattan federal prosecutor who oversaw sex crimes cases against Sean Combs and Peter Nygård, to lead the reopened investigation into a former student's allegation that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024. Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor on Oct. 1 after losing faith in Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024, and two men named in the student's lawsuit are now seeking James' removal over a social media post supporting the accuser that she made before her appointment. Kelly, who will remain at Boies Schiller Flexner during the probe, said "All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case".
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

item.title: What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
item.description: The NTSB investigation into the Bahamas-bound Learjet that crashed in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm, killing all nine aboard, will likely take more than a year, though a preliminary report without analysis of the cause is expected about 30 days after the crash. Pieces of the tail's elevator found more than a mile from the main crater confirm the jet began breaking apart before impact, and NTSB member Tom Chapman said the cockpit voice recorder would be "very important data" but that not finding it wouldn't doom the probe. Weather will be an early focus, with retired airline pilot John Cox saying "I don't understand why they came down" from 41,000 feet near the storms, while investigators also review maintenance records and interview the operator, Upper Jets, and air traffic controllers.
item.dc:creator: Josh Funk, Associated Press

item.title: Romney blames GOP midterm losses on 'bad policy, bad character'
item.description: Former Sen. Mitt Romney wrote on social media that Republicans' midterm losses came down to "Bad policy, bad character", listing grievances from erratic tariffs and the Iran war to blanket pardons, ICE brutality and hiding Epstein, and said he hoped for a course correction. Other Republicans offered their own explanations: Vice President JD Vance said the Iran war was "the reason we lost," while Utah Sen. John Curtis called the election a wake-up call for a party he suggested had abandoned core conservative principles. Democrats, who flipped both chambers with some races still pending, credited affordability and dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Salt Lake County continues processing more than 100,000 ballots as key races remain unsettled
item.description: Salt Lake County is still verifying more than 100,000 mail ballots dropped off on Election Day, a process Clerk Lannie Chapman said now takes roughly 12 seconds per ballot instead of two to three because a new state law adds a check of the last four digits of a voter's Social Security number or Utah ID to signature matching. Early returns suggest Democrats could gain control of the County Council and voters appear to be backing a $128 million parks and recreation bond, though Chapman cautioned "we still have a lot of ballots to count." Officials hope to release more totals Thursday evening and Friday, provisional ballots will be added next week, and certification will follow the two-week canvass period in which voters can cure ballot problems.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Florida authorities say 2 dead at Tampa office complex, including gunman shot by security guard
item.description: A gunman drove a car into a courtyard where people were eating lunch on Citibank's Tampa business campus Wednesday and killed a woman with a rifle before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria and fatally shot him, according to the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, which gave no motive and did not say whether the two knew each other. Chief Deputy Frank Losat said about 3,200 people were working on the campus, four others were hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries and more than 360 deputies spent 2 1/2 hours clearing buildings, and he offered "kudos to that security guard" for preventing potential further violence. A nearby Sheraton sheltered an estimated 300 Citibank workers, and a Citibank vice president recalled an "incredible clatter" he later realized was gunfire.
item.dc:creator: Russ Bynum and Chris O'Meara, Associated Press

item.title: Ogden man sentenced to 15 years to life imprisonment in killing of his mother
item.description: Alec Conrad Martinez, 27, was sentenced Monday in 2nd District Court to 15 years to life in prison for murdering his mother, Jennifer Martinez, in Ogden in 2025, after pleading guilty in July while citing a mental condition. Under the plea deal, the Weber County Attorney's Office dismissed counts of attempting to disarm an officer of a taser and use of a dangerous weapon by a restricted person. According to the account of the June 19 emergency calls, the mother screamed "He has a knife!" before the line went silent, and Martinez then called dispatchers to say he thought he had killed her.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: The Southern Taurid meteor shower will bring rare fireballs tonight
item.description: The Southern Taurid meteor shower produces only about five meteors an hour but is known for bright fireballs from marble- to boulder-sized debris shed by comet 2P/Encke, with viewing expected to be best around midnight Thursday and the peak estimated around 3 p.m. ET on Nov. 5, according to EarthSky. NASA's Bill Cooke said "when you see one, you'll remember it" and advised finding a dark spot and giving eyes at least half an hour to adjust without a phone, while astronomer Bethany Cobb Kung suggests locating Orion's belt and looking to the right toward Taurus. Cooke said Earth is predicted to pass through a denser swarm of Taurid debris in 2032, describing the present as "a lull before the thunderstorms occur."
item.dc:creator: Dharma Niles, CNN

item.title: Southern Utah couple accused of abusing young daughter
item.description: Trevor Dean Noffsinger, 22, and Mariah Faith Calapp, 21, of Cedar City were booked into the Iron County Jail on Tuesday for investigation of aggravated child abuse after an investigation that began in February, when doctors found their 4-month-old daughter had clavicle and rib fractures in different stages of healing along with grip-pattern bruising that medical staff deemed non-accidental. According to a police affidavit, Calapp admitted lying to a nurse about the cause, while Noffsinger told police "I believe it might have been me" but said he didn't hurt the baby on purpose and blamed palm bruising on not knowing his own strength. Police also noted Noffsinger's prior child abuse conviction and the 2024 death of the couple's infant son, ruled a sudden unexplained infant death, whom Calapp said had the same palm bruising.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'It wasn't just a home': Flooding displaces generations of a family near Bluff
item.description: Kayla Atcitty's grandmothers, cousins and other relatives were displaced when San Juan River flooding near Bluff reached homes in a family community whose roots trace back to her great-great-grandfather, with water rising from shin- to thigh-deep within about an hour as they fled with documents, medications and animals. One grandmother and four cousins are now in Atcitty's basement, bringing her household to 10, while another grandmother is in an RV park cabin near Blanding, and the family doesn't know whether the homes will be livable given worries about water under the structures and mold. Atcitty, whose own parents lost their home there in a 2003 flood, said "It wasn't just a home that they lost," and has started a GoFundMe for the family.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: A 24-year-old running the NYC marathon collapsed 2 miles from the finish line and died
item.description: Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, collapsed a couple of miles short of the finish in her first New York City Marathon on Sunday and died at a hospital; the medical examiner is still investigating, though her father told the New York Times the cause was rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which skeletal muscle breaks down and poisons the body. Mount Sinai nephrologist Doug Farrell, who documented 24 rhabdo cases at the unusually hot 2022 race, said heat speeds muscle breakdown, though Sunday's temperatures hovered in the mid-60s. Emory sports cardiologist Jonathan Kim said deaths from rhabdo "would be really, really rare", noting that heart attack is the most common cause of cardiac arrest in marathons and that runners' chance of dying from sudden cardiac arrest fell by half from 2010 to 2023.
item.dc:creator: Jen Christensen, CNN

item.title: JetBlue raises baggage fees a second time as jet fuel prices stay elevated
item.description: JetBlue has raised checked bag fees for the second time this year, so most economy passengers on tickets bought on or after Nov. 3 will pay at least $50 each way for a first bag, up from $39, and as much as $70 when paying within 24 hours of a peak-period departure. The airline's March increase helped set off bag-fee hikes at Delta, United, American and Southwest, and JetBlue said in the spring that the increases help offset higher operating costs while keeping base fares competitive. Jet fuel prices have stayed elevated because the unresolved Iran war has largely restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, and JetBlue expects its average fuel price to reach $4.64 a gallon in the final three months of the year, up 85% from a year earlier.
item.dc:creator: Rio Yamat, Associated Press

item.title: These Salt Lake City blocks inspired Smith Entertainment Group's downtown plan
item.description: New design guidelines from Smith Entertainment Group for its planned downtown district draw on Salt Lake City areas such as Main Street, Regent Street, the 2nd & 2nd District and 9th & 9th, which executive Mike Maughan said the company wants to learn from rather than recreate, aiming for something "uniquely Salt Lake" instead of the mountain and red rock motifs common in Utah pitches. City leaders were surprised that building heights may top out near half the zone's 600-foot maximum, Council Chairman Alejandro Puy said, but they're encouraged by plans to break up the Salt Palace and raise 200 West, and they believe a proposed 6,000-seat music venue was placed to limit impacts on Japantown, where community members raised concerns. An updated development agreement could be drafted by year's end, with a Planning Commission presentation tentatively set for Dec. 9 and a partial demolition of the convention center slated to begin in February or March.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Sen. Riebe says she won't resign, pushes back on misconduct allegations
item.description: Utah state Sen. Kathleen Riebe of Cottonwood Heights said Wednesday "I am not going to resign" after fellow Senate Democrats voted to remove her from their caucus and called for her resignation, citing an investigation they say found workplace harassment and discrimination. Riebe said she was not allowed to review the report or invited to meet before the vote, and told KSL she believes the matter stems from concerns she raised about a legislative staffer allegedly doing campaign work for Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, who did not immediately respond. She also questioned the timing of the announcement, released late Tuesday just before polls closed on a big election night for Democrats.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Davis County man who wanted to 'go out in a hail of glory' faces felony charges
item.description: Kelly Scott Dicus, 43, of Clearfield, is charged with aggravated kidnapping and other domestic violence-related counts after charging documents say he appeared inside his estranged wife's home shortly after midnight Oct. 9, days after she served him an eviction notice, took her phone and kept her from leaving while a gun in his lap pointed toward her. According to the charges, he said that if the children called police he would "make sure he took officers with him," and police say he later brandished a gun at officers during an armed standoff in Syracuse and was shot. Police asked that Dicus be held until trial as a "lethal threat", and Syracuse police said more charges may follow once the officer-involved shooting investigation concludes.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah House Republicans may lose supermajority for first time in decades
item.description: Utah Republicans appear on track to lose their two-thirds supermajority in the state House for the first time this century, with 15 sitting GOP lawmakers trailing their challengers on Wednesday and the caucus possibly shrinking from 61 seats to as few as 44, which would leave it unable to override vetoes or propose constitutional amendments without Democratic votes; Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore also trailed Democrat Shana Anderson by more than 4,000 votes. Incumbents blamed a national wave compounded by their own missteps, with Rep. Matt MacPherson calling the decision to put Amendment B on the ballot a likely strategic error, though Rep. Norm Thurston, trailing by nearly 600 votes, noted that only about half of Utah County's ballots had been counted. Taylor Morgan of Morgan May Public Affairs described "the blue bludgeoning" reaching Utah, while BYU political scientist Adam Brown attributed the losses chiefly to dissatisfaction with the Trump administration, saying down-ballot races are driven by "what's happening at the top".
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff and Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after 2 decades studying cosmic explosions
item.description: NASA's Swift Observatory reentered the atmosphere near Indonesia on Wednesday, ending a study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars that was planned for two years but lasted 22, after solar activity dragged down its orbit and a robotic orbit-boost attempt by Katalyst Space failed when that craft came down in September. NASA anticipated that some denser pieces of the 1 1/2-ton spacecraft would survive reentry. The agency is now asking private companies how they might boost, upgrade or safely deorbit the Hubble Space Telescope, which recent analyses expect to come down by the mid-2030s, and Administrator Jared Isaacman said the telescope "still has important science ahead of it".
item.dc:creator: Marcia Dunn, Associated Press

item.title: 'The Chosen' is fully funded. What's next?
item.description: Come and See, the nonprofit behind The Chosen, has reached the $78 million goal to fund the seventh and final season with help from more than 86,000 supporters in 175 countries, and can now focus on reaching 1 billion people and translating all seven seasons into 600 languages at about $75,000 per season per language. Come and See's Stacey Baxter said "Now the work is to take it to the world," noting that the series app drew 2.2 million international users in October, compared with 1.6 million in the United States. Season 6 premieres Nov. 15 on Prime Video, and the first season already holds a Guinness World Records title as the most-translated television season, in 125 languages.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: 'We have kids,' victim told gunman before being fatally shot during robbery
item.description: Ryley Jilberto Avila, 26, of Taylorsville, has been charged with murder, aggravated robbery and other counts in the Oct. 24 killing of Abraham Martinez, 24, in a West Valley City IHOP parking lot, where charges say Avila showed up "under the guise of buying cocaine" without money and pulled a gun. Martinez was in the back seat next to his children, ages 2 and 4, and his girlfriend heard him repeat "We have kids" before Avila allegedly shot him in the head inside the car and fired a second round as the car drove away. A man who was with Avila told police he suspected a robbery but knew of no plan to shoot anyone, and Avila was arrested at a Taylorsville apartment with help from a SWAT team.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Pleasant Grove students put together care packages for military families
item.description: Utah National Guard members, including Master Sgt. Greg Annis, visited Grovecrest Elementary in Pleasant Grove to thank its Purple Star Club, which assembled care packages of handwritten cards, stickers and school items for children with a family member deployed or about to deploy. Sixth grader Spencer, whose brother deployed about two years ago, said the project grew from knowing other kids face the same separation. Annis called it a personal thank-you from "probably the most affected members of a family when a loved one has to deploy".
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Democratic sweep of Congress ushers in new era; Trump acknowledges impact of the Iran war
item.description: Democrats won unusually wide majorities in both chambers, with Senate Democrats holding at least 54 seats after long-shot pickups in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, and they plan a 100-day agenda on gas, grocery and health care costs alongside broad oversight of the Trump administration, with impeachment an option. Trump signaled he could work with Democrats while threatening vetoes and acknowledged the Iran war affected the vote, and Vice President JD Vance pointedly wrote that "The reason we lost is the war". House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek reelection as GOP leader, according to two people familiar with his decision, setting up a potentially brutal leadership fight as some races remain too early to call.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press

item.title: Blake Moore will run again in leadership despite GOP midterm losses
item.description: Utah Rep. Blake Moore plans to seek reelection as House Republican conference vice chairman in next week's leadership elections, though he is also vying to be the top Republican on the House Budget Committee and said "I would not serve as both". Moore said the messaging role would become "more reactive to what Democrat leadership is doing" once Democrats take control of the House, with less emphasis on touting legislative wins. The Budget post likely won't be decided until December and could go to Rep. Lloyd Smucker, who is next in line, while GOP leaders including Speaker Mike Johnson may face pushback from rank-and-file members after the midterm losses.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Mayor Karen Bass and democratic socialist Nithya Raman in tight race to lead Los Angeles
item.description: Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and council member Nithya Raman, a challenger backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, were in a tight race in early returns Wednesday, with Raman holding a slim advantage and an estimated one-third of ballots still uncounted. Bass, backed by Gavin Newsom, Kamala Harris and Nancy Pelosi, has called Raman "not ready for primetime" and her views on policing and homelessness extreme, while Raman has pledged to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least 50% by 2028. The incumbent still faces fallout from the 2025 Palisades Fire, and a Raman win would place her alongside New York's Zohran Mamdani among democratic socialists leading city governments.
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Blood, Associated Press

item.title: County commissions in Weber, Davis counties will each get 2 new members
item.description: The Davis and Weber county commissions will each gain two new members after Tuesday's election, with former Bountiful Mayor Kendalyn Harris and former Plain City Mayor Jon Beesley having run unopposed for open seats. The other two races were still being counted: in Davis County, unaffiliated former commissioner Bret Millburn narrowly led Republican Susan Lee 50.7% to 49.3%, though Millburn noted as many as 30,000 ballots remain uncounted, and in Weber County, Republican Duane Kearsley led Democrat Alvin Thurgood 49.2% to 45.2%. Harris, who will take the seat Bob Stevenson left to run for the Utah House, said the first priority is to "get our fiscal house in order".
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: CVS to split into two companies, in major breakup of its $117B healthcare empire
item.description: CVS Health will separate into two companies in a tax-free transaction expected to close in early 2028, reversing a strategy that began with its 2007 Caremark merger and continued with its $69 billion purchase of Aetna in 2018. CEO David Joyner described the move as "taking what I believe is one great company and making it two," and the split isn't expected to change how people shop at CVS or what patients pay for prescriptions. It cuts against an industry trend toward integrated conglomerates that consumer advocates and lawmakers blame for higher costs, and CVS shares fell 10% in early trading even as the company reported stronger third-quarter results and raised its guidance.
item.dc:creator: Chris Isidore and Tami Luhby, CNN

item.title: First lady Abby Cox wrote a children's book
item.description: Utah first lady Abby Cox read her new children's book, Jennie Makes Room, to students in the Governor's Mansion ballroom, telling the story of philanthropist Jennie Judge Kearns, whose giving helped fund an orphanage that became Kearns-Saint Ann Catholic School, helped finance the Cathedral of the Madeleine and supplied the mansion now used as the governor's residence. Cox said she "realized how much my work intersected with the things that she was passionate about", and said proceeds will go to the Mansion Foundation to preserve the home, whose details are hidden throughout Matt Loveridge's illustrations. The school's principal, a great-great-granddaughter of Kearns, noted that the students were walking through the home of the family whose generosity helped make their school possible.
item.dc:creator: Reagan Campbell, Deseret News

item.title: Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, will be first Muslim senator
item.description: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat and will become the nation's first Muslim senator, after a grassroots campaign built on Medicare for All and sharp criticism of Israel that survived nearly $30 million in AIPAC spending against him in the primary. Rogers struggled to stay aligned with Trump amid high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran, while Republicans sought to link El-Sayed to terrorist organizations without evidence. "They might have been pointing to my name and my faith, but we all know my name and my faith are not why you can't afford your gas," El-Sayed said in his victory speech, a result that gives progressives an argument heading into 2028 that their agenda can win in battleground states.
item.dc:creator: Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press

item.title: 2 rescued from southern Utah reservoir that received a rare fall surge
item.description: Washington County search and rescue crews and local firefighters pulled two people from the roof of their Toyota Tacoma on Monday after it became stuck crossing the river near the Gunlock Reservoir waterfalls and water began entering the cab. The reservoir surged from 37% capacity last month to 109% as of Tuesday after several nearby mountain locations received more than 8 inches of precipitation in October, a sharp contrast with its typical fall rise of about one percentage point. With record-high soil moisture and long-range forecasts showing no sign of a break in the stormy pattern, sheriff's officials warned that "Even familiar crossings can quickly become dangerous" and urged people never to drive through swift-moving water.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Power customers in 16 Utah communities face fee hike for renewable energy program
item.description: About 250,000 Rocky Mountain Power customers in 16 communities, including Salt Lake City, Park City, Moab and Ogden, will be automatically enrolled Jan. 1 in the Community Clean Energy Program, which adds $4 a month to residential bills and a usage-based fee for businesses to fund wind, solar and other renewable resources under HB411, a 2019 law. Customers can avoid the fee by opting out by Dec. 31 and can leave without a termination fee through May 1, after which a one-time $30 charge applies, a charge Salt Lake City's Glade Sowards said "isn't punitive" but meant to gauge interest. Kamas-area resident Dee Warner, surprised by the notification letter, opted out and accused those behind the program of "going behind our backs".
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Volunteers work to clean up Bluff Historic Fort after flooding in San Juan County
item.description: Recent flooding sent water and mud through the Bluff Historic Fort in San Juan County, forcing volunteers to empty 13 cabins and wash, dry and treat the chairs, beds and other furniture before returning them. Co-director Connie Hunt said people from every state have called to ask whether the fort, which tells the story of pioneers who reached Bluff in 1880 and remains open, was saved, and she joked that unlike the settlers she has "a pressure washer" and a crew of 100.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff wins reelection, defeating Rep. Mike Collins to hold a key Democratic seat
item.description: Sen. Jon Ossoff, 39, won a second term Tuesday by defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Rep. Mike Collins, holding what had been a top GOP target as the only Senate Democrat seeking reelection in a state Trump carried in 2024. Ossoff ran as an aggressive Trump critic, raised more than $100 million amid 2028 speculation, and repeatedly branded Collins a "bigot" over past posts and associates' white nationalist ties, while Collins struggled with fundraising and an unresolved House ethics investigation. The AP calls the win a "notably bitter confirmation" of Trump's slide toward lame-duck status in the state where he anchored his false claims about the 2020 election.
item.dc:creator: Bill Barrow and Sudhin Thanawala, Associated Press

item.title: Jury begins deliberating at Russell Brand's rape and sexual assault trial
item.description: Jurors at London's Southwark Crown Court began deliberating Tuesday in Russell Brand's trial after three weeks of evidence, with Judge Joel Bennathan telling them their verdict must be unanimous.
