Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009, and he testified that his encounters were consensual. His lawyer, Ian Winter, argued the women went to police only after a 2023 documentary that left the "well of justice" tainted, and told jurors, "It is not criminal to treat women unkindly before, during or after sex."
item.dc:creator: Jill Lawless, Associated Press

item.title: 'Drop what you have and just come talk to us,' police order before fatal shooting
item.description: West Valley City police released body camera video Tuesday showing an officer spending about three minutes urging Sebastian Enrique Cerda-Monti, 40, to drop what he held and leave a storage shed outside a TownePlace Suites hotel on Oct. 25, at one point using pepper spray, before Cerda-Monti charged him waving two silver objects 2 to 3 feet long. The officer fired 10 to 12 shots and Cerda-Monti died at the scene despite immediate aid, after a hotel employee's 911 call reported he had threatened to shoot workers trying to enter. West Jordan police will investigate for the Salt Lake County District Attorney's Office, and court records show Cerda-Monti had been sentenced to time served a week earlier for mail theft and failing to stop for police.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: It's Election Day: Here's why 12 election monitors are in Utah
item.description: Twelve of the Justice Department's 1,000 federal election monitors were assigned to Utah, all in Salt Lake County, where Clerk Lannie Chapman said she has "No concerns" and noted the monitors, mostly Utah residents, are expected to check compliance with Spanish-language materials and disability access laws. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said they will work in pairs at six or seven sites under the standard observer rules, such as staying six feet from booths, and that while the scale is unusual, federal monitors visiting states is normal. The Utah League of Women Voters and ACLU of Utah, which have trained about 150 poll watchers who will also watch the monitors, warned the lack of specifics could intimidate voters, with Helen Moser calling the effort "kind of capricious."
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Salt Lake City plan for a year-round Downtown Farmers Market building fizzles
item.description: The Salt Lake City Downtown Alliance has dropped its plan for a permanent, year-round Downtown Farmers Market building at Pioneer Park, an estimated $20 million to $25 million project endorsed by Mayor Erin Mendenhall, after a year and a half of talks failed to settle ownership and financing. City real estate adviser Blake Thomas said "it came down to the funding" because the city had no budget allocation for the building, though it would revisit the idea if that changed. The alliance will instead pursue a permanent winter market home, returning to the old Leonardo Museum building for a market starting Nov. 14, the day after the renovated park reopens.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Polls begin to close in midterm elections as voters pass judgment on Trump's second term
item.description: Polls began closing Tuesday in midterm elections framed as a referendum on President Donald Trump's second term, with Republicans bracing to lose the House and fighting to hold the Senate, where Democrats need a net gain of four seats, after more than 59 million early ballots surpassed 2022's early turnout. The AP Voter Poll found about three-quarters of voters angry or dissatisfied with the country's direction and about 8 in 10 reporting inflation-related hardship, even as Trump told Fox News that "inflation is solved" despite 3.6% annual price growth in September. Key contests include Texas, where Trump-backed Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico, plus North Carolina, Georgia, Ohio and Alaska, and a Democratic chamber could open investigations into figures such as Pete Hegseth and Elon Musk.
item.dc:creator: Jill Colvin, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert, Associated Press

item.title: Ballot drop boxes fill early as Salt Lake County voters make final Election Day push
item.description: Last-minute voters filled some Salt Lake County ballot drop boxes to capacity by mid-morning on Election Day, and County Clerk Lannie Chapman said many people waited until the final 24 hours, so collection teams kept emptying boxes throughout the day. Voter Nicole Masco said the older she gets, the more important it is to have a say, calling it "a no-brainer" to do her civic duty. Collected ballots go through signature and registration checks before counting, and officials urged anyone still holding a ballot to use an official drop box before polls closed at 8 p.m.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell and Cameron Elliott, KSL

item.title: Death toll hits 31 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, with dozens still missing
item.description: Russian strikes with bunker-busting bombs on a former school and a shelter where people were lining up for humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, killed at least 31 people, including four police officers and two rescue workers, with more than 45 still missing. Acting regional head Mykhailo Semikin called it "one of the worst tragedies" for civilians in the region since the full-scale war began, and the attack came after a six-day ceasefire in Oleshky expired, which Zelenskyy said Ukraine had offered to extend. An overnight barrage of 289 drones and 76 missiles also hit power plants and hospitals across nine regions ahead of U.S.-mediated peace talks set for Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi, where Zelenskyy wants a halt to strikes on energy infrastructure.
item.dc:creator: Derek Gatopoulos and Geir Moulson, Associated Press

item.title: Election Day unfolds with relatively few problems including weather, machine issues
item.description: Relatively few voting problems had been reported by 4:30 p.m. MST Tuesday, with the biggest disruptions caused by flooding in Florida and the Southwest, where Navajo Nation officials moved polling sites and Utah's San Juan County let voters cast ballots electronically. In New York's Westchester County, a program update left scanners rejecting paper ballots, which went into emergency bags for later counting, and Broward County, Florida, started 20 minutes late after a new safety feature malfunctioned. Despite the Justice Department's largest-ever poll-monitoring effort and an ICE post warning noncitizen voters "There will be no escape," none of the federal steps Democrats most feared had happened, and David Becker of the Center for Election Innovation and Research called the smooth day "remarkable."
item.dc:creator: Ali Swenson, Associated Press

item.title: Weber County officials discuss election preparations, federal concerns
item.description: Weber County Clerk/Auditor Ricky Hatch, whose team set up 100 voting booths at the county fairgrounds on election eve, said this year has been a struggle of "seeing them as a threat" rather than a partner, referring to the federal government, which had sought voters' Social Security and driver's license numbers in a Justice Department suit a judge dismissed 10 days ago. Turnout was 38% Monday morning, on par for a midterm, and Hatch expects 60% to 65%, adding, "We love boring elections." Ballots must arrive by 8 p.m., and those dropped off late on Election Day may not be counted until Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Brittany Tait, KSL

item.title: Fresh snow fuels excitement, but Super El Niño's effect on Utah winter is unknown
item.description: A weekend storm dropped 17 inches at Snowbird and let several resorts begin making snow, with Solitude scheduled to open Nov. 20 and Alta pausing uphill travel for snowmaking. Brighton's Jared Winkler said crews must take advantage of cold temperatures because it "can warm up (in) late November," and he hopes for at least an average winter after a rough last season. Super El Niño projections vary, but an Alta spokesperson said the odds favor more snow than last year.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Flights across Europe face disruption after false bomb threats
item.description: Hoax bomb threats Tuesday targeted LOT, SAS and Ryanair flights across Europe, prompting diversions, searches and an Italian Air Force Eurofighter escort for a Dublin-to-Rome plane, a day after a Wizz Air flight from Luton was diverted to Budapest; no explosives were found and no one was hurt. Matthew Borie of Osprey Flight Solutions said the focus on Europe means "there could be a Russian angle," though Iranian hybrid warfare is also active there, and his advice to travelers was "Don't be alarmed." Greek authorities separately searched and evacuated the Israeli-run cruise ship Crown Iris at Syros as a precaution after a bomb threat.
item.dc:creator: Kirsten Grieshaber, Stefanie Dazio and David Biller, Associated Press

item.title: Job postings jumped sharply in September, potentially good sign for those seeking employment
item.description: Job openings rose to 7.5 million in September from a revised 7.19 million, the most since May, while gross hiring increased, layoffs fell to 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025, and quits reached an 18-month high, so openings now exceed the number of unemployed. Navy Federal Credit Union economist Heather Long called the data "an encouraging sign" despite high fuel prices and inflation, but ZipRecruiter's Nicole Bachaud warned that inflation and higher interest rates will likely remain "a downward pressure on hiring." Friday's October jobs report is forecast to show 65,000 jobs added, a modest figure that the AP notes can still keep unemployment low as baby boomers retire and immigration falls.
item.dc:creator: Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press

item.title: Utah teacher accused of pulling gun during drill resigns
item.description: A 40-year-old Hillcrest High School health sciences teacher who has not been charged resigned Monday, and Unified police forwarded his case to the Salt Lake County District Attorney's Office after saying he pointed his concealed handgun at his classroom door during a Sept. 30 lockdown drill as administrators and officers checked doors. A search warrant affidavit says 27 students were inside as he knelt behind a table aiming through the door's window, and that he told police he didn't know about the drill but couldn't describe any threat that justified his actions. Canyons School District spokesman Jeff Haney said drills are announced in advance and teachers with valid permits may carry guns, and that the teacher, with the district since 2018, was placed on paid leave the day of the drill.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 911 call released from the man who killed a shooter inside an Ore. elementary school
item.description: A newly released 911 recording captures Kaylub Giamanco telling a dispatcher "I have a gun, and I will shoot them right now" after spotting a gunman at his daughter's school, Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old killed three children and a teacher on Oct. 15, as the operator urged him to wait for police. Giamanco climbed in through a window and shot the attacker, Griffin J. John II, who was struggling for his weapon with learning specialist Cassidy Schutz, newly identified by the district, after she threw her phone and tackled him. Giamanco credited Schutz with giving him an opening, calling her "a real true hero," and said he regrets not arriving soon enough to save everyone.
item.dc:creator: Martha Bellisle, Associated Press

item.title: Election Day: Here's a look at the 8 state school board races for 2026
item.description: Eight Utah State Board of Education seats are on this year's ballot, and four are uncontested, with Democrats Kacee Weaver and Sarah Reale and Republicans LeAnn Wood and Linda Hanks set to take or keep seats. In contested races, Republican incumbent Jennie Earl, seeking a third term, faces Democrat Cathy Callow-Heusser, who opposes state management of federal education funds and warns it could "weaken civil rights protections," while appointed Republican incumbent Erin Longacre faces Democrat James Martin. Open seats left by Republicans Christina Boggess and Cindy Bishop Davis pit Democrat Araueni Olivares against Granite school board president Nicole McDermott and Democrat Lacey Peterson against legislative attorney Tracy J. Nuttall.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: High school athletes can now earn college credits for participating in events at SUU
item.description: Southern Utah University has expanded a credit program that began this year at the Larry H. Miller Utah Summer Games, so high school juniors and seniors competing in sporting events held on its Cedar City campus can earn three elective credits for a $30 fee. Students must compete in two different sports or event categories through the Utah High School Athletic Association, the Summer Games or both, and qualifying events this month include Special Olympics Utah Unified Flag Football and the 1A-3A Eight-Player Football Championships. Parowan High senior Cooper Heath said it lets him "get a head start" on college, and his mother, an SUU employee, called it "the cheapest way to get three college credits that you can even imagine."
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Hybrid Utah school offers students the best of both worlds
item.description: Jordan Virtual Learning Academy, made up of Rocky Peak Virtual Elementary, Kesley Peak Virtual Middle School and Kings Peak High School, pairs online instruction from certified teachers with in-person sessions two to three times a week and serves about 4,500 K-12 students. Any student with a Utah address can enroll, and Principal David Hullinger said families ranging from traveling athletes to students with anxieties want virtual school but "don't like their student only in front of a computer all day." Students and a parent cited working at their own pace and the social time on campus, and school leaders credit that flexibility for growing enrollment.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Utah's soil moisture levels jump to 'uncharted territory.' Here's why that matters
item.description: After what is expected to be one of Utah's wettest Octobers on record, statewide mountain soil moisture reached nearly 78% saturation, about four points above the usual spring-runoff peak, a reading Utah Snow Survey director Jordan Clayton called "uncharted territory." Wet fall soils typically make spring snowmelt more efficient, and reservoirs have already risen from 46% to 49%, but the saturation has also fueled flash flooding and landslides, and Clayton cautioned that "The snow has to come." Last year shows the risk: strong fall soil moisture was followed by Utah's worst snowpack on record.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Dementia-Friendly Choir brings people together through music and love
item.description: The Janet L. Herrick Dementia-Friendly Choir in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, brings together more than 30 people living with dementia, caregivers and others touched by the disease, and director Carra-lyn Conger said music helps people with memory loss stay active by triggering different parts of the brain. Julie Messner, who has never missed a rehearsal and whose mother and husband both had dementia before dying in 2019, urged people to love such family members "like they were still ones you fell in love with." Members step in when someone loses their place in a song, and 96-year-old Marilyn Zimmerman said people in the choir are "very understanding and helpful" ahead of a Nov. 21 performance at Uptown Social.
item.dc:creator: John Kim, WTMJ via CNN

item.title: Utah's new blue district could help Democrats deliver their verdict in a midterm test
item.description: The University of Virginia Center for Politics' final midterm rating projects Democrats winning the House by a 21-seat margin and calls Utah's 1st District, a court-ordered Salt Lake County seat Kamala Harris won by 24 points, a safe Democratic pickup for former Rep. Ben McAdams over Republican Riley Owen. McAdams, who once voiced anti-abortion views and was among the last to back impeaching Trump in 2019, now promises to end tariffs, halt military action in Iran and undo Trump's signature legislative achievement, and Crystal Ball editor J. Miles Coleman expects him to be "more mindful of his left flank" in office. Notre Dame political scientist James Curry likened the moment to Republicans' 2006 losses under George W. Bush and called the Utah seat "a huge win for Democrats nationally."
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Man pleads guilty to assaulting family members, driving car into Layton home
item.description: Marco Jamie Rodriguez, 28, pleaded guilty Oct. 20 to about half his charges, including domestic violence-related aggravated assault, DUI and failing to stop for police, from an August incident in which charges say he hit relatives and then accelerated toward them in a Layton carport, striking the home's brick. Police say the episode ended after a chase of up to 100 mph on U.S. 89, when a trooper's contact sent his car into a concrete wall and officers recovered a bag of meth, cocaine and LSD he had thrown over the freeway wall. He was out on release at the time in a January Bountiful trespassing case involving a loaded gun, where he also pleaded guilty, and sentencing in both cases is set for Dec. 1.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City's housing is 'out of whack.' This new complex seeks to help
item.description: Latitude Apartments, a 105-unit complex at 940 W. 200 South on Salt Lake City's west side, has opened with every unit reserved for households at or below 60% of area median income, 16 of them at 30%, and about 30% of units offering two or three bedrooms. Council Chairman Alejandro Puy, whose district includes Fairpark and Poplar Grove, said "Things are out of whack in society right now," noting the city can't control wages but put about $2.8 million into the nearly $39 million project, one of several developments adding about 1,000 units nearby. New resident Lynda Davison, who came to Utah after her husband entered a nursing home, said she feels "at peace," though officials acknowledge the state still lacks about 44,000 affordable rentals.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Stroke survivor grateful for therapy that helped him with new passion of woodworking
item.description: David Wilson, 64, a retired principal who skied and golfed avidly before a January 2024 stroke, regained use of his left hand through an emerging therapy that combines transcranial electrical and magnetic stimulation with intense hand exercises, now under study at the University of Utah. Dr. Amit Sethi said the treatment, given three times a week for six weeks, helps intact brain areas take over for damaged ones, and his five-year study is still seeking participants. Wilson has since found a new passion making wooden bowls, including a walnut chopping board for Sethi, and said "The stroke closed doors, yet at the same time, it opened other doors."
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Conservative climate group faces a midterm reckoning. Its Utah founder still sees hope for the movement
item.description: The Conservative Climate Caucus that Sen. John Curtis founded in 2021 as a House member could lose up to a third of its members, with 15 retiring in January and 11 in competitive races, including chairwoman Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and both vice chairs. Curtis attributes the vulnerability to "a little bit of a blue wave" hitting seats whose holders talk about climate, and argues that newcomers are more receptive than longtime members who have "become hardened" on the issue. He says rising energy demand has narrowed the partisan gap and points to his own Senate win in a deeply red state as proof the message works, even as a Senate permitting deal leaves wind and solar language unresolved.
item.dc:creator: Cami Mondeaux, Deseret News

item.title: Trump administration has slow-walked 380K potential immigrant voters
item.description: USCIS approved about 55,000 citizenship requests from April to June, down from more than 230,000 a year earlier, and Stateline estimates almost 380,000 more immigrants, nearly all adults, could have become citizens and potential midterm voters had the earlier pace held. USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler attributed the slowdown to tougher vetting, including social media screening and stricter English and civics requirements, writing that "Naturalization is a privilege, not a right," while the National Partnership for New Americans accused the administration of deliberately delaying people's civil and voting rights. How they would vote is unclear, since naturalized citizens split almost evenly in 2024 after favoring Democrats in 2020, and Texas demographer Lloyd Potter said a Census jump in self-reported citizens may reflect fear of answering surveys.
item.dc:creator: Tim Henderson, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Henderson issues emergency elections order for voters affected by San Juan County flooding
item.description: Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson issued an emergency declaration Monday letting San Juan County voters who can't reasonably reach a drop box or polling place because of flooding, including residents of Bluff, Aneth, Mexican Hat and Navajo Mountain, vote electronically, much as military and overseas voters do. Eligible voters will be emailed Tuesday morning and must request ballots by 5 p.m. and return them by 8 p.m., while those without an email on record can call the county clerk. Bluff Mayor Josh Ewing said flood-related building closures have cut off some drop boxes and he even saw a ballot floating in debris, and Clerk/Auditor Lyman Duncan said voters who lost ballots can cast provisional ones at polling places.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson and Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Lehi man pleads guilty in $60 million Ponzi scheme
item.description: Matthew Morrison Bates, 42, of Lehi, pleaded guilty Monday in federal court to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and money laundering in a Ponzi scheme that prosecutors say took more than $60 million from "hundreds of investors" between May 2020 and June 2025. Prosecutors said his company, Hedgehog Investments LLC, promised returns of 20% to 100% from bridge loans to businesses that it never actually made, paying investors with new investors' money. He is scheduled to be sentenced Jan. 12 and also faces a former investor's securities fraud lawsuit in state court.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Motorcyclist dies after Ogden Canyon crash involving local sheriff
item.description: Katie Huggins, who was critically injured last Tuesday when her eastbound motorcycle collided with a vehicle turning onto Canyon Road near the mouth of Ogden Canyon, has died, her family said Monday. Authorities have confirmed the vehicle's driver was Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter, who is on voluntary administrative leave during the investigation. The family thanked the community, said it hopes those responsible will be held accountable and noted that Huggins' organ donation will help others.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia and Payton Davis, KSL

item.title: Utah weighs a 60% threshold for tax initiatives as California considers taxing billionaires
item.description: Amendment B, placed on Utah's ballot by the Legislature in 2025, would raise the vote needed for citizen initiatives that change taxes from a simple majority to 60%, and supporters including Sen. Lincoln Fillmore point to California, where voters are weighing Proposition 40, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires. Fillmore said a 2024 Utah Supreme Court ruling leaves lawmakers treating citizen initiatives as "untouchable," and California-focused policy analysts said a higher bar would guard Utah against special interests seeking tax increases. Vote No spokesperson Scott Cuthbertson called the measure a "power grab" by a Legislature out of step with voters, and Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla said initiatives are already rare in Utah and lawmakers can still refine them.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Supermarket freezers in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks
item.description: Fridges and freezers in supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland and Estonia malfunctioned Monday in apparent cyberattacks, following a case last month in which attackers remotely seized refrigeration systems in hundreds of French stores. A Swedish ICA Kvantum store said its units were hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius, Delhaize reported an "IT incident" at several dozen stores, Carrefour said 15 of its more than 700 Belgian stores were hit, and Ireland's Musgrave Group pulled chilled and frozen goods at 13 SuperValu stores. An Estonian refrigeration firm said it stopped an attack on a client's system within minutes.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Annual Heels 2 Heal walk expanded this year to include focus on recent community violence
item.description: Utah-based Pacific Island Knowledge to Action Resources held its 12th annual Heels 2 Heal walk Saturday at Salt Lake City's International Peace Gardens, closing Domestic Violence Awareness Month and broadening its focus this year to community violence. Men were invited to walk in high heels as active partners in prevention, with CEO Susi Feltch-Malohifo'ou saying "we must have men be part of this movement." The story cites CDC survey data showing about one in five U.S. women and one in 23 men have experienced contact sexual violence.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Haven't voted yet? Here's what you need to know
item.description: Statewide turnout was about 27% as of Monday, and elections director Ryan Cowley urged remaining voters not to mail ballots but to use a drop box or county clerk's office, or vote in person with ID, by 8 p.m. Tuesday. Cowley said flooding has made access hard for some San Juan County voters, though polling places and drop boxes there will be open, and that 12 Justice Department monitors in Salt Lake County may "come in and watch the process" but can't be armed or approach voters. He attributed the lackluster turnout partly to the absence of high-profile races such as governor or U.S. Senate.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Argentina's Milei pitches a regulation-free AI haven at the end of the world
item.description: Argentine President Javier Milei is courting AI data centers with a no-regulation pitch, telling the U.S. Chamber of Commerce "We are not going to regulate artificial intelligence," and proposing to cut the corporate tax rate to 15% from 25% for projects of at least $1 billion, while Patagonia offers cold weather, wind, open land and Vaca Muerta shale gas. Polish firm Green Capital, which has yet to secure a customer, plans a $3 billion Patagonian campus on land leased from sheep ranchers that at peak would use about 2.7 times Buenos Aires' 2025 electricity, according to an AP calculation. Critics note the incentives require no local computing capacity or disclosure of energy and water use, a Córdoba computer science professor warned Argentina could become "a laboratory," and a small group of Trelew residents has rallied against data centers.
item.dc:creator: Isabel Debre, Associated Press

item.title: Which party cares about passing down their politics? New survey finds answer
item.description: The American Family Survey of 2,000 Americans, by the Deseret News, the Wheatley Institute and BYU's Center for the Study of Elections and Democracy, found most Americans don't consider passing their political beliefs to their children important, but Republicans are twice as likely as Democrats to say it is. Co-author Jeremy Pope said researchers "don't know why that difference exists" and speculated that Democrats may focus on passing down values rather than beliefs, while a 2023 Pew study found teens of Democratic parents matched their parents' party more often (89% vs. 81%). University of Utah student organizer Samantha Reagan, raised by Democrats and now a self-described socialist, said she kept her parents' moral values, such as caring for the poor, more than their politics.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Logan warming center opens for 5th season, adds space for families
item.description: The William A. Burnard Warming Center, housed in Logan's St. John's Episcopal Church, opened its fifth season Nov. 2 and will stay open six weeks longer than before, through April 30, thanks to donations and a state grant, with 60 beds, breakfast and dinner, pet-friendly space and a new separate area for families. Executive director Heather Crockett said shelter demand rose 34% last winter despite it being the warmest on record, which she attributes largely to the economy, and the center needs 63 volunteers a week. "I can't fix everything, but I can do this," Crockett said, as the nonprofit runs a capital campaign aiming for its own facility next season.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration push to set aside thousands of California ballots
item.description: On the eve of the final day of midterm voting, the Supreme Court, with no public dissents, refused the Trump administration's request that California set aside mail ballots in a case involving 20,000 people it flagged as likely noncitizens, a list state officials said was filled with errors. Lower courts had sided with California, and the same day Chief Judge James Boasberg ruled that the administration's last-minute demands on state election officials likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause. In a separate hearing, a Justice Department attorney agreed that a high error rate was "a fair statement," and California Attorney General Rob Bonta said the appeal "reeks of desperation."
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Whitehurst and Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press

item.title: 2 amendments, 1 fight: What's on Utah's ballot this November
item.description: Utah voters will decide two constitutional amendments: Amendment A, which passed the Legislature without opposition, would replace the requirement to publish proposed amendments in newspapers in every county for two months with a method lawmakers choose at least 60 days before the vote, fixing the rule that voided Amendment D in 2024. Amendment B, sponsored by Sen. Lincoln Fillmore, would require 60% approval for citizen initiatives that create or raise taxes, which Fillmore framed as asking "How easy do you want it to be to raise taxes on your neighbors?" Opponents, including the Vote No campaign led by Elizabeth Rasmussen, call it a power grab; the 2018 Medicaid expansion passed with 53.3% and would have failed under the rule, while a September poll found 50% support and 21% opposition.
item.dc:creator: Reagan Campbell, Deseret News

item.title: Parents of 1-year-old fatally shot by police protest at Mississippi Attorney General's Office
item.description: The parents of Kohen Wiley, a 1-year-old killed in June when Senatobia police Sgt. Hunter Foster fired into a moving car outside a Walmart during a shoplifting call, led a protest Monday at the office of Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch, which ruled last month that the shooting was justified. Body camera footage shows the car reversing into another vehicle and then accelerating toward Foster, who fired through the front passenger window where Kohen sat on his mother's lap; Foster's attorney says he had "no choice." Kohen's father, Davion Williams, said he wants Foster prosecuted and Fitch out of office, and the ATF is investigating a Saturday fire that damaged the Senatobia police building.
item.dc:creator: Sophie Bates, Associated Press

item.title: Rubio meets Venezuelan counterpart as US presses for progress on election preparations
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco in Washington on Monday, two weeks after Venezuela's interim authorities and opposition agreed on a blueprint for electoral reforms ahead of elections that could come in 2027. The State Department said they discussed reforms laying "the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections," and Rubio urged the release of Venezuela's remaining political prisoners. The meeting was one of the highest-level contacts with acting President Delcy Rodríguez's government since a U.S. military raid in January captured Nicolás Maduro, who denies drug trafficking charges.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Lee, Associated Press

item.title: Law enforcement to beef up in Dallas entertainment district after shootings and nationwide violence
item.description: Federal and local authorities announced Operation Deep Cover to increase law enforcement in Dallas' Deep Ellum entertainment district, where three shootings early Sunday killed four people and wounded 15 within about an hour and 15 minutes. Halloween-weekend mass shootings killed at least eight people nationwide, including at a Jackson, Mississippi, nightclub costume party, outside Birmingham's Legion Field after the Magic City Classic and in a Bloomington, Indiana, nightlife area. U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould said "The violence has to end, and it will end," even as FBI figures show the U.S. homicide rate fell to a 75-year low in 2025.
item.dc:creator: Jamie Stengle and John Raby, Associated Press

item.title: UDOT closes Alpine Loop for winter as seasonal road closures begin
item.description: UDOT has closed the Alpine Loop, state Route 92, between Pine Hollow in American Fork Canyon and Aspen Grove above Sundance for the winter, making it and Guardsman Pass the first two of the eight seasonal roads the agency shuts each year. UDOT public relations director John Gleason said plowing the high-elevation routes "doesn't make any sense" from a budget standpoint and they couldn't be kept safe, with reopening targeted around Memorial Day weekend. Sundance remains reachable through Provo Canyon, as does Tibble Fork Reservoir through American Fork Canyon, conditions permitting.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: SUU theater class looks to engage community in Greek mythology, performing arts
item.description: Southern Utah University's theater education capstone class created Killer Quest, a set of Percy Jackson-inspired challenges for Iron County students and families, such as finding a Greek mythology book at a library, photographing the Randall L. Jones Theatre and making a Greek mask, ahead of SUU's production of The Lightning Thief: The Percy Jackson Musical. Students who finish the required quests earn 50% off up to eight tickets, and every participant gets a 15% family discount. Class member Brooke Wilson called it a way to learn Greek mythology "in an arts-integrated way," and the show runs Nov. 6 through 14.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Prosecution, defense exchange arguments as Lori Daybell asks for new trial
item.description: Lori Vallow Daybell's attorney Craig Durham asked the Idaho Supreme Court on Monday for a new trial, arguing she was denied her counsel of choice when the trial judge disqualified attorney Mark Means over his representation of her husband, Chad Daybell, a ruling Durham called "unconstitutional." Assistant Attorney General Jeff Nye countered that Means had served as Chad Daybell's attorney and kept filing inappropriate documents while Lori Daybell was deemed incompetent, saying "Nothing that happened here is normal, but that doesn't mean there was error in any of it." Asked whether a reversal could reopen the death penalty, Durham said his client is aware of the risks, and the court will rule later on her appeal of the 2023 convictions in the deaths of JJ Vallow, Tylee Ryan and Tammy Daybell.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: A mystery skeleton found in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally have an identity
item.description: The man buried in a fourth-century Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey, inscribed to "Valerius Amandinus," was likely a late Anglo-Saxon abbot, most probably Ælfwig, abbot from A.D. 993 to around 1020, according to a study by abbey consultant archaeologist Warwick Rodwell published Oct. 20. Radiocarbon dating placed the man, who died between 35 and 49, between A.D. 987 and 1052, and traces of a lime-packed timber coffin inside plus an Anglo-Saxon cross on the lid pointed to a high-status burial. Rodwell said the reuse was likely an honor because stone coffins had become scarce, and "Acquiring a secondhand stone coffin was considered a 'prize.'"
item.dc:creator: Mindy Weisberger, CNN

item.title: Utah County couple accused of abusing infant daughter
item.description: Steven Charles Schoebinger, 30, and Kayla Rae Schoebinger, 29, of Santaquin were charged Monday in 4th District Court with first-degree felony aggravated child abuse, nearly three months after their arrests. Charging documents say a skeletal survey of their 2-month-old daughter, brought to a hospital July 29 because she wasn't moving her arm, found multiple fractures in various stages of healing, including in her ribs, wrist, hands and feet, which doctors determined were "all non-accidental." A doctor rejected the parents' suggestion that a sibling caused the injuries, saying the arm fracture would have come from a yanking or twisting motion.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Immigration could be a solution to Utah's 'wicked' demographic woes, researchers say
item.description: At a Sutherland Institute roundtable, University of Illinois law professor Robin Fretwell Wilson said the country's coming demographic imbalance, with the CBO projecting more deaths than births starting in 2030, is "wicked in a way that even the culture wars are not," and that migration could help. Olivia Whiteley of Reliable Refuge noted net international migration fell from 2.7 million in 2024 to 1.3 million in 2025 and is expected to drop to about 321,000 in 2026, even though it drove nearly 21% of Utah's 2024-25 population growth. She said Utah, long able to resettle more than 1,000 refugees a year, welcomed only 152 this year, and urged Congress to codify a refugee floor shaped by state input.
item.dc:creator: Alixel Cabrera, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Intoxicated driver accused of hitting, killing woman changing flat tire
item.description: A booking affidavit says Peter Joseph Hoffelmeyer, 47, told a trooper he had "four mixed drinks prior to driving" before his car left its lane on westbound I-80 in Parleys Canyon late Friday and struck a disabled vehicle on the shoulder. Taylor Breanne Giles, 36, of Sandy, who was outside changing a flat tire on her Subaru Forester, died at the scene. A breath test put Hoffelmeyer's blood-alcohol level at 0.14%, nearly three times the legal limit, and he was booked for investigation of automobile homicide and DUI.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Utah prosecutor seeks fifth term as he leads national discussion on holding ICE agents accountable
item.description: Salt Lake County District Attorney Sim Gill, seeking a fifth term against Republican Kent Davis, gave a July presentation to the Major County Prosecutors Council on charging ICE agents who violate state law, saying "ICE does not get to violate rights of our citizens." Utah ICE arrests hit a record 613 in June, and Gill, who says he does not seek to obstruct deportations, fears surging enforcement leaves immigrant residents afraid to report crimes. Davis, Gill's former deputy, says the DA has no role in civil immigration enforcement and points to a December 2025 legislative audit finding that about half of declined felony cases lacked detailed explanations and that diversion programs don't track recidivism, while Gill cites county crime at a decade low.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Tomco, Deseret News

item.title: Bluff residents shelter in place, San Juan County schools closed due to flooding
item.description: Bluff residents were told around 3 a.m. Monday to shelter in place or move to higher ground after the Cottonwood Wash slot canyon flooded, and an evacuation order was lifted later in the day. San Juan County said floodwaters washed out the Comb Wash Bridge and closed Highway 163 west of town, county offices and all district schools closed Monday, and Montezuma Creek Schools will hold virtual classes Tuesday. The sheriff's office expects another surge from Colorado storms to raise the San Juan River through Aneth, Montezuma Creek and Bluff, and the Utah Division of Emergency Management promoted a disaster distress helpline, saying "You do not have to lose your home or experience physical damage to be affected by a disaster."
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
item.description: Iran said Monday it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume nuclear talks within two days rather than seven if the U.S. meets its demands, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, though Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei gave no sign Tehran had softened its conditions or that Washington had agreed. The U.N. migration agency said more than 300,000 Yemenis have fled renewed fighting between Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, and China said it will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia. Israel's military also said it had concluded an operation in Hebron, begun last month after a shooting killed two soldiers, that displaced hundreds of Palestinians.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Do Utahns benefit when their governor travels the world? Cox responds
item.description: Interviewed at the end of a trade mission to Ireland and Northern Ireland, Gov. Spencer Cox said the trips, 16 abroad since he took office, are mostly paid for by participating businesses and chosen by data rather than preference, and argued they bring higher-paying jobs and tax revenue to all Utahns. World Trade Center Utah director Jonathan Freedman said the governor's presence opens markets usually closed to small businesses, adding, "We want to export our goods and services, not our children." The delegation, focused on medical tech, heard Northern Ireland pitch its EU and U.K. market access and met former Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern, and Cox said he agrees with the Trump administration on some strategic industries but warned against becoming "too isolationist and too protectionist."
item.dc:creator: Suzanne Bates, Deseret News

item.title: Washington reports first US bird flu death of 2026; health officials say risk to the public is low
item.description: A Yakima County, Washington, resident with underlying health conditions who caught bird flu from infected dairy cows died Nov. 1, the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third since the virus entered dairy cattle in February 2024. County officials are monitoring the person's contacts, and a third Washington case, also tied to infected cows, has mild symptoms; the state has reported 33 infected dairy herds since Oct. 8. No human-to-human spread has been documented in the U.S., and health officials say the risk to the public remains low.
item.dc:creator: Brenda Goodman, CNN

item.title: Ukraine and Russia report fake emergency alerts after cyberattack targets apps
item.description: Ukraine and Russia both said their emergency alert apps were hacked late Sunday, with Ukrainians receiving false warnings of high radiation, a chemical threat and an incoming Oreshnik missile, and Russia saying a fake alert reached 33 of its 89 regions; it was unclear whether the attacks were linked. A Russian Telegram channel said a group called Hitcore claimed the Ukrainian breach, which could not be verified, and Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said state agencies face constant cyberattacks, a growing number of them using AI. Separately, Russian drones struck Kherson hours after a localized ceasefire for an evacuation from occupied Oleshky expired, a mission Ukraine's ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets hopes can serve as a "pilot model" for others.
item.dc:creator: Derek Gatopoulos and Susie Blann, Associated Press

item.title: 'Oil pulling': Natural, stronger mouthwash or waste of time?
item.description: Dentists say oil pulling, the Ayurvedic practice of swishing coconut or another edible oil for up to 20 minutes that has resurfaced on social media, adds little to brushing and flossing; a 2022 meta-analysis found lower bacterial counts but limited evidence of less plaque or gum inflammation. Dr. Matthew Messina, a consumer advisor for the American Dental Association, said there is no evidence it helps or harms, and San Diego-area dentist Dr. Kami Hoss said it offers a "false sense of protection." Oil pulling is no substitute for antibiotics for a gum infection, and Messina said mouthwash, unlike oil, has antibacterial and fluoride benefits but should still only supplement brushing.
item.dc:creator: Sneha Dhandapani, CNN

item.title: Registration opens for Tabernacle Choir's Christmas Concert tickets
item.description: The Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square is taking registrations through Nov. 15 for its Dec. 17-19 Christmas concerts, with up to four tickets per household awarded by random selection by Dec. 1 and a standby line forming 90 minutes before each 8 p.m. show. Choir president Michael O. Leavitt said the objective is "to celebrate the life and birth of Jesus Christ." Last year's concert with Broadway couple Stephanie J. Block and Sebastian Arcelus airs on PBS Dec. 14 and 24, and the choir also appears in a CW holiday special on Dec. 17.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Here's where Thanksgiving, Christmas holidays mean better deals for homebuyers
item.description: Most U.S. housing markets now favor buyers because of high prices and mortgage rates pushed up by the war against Iran, and Redfin says the late-year seasonal advantage may be stronger than ever this year. Fall is the cheapest season in most of the country, but in seven metros, including Milwaukee, Tampa, Detroit and three South Florida areas, deals peak in November or mid-December, with Florida's timing shaped by hurricane season and snowbirds who arrive after the new year. Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said late-year shoppers see fewer fresh listings but "face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal."
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Utah students wanted a say in classroom AI rules. Now they're getting it
item.description: The Utah State Board of Education gave final approval Oct. 1 to an Artificial Intelligence Student Task Force under its Student Advisory Council, capping a roughly yearlong push that began when Skyline High senior Rahul Nair found little student voice in the state's AI framework for schools. Nair, who uses AI for practice problems and research, wants clearer rules rather than tighter restrictions, while Hillcrest High senior Kennedy Mickelson worries students can skip real learning, saying "There's a struggle that needs to be done." The task force arrives as the board drafts model AI policies required by HB273, and Nair hopes to bring in students from beyond the Salt Lake Valley.
item.dc:creator: Brooke Nally, KSL

item.title: All 9 people aboard a jet that crashed in Florida have died, transportation secretary says
item.description: All nine people aboard a Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 from Austin were killed, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said, after the jet nose-dived into a Palm Beach County neighborhood on Sunday and exploded beside a busy road, only feet from homes. Flight tracking data and air traffic recordings show the jet's descent reached up to 30,000 feet per minute after the crew, cruising at 35,000 feet, reported icing and turbulence and asked to climb. Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of injuries on the ground, describing a crash that "looked like a missile going down."
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Flash floods trigger evacuations in Arizona and Colorado amid heavy rains in southwest
item.description: A series of Pacific storms brought flash flooding and mandatory evacuations across the Southwest on Sunday, with Pagosa Springs, Colorado, bracing for the San Juan River to crest above 20 feet, higher than the roughly 17.8 feet of a 1911 flood that destroyed most of the town. In Arizona, officials ordered evacuations near Oak Creek in Sedona, in Camp Verde and across the Tonto Creek community of Gisela; Tucson saw boat rescues; and a weather service meteorologist said the region was getting "two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days." Flood warnings and watches extended into southern Utah, where forecasters flagged runoff risk in Washington County and Zion and Capitol Reef national parks.
item.dc:creator: Philip Marcelo and Michael Casey, Associated Press

item.title: Judge dismisses lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate race if GOP incumbent loses
item.description: U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason on Sunday dismissed a Justice Department lawsuit, pushed by President Donald Trump, that sought to block certification of Alaska's Senate race if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, calling the requested relief "infeasible" because many ballots were already cast. The suit sought an investigation into whether votes for a second candidate, retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, were meant for the senator, and Gleason wrote the government offered no workable plan to do that while preserving voter secrecy. The senator told CNN he expected to lose votes to "that trickery" and accused Peltola of lying about her aides' role in recruiting the other Sullivan.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Riccardi and Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

item.title: Remember 'Light the Fire Within'? Here's the motto for LA's 2028 Summer Games
item.description: LA28 organizers unveiled "Stars Align" as the motto for the 2028 Summer Olympics and Paralympics, with marketing chief Alex Merchán calling it a rallying cry for athletes and a call to volunteers and fans. The Hollywood-tinged slogan follows recent mottos such as Paris' Games Wide Open and Milan Cortina's IT's Your Vibe, and differs in tone from Salt Lake's 2002 "Light the Fire Within," which Fraser Bullock said was meant to inspire people to grow and help others. Bullock, now president and executive chair of Utah's 2034 Winter Games, credited the 2002 motto to volunteer advertising executive Gordon Bowen during a brainstorming session.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Provo Community Church gathering funds for renovation, restoration
item.description: Provo Community Congregational United Church of Christ, whose University Avenue home pairs the 1924 Spanish Colonial Revival Meno Trope Hall with a 1956 mid-century modern sanctuary, needs more than $10 million for renovations and expansions, and the church and community groups have raised $1 million so far. Plans include a new central bell tower with an elevator for accessibility, a lengthened sanctuary to hold an organ donated by Salt Lake City's First Congregational Church, and a new fellowship hall, after leaders turned away developers who offered to bulldoze the century-old building. Council moderator Dave Lewis said the aim is to complement rather than copy the original and keep a place where people can "build interfaith friendships, serve their neighbors" for generations.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Trump administration promises US farmers $15 billion in the weeks before the midterms
item.description: In the weeks before the midterms, the Trump administration has promised more than $15 billion to agricultural producers to offset diesel and fertilizer costs driven up largely by tariffs and the war in Iran, led by an $8 billion one-time payment for farmers hit by soaring diesel prices. The package also includes at least $5 billion in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen, $1.8 billion for conservation program participants and $573 million for fertilizer manufacturing, mostly USDA money that needs no immediate congressional approval. Kansas State's Gregg Ibendahl estimated the payments would "more than cover the increase in fuel costs," though it is unclear whether the money will sway voters in farm states where Republican seats have become competitive.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Raza, Associated Press

item.title: 509 Utahns told us their hopes and concerns for Great Salt Lake. Do you feel the same?
item.description: An open-response survey of 509 Utahns by the Great Salt Lake Collaborative found most respondents want the lake to rise under a lasting plan, and many worry about dust and public health, development and whether state leaders are taking the problem seriously. The responses come as lake levels fell below 30% in October, exposing more than 57% of the lakebed, and as Gov. Spencer Cox pursues a goal of a healthy lake by the 2034 Olympics. One Ogden respondent warned, "Collapse this lake, collapse this culture," while a Layton resident said they feel "powerless over its fate."
item.dc:creator: Will Ruzanski, The Daily Utah Chronicle

item.title: Box Office: 'You Can See Everything,' 'Clayface' lead sleepy Halloween weekend
item.description: With Halloween competing for Saturday crowds, North American ticket sales were on track for no more than $56 million, which would be the year's second-lowest weekend, though the domestic box office remains up more than 17% from last year. The Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything reached No. 1 for the first time in its third weekend with $10.6 million, edging DC's Clayface by about $200,000 as the Batman-villain film fell 57% in its second weekend.
item.dc:creator: Lindsey Bahr, Associated Press

item.title: Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across US
item.description: At least six people died and dozens were wounded in shootings at nightlife districts in about half a dozen U.S. cities over Halloween weekend, the deadliest in Dallas' Deep Ellum, where three separate shootings over roughly 75 minutes left four dead and 15 injured despite a stepped-up police presence. In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight wounded near Legion Field after the Magic City Classic, a rivalry game between historically Black universities that drew nearly 70,000 fans. Shootings were also reported in Fayetteville, Arkansas; Newark, Delaware; and Bloomington, Illinois, and Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators were still working out whether the Deep Ellum shootings were connected.
item.dc:creator: John Raby, Associated Press

item.title: What to know about the Affordable Care Act's open enrollment period now underway
item.description: Affordable Care Act open enrollment runs from Sunday through Jan. 15 in most states, with KFF projecting marketplace premiums to rise an average of 13% in 2027 as financial help is restricted for many previously eligible groups, new limits apply to immigrants and enrollment checks tighten. KFF's Cynthia Cox warned that some enrollees who don't qualify for subsidies may be unable to keep their coverage, noted many have already shifted to the cheapest bronze plans, and expects fewer enrollees overall. Costs have soared since Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies, a change that led to 1.2 million fewer sign-ups, while a CMS fact sheet promises "robust access to low-cost plans."
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein, Associated Press

item.title: Anthropic says you can't be mean to Claude. It's not about feelings
item.description: Anthropic's October update to its usage policy bars users from engaging in "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior" toward its Claude models and could lead to permanent bans in extreme cases, though a spokesperson told CNN that Claude ending conversations remains the main enforcement tool and that frustration, blunt feedback and research are not targeted. The rule drew mockery, including a melting-face emoji from Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, but experts say it reflects more than concern for a machine's feelings. Former Reddit CEO Yishan Wong argued abusive inputs could end up in training data, and William and Mary professor Jindong Wang said research shows prompt tone can affect AI performance without implying emotion.
item.dc:creator: Hadas Gold, CNN

item.title: Russia's security service detains a teenager planning a 'terror attack' after a US tip-off
item.description: Russia's FSB said it detained a teenage Russian citizen suspected of planning an attack on Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve after U.S. law enforcement shared information, a day after the U.S. Embassy warned of a "credible threat of a mass casualty event" there. According to the FSB, the suspect followed a neo-Nazi Telegram channel and posted TikTok photos of himself in tactical gear with an apparent weapon and of the museum captioned "I found a place," and airsoft weapons were found at his home. The agency thanked the U.S., a contrast with Vladimir Putin's dismissal of a 2024 U.S. warning days before the Crocus City Hall attack killed more than 140 people.
item.dc:creator: Ivana Kottasová, CNN

item.title: 81 years later, a son pays tribute to his father's WWII mercy ride
item.description: In early September, 56-year-old Greg Hoole rented a heavy town bike and rode 175 kilometers from Amsterdam to Assen over two days, retracing the trip his father, Hank, made at 14 on a bicycle with metal rims in the spring of 1945 after carrying food to his own father in Nazi-occupied Amsterdam. Greg found the story while rereading his late father's autobiography, which he had helped write and edit, and said he spent the ride wishing he had asked questions such as "How did you know where to go?" Unlike his father, he had rubber tires, a bike path the whole way and Apple Maps, and at the finish he said "I felt like I was on top of the world."
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: A drone motor in a garage. Natural gas to jet fuel. A power grid under pressure. What Utah builders made in days
item.description: At the Hard Tech Hackathon during Utah Hard Tech Week, builders had about two days to turn ideas in energy, AI infrastructure, defense and aerospace into working prototypes, and Rogue Technologies co-founders Nate Roberts and Peter Hartvigsen won the Nucleus challenge's $10,000 bounty with a custom AI model that ran 51 times faster than conventional simulations of a reactor turning natural gas into jet fuel. Other entries included Joe Blash's garage-built machine for winding drone-motor coils, a first step toward U.S.-made drone motors, Juan Lizarazo's DETOUR software for timing business energy storage around grid prices, and an AI-to-3D-printing site called Printerest. State entrepreneurship official Tyler Jennings said Utah favors hackathons over pitch contests because "anybody can tell a story," describing the state's culture as one of "scrappy builders."
item.dc:creator: Frizz Flake, Deseret News

item.title: Churches celebrate All Saints' Day after Halloween
item.description: Several Salt Lake-area churches marked All Saints' Day on Sunday, including First United Methodist, where Pastor Kelsie Parrish planned to read the names of community members lost over the past year during Holy Communion, and the Cathedral of the Madeleine, whose choir was scheduled to sing works by Victoria and Britten. Rev. Dr. Hank Malone of St. John's Lutheran Church described the preceding Halloween as a way to mock the devil, since Christ has taken away death's sting. Parrish said simultaneous observances worldwide remind believers "we are the body of Christ," and a diocesan Mass at Mount Calvary Catholic Cemetery was set for All Souls' Day on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: What new earnings data reveals about Utah's college grads vs. Utah's high school grads
item.description: Utah ranks No. 2 nationally, behind only Delaware, for how much its college credential holders out-earn high school graduates, according to HEA Group analysis of federal College Scorecard data: four years after finishing, alums typically earn $74,202 versus $37,112 for Utahns with only a diploma. Utah bachelor's graduates in computer and information technology administration ranked first in the nation on the earnings premium at $127,178, while the state's cosmetology graduates typically earn $9,000 less than high school graduates. The gap carries new stakes under a Department of Education framework that will cut federal loan eligibility for programs whose graduates repeatedly fail to out-earn diploma holders, which Under Secretary Nicholas Kent said ensures taxpayers back only programs that leave graduates "financially better off."
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Does your life have meaning? Start by answering these 2 questions
item.description: Accepting the Sutherland Institute's George A. Sutherland Award, Harvard business professor and author Arthur Brooks described happiness as a balance of enjoyment, satisfaction and meaning, and said half of his students can no longer answer his two-question exam on why they are alive and what they would give their lives for. Brooks blamed smartphones for the decline since 2008, saying his students "have eradicated every moment of boredom from their lives — and their lives are boring." He praised Utah as a model, saying that if America were more like it, "we'd have a lot fewer problems," and the institute gave its Family Values Award to former Gov. Mike Leavitt and Jacalyn Leavitt.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Mother-daughter duo creates pirate Halloween displays
item.description: Staci Gifford of Eagle Mountain and her daughter, Kailee Burdette of Saratoga Springs, have built Pirates of the Caribbean-themed Halloween yards every year since 2018, Pirates of Thunder Gulch and Pirates of Utah Lake, adding homemade props and animatronics that come alive after dark. Burdette's social media posts now draw visitors from well beyond the neighborhood, who hunt for hidden Mickeys to earn a treasure and get homemade Disney churros and popcorn. Gifford, whose decorating began with three scarecrows dressed in her kids' clothes, said the point is family time, calling Halloween "a really fun time for families to grow close."
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Nonprofit temporarily closes its doors, impacting more than 20,000
item.description: Community Action Services and Food Bank, a Provo nonprofit founded in 1967 that served more than 24,000 people last year in Utah, Wasatch and Summit counties, closed until further notice Sunday while its board weighs next steps, after an effort to raise $1.5 million to stay open into next year. Utah County Commissioner Skyler Beltran called the closure a travesty and blamed what he called "financial and operational mismanagement" rather than any lack of government support, saying the county is working to protect the roughly 20,000 people who rely on its services. The county has taken over the warming center, which was scheduled to open Nov. 1 as planned, and CEO Caitlin Rangel said the need for the services "has not gone away."
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: Family identifies Ogden Canyon crash victim, prepares to say goodbye
item.description: In a statement released on Halloween, the 14th anniversary of her adoption at age 7, the family of 22-year-old Katie Sue Ruth Huggins said she is on life support and not expected to survive, and that as an organ donor her gift will "carry her love forward." The family remembered her love of motorcycles, animals, family and friends and asked for privacy. She was critically injured Oct. 27 when her motorcycle collided at the mouth of Ogden Canyon with a vehicle authorities confirmed was driven by Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter, who is now on voluntary administrative leave.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Longtime homeless cleanup nonprofit shuts down, leaving 125 unemployed
item.description: Advantage Services, a Utah social enterprise founded in 1992 that employed about 125 people, most of them experiencing homelessness or other hardships, ceased operations Saturday after the state Office of Homeless Services declined CEO Rob Ferris' request for emergency bridge funding. Its troubles deepened when its largest contract, with Salt Lake City's Urban Services Division, was cut roughly in half from about $2 million, and Ferris had furloughed about 110 workers earlier this month after missing payroll; he now plans to sell assets, including the vehicle fleet, to pay out unused vacation as severance. Former office manager Megan Belagam said she feels betrayed and that the shutdown "has dehumanized" the workers.
item.dc:creator: Katie McKellar, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Race for Campus Safety draws record turnout as awareness of relationship violence grows
item.description: More than 800 people took part in Saturday's Race for Campus Safety at the University of Utah, up from about 100 at the 2022 inaugural event honoring Lauren McCluskey, a student killed on campus by her ex-boyfriend in 2018. Her mother, Jill McCluskey, credited students' growing awareness of relationship violence and said safeguards the university now has, such as parole checks, lethality assessments and victim advocates, "would have made a difference." Proceeds will help the Lauren McCluskey Foundation expand programs nationwide, including Lauren's Promise, a pledge to listen to and believe people facing threats that faculty at 480 universities have taken.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: St. George woman donates wind phone to help individuals 'talk' to loved ones lost
item.description: A phone-booth-style wind phone, where visitors can dial a number that reminds them of someone who has died and say what they never got to, now stands beside a bench at St. George's Tonaquint Nature Center near the Rainbow Bridge pet memorial. Shaelynn Del Toro, 23, created it after her uncle died unexpectedly in August 2025 without a chance to say goodbye, hand-painting the box with butterflies and a rainbow and adding the 988 crisis number and a QR code. City parks official Ben Neumann steered the project away from a park to the quieter spot, saying visitors can simply sit and "let your words go in the wind," an idea that traces to a Japanese garden designer in 2010.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Republicans on defense in Texas while Democrats in Michigan can't get on the same page
item.description: Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico made closing pitches Saturday in a tossup Texas Senate race that has become a gauge of frustration with President Donald Trump, with Talarico casting Paxton as corrupt and his fight against Elon Musk, who has spent more than $150 million to help Paxton, as "David vs. Goliath," while Paxton called Talarico too liberal for Texas. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed tried to quiet talk of friction with primary rival Rep. Haley Stevens in his competitive open-seat race against Republican Mike Rogers, a seat Democrats can ill afford to lose. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate edge, early ballots were nearing 50 million, and Trump campaigned by phone Saturday before planned Sunday rallies in Iowa and Kansas.
item.dc:creator: Bill Barrow, Associated Press

item.title: Man sentenced for assault, attempted kidnapping of woman who said he wanted to 'mark her'
item.description: Arnold Nelson, 54, of West Jordan, will serve a year in jail and three years of probation after pleading guilty to aggravated assault and a reduced attempted aggravated kidnapping charge over a June attack in which a witness said he beat the woman he lived with using a stick and a hammer or tomahawk knife. According to a police affidavit, he had ordered her into the backyard so he could "mark her," and officers found her covered in blood. Judge Dianna Gibson suspended a prison term of up to five years but ordered addiction treatment and denied good-time credit.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Weber State students press to resurrect centers geared to Latino, Black and other students
item.description: Weber State seniors Nick Eckstrom, Evan Burnett and Kolby Ferrell have started a petition and met with President Chris Mallett seeking to revive the cultural centers for Black, Latino, LGBTQ and other students that the university closed in 2024 after HB261 required dismantling DEI programming. Burnett said Mallett was open to the idea but raised questions about logistics and legality, and state guidance allows such centers only if they focus on cultural awareness, are open to all students and win Board of Higher Education approval. A university spokeswoman said closing the centers was a choice to customize support rather than a legal mandate, while Eckstrom rejected the law's premise, saying the centers "are about inclusion not exclusion."
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Rubio says the US government did not facilitate Bolsonaro's flight to the US
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that the Trump administration "didn't facilitate anything" in defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro's arrival in Miami, saying Bolsonaro had previously held a visa and Trump decided to let him in. Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and declared himself the "true president-elect of Brazil," is under investigation at home for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion and had been ordered to surrender his passport.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Don't give up on buying your first home, Utahns advised
item.description: A study commissioned by the Salt Lake Board of Realtors found 50.1% of Utah households headed by 25- to 34-year-olds owned their homes in 2024, well above the 40.4% national rate, which board president Scott Colemere partly credits to young Utahns being better at "adulting." Colemere argues buyers who save at least $15,000, shore up their credit and consider condos or townhomes can still get in, as 37-year-old Michael Peterson did in Herriman, even though a Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute report puts homeownership out of reach for about 91% of renters. State housing coordinator Steve Waldrip praised young buyers' resilience but warned "the headwinds are getting tougher," with Gov. Spencer Cox's goal of 35,000 starter homes by 2028 only about a quarter met.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Virginia, DC sue over Trump's arch, adding to legal challenges
item.description: Washington, D.C., and Virginia sued Saturday to stop President Donald Trump's planned 250-foot memorial arch near the bridge to Arlington National Cemetery, arguing that three years of construction would snarl traffic, pollute the Potomac and hamper emergency response. It is the third lawsuit against the project, which the administration hopes to approve as soon as Thursday and possibly start building the same day, while Judge Tanya Chutkan weighs halting it and asked what harm a delay would cause "apart from the executive's desire to bedazzle the city." A 106-page plan filed Friday envisions a winged bronze Lady Liberty, an observation deck and offices, and officials say the arch will also serve a national security function.
item.dc:creator: Gary Fields, Associated Press

item.title: Salt Lake County hosts first-ever Halloween early voting
item.description: Salt Lake County offered in-person voting on a Saturday for the first time, letting residents cast ballots at the county government center on Halloween before trick-or-treating in the county's final early-voting window. County Clerk Lannie Chapman said voters can still use 29 drop boxes or vote in person starting at 7 a.m. Tuesday, with ballots due by 8 p.m., and that unregistered Utahns may register on Election Day, though those ballots stay provisional until eligibility is verified.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: 'Grasping at straws': Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein letter
item.description: U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami dismissed with prejudice Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation suit against The Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over its report on a sexually suggestive birthday letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album for Jeffrey Epstein, saying the president was "grasping at straws." Citing New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, Gayles ruled that the amended complaint, filed after he first dismissed the case in April, still failed to plead actual malice, and he noted the story had reported Trump's denial.
item.dc:creator: Dave Collins, Associated Press

item.title: 1 dead, 6 wounded in targeted shooting at California Spirit Halloween store, police say
item.description: A shooting inside a Spirit Halloween store at Fairfield, California's Solano Town Center on Friday night killed Constance Hages, 31, whom family members said was pregnant, and wounded six others, three of whom remained in critical condition Saturday. Police said the shooting appears to have been a targeted incident involving one suspect, detectives are still working to identify the person responsible, and the FBI sent an evidence response team. The mall canceled its Saturday trick-or-treating event, and the store will stay closed.
item.dc:creator: Sydney Bishop, Karina Tsui, CNN

item.title: Rick Ross no longer faces felony charge in Miami Beach domestic violence case
item.description: Miami prosecutors declined to file a felony battery-by-strangulation charge against rapper Rick Ross, citing insufficient evidence, and instead charged him with one misdemeanor count of domestic violence battery. A woman told police Ross slapped and struck her and restricted her breathing by grabbing her hoodie collar during an Aug. 28 dispute over an Instagram photo at his Star Island home, allegations he calls fabricated. His attorney, Bradley Horenstein, said her injury photos showed no sign of strangulation and asked the public to "wait for it all to play out in court."
item.dc:creator: Camila Fernandez, WFOR via CNN

item.title: Attorneys for Alaska say 'meritless' Trump demand to set aside Senate ballots 'not even possible'
item.description: Alaska's Republican-led state government asked a federal judge Saturday to dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit, filed at President Donald Trump's direction, that seeks to block certification of a possible win by Democrat Mary Peltola in the U.S. Senate race because a second candidate named Dan Sullivan is on the ballot. The state called a new request to segregate ballots cast for that Sullivan "both disturbing and impossible" without violating voter privacy, noting the incumbent is listed as a Republican while the other appears simply as Daniel J. Sullivan. Trump has also called for Peltola's prosecution after The New York Times reported that Democrats' campaign appeared to have helped recruit the second Sullivan.
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Riccardi and Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

item.title: Former church building in Rush Valley prepares to reopen as museum
item.description: Volunteers have logged more than 4,000 hours over five years restoring Rush Valley's 1907 Clover Ward meetinghouse, which had been converted to house the town's fire truck, and it will be dedicated as a museum on April 28, 120 years to the day after its original dedication. That date was set only after project manager John Cluff, following five years of fruitless archive searches, obtained a handwritten program from the Church History Library confirming that then-Elder Heber J. Grant performed the first dedication. Donated and discounted work worth more than $200,000 cost the project $90,000, and Carol Cluff said she hopes the building becomes "an asset to the whole county."
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Advisories issued as more rain, snow return to Utah, including areas recovering from floods
item.description: An atmospheric river colliding with a cold front is expected to bring heavy mountain snow and valley rain to Utah from late Halloween night into Monday, prompting a National Weather Service winter weather advisory and flood watches. Areas above 10,000 feet in the Cottonwood Canyons and Uintas could get 18 to 24 inches, one model gives Alta a 40% chance of at least 18 inches, and forecasters raised parts of southwest Utah and the Four Corners to a moderate flood risk. Grand Junction hydrologist Erin Walter said her office is most worried about the Four Corners area that flooded last week, where some San Juan County families still cannot return home.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls: analysis
item.description: In the first outside analysis of the list, UCLA Voting Rights Project researchers told a court that 8,880 of the 20,930 names the Justice Department flagged as possible noncitizen voters in California, 42% of the total, match no one on the state's current voter rolls, and at least 22 are U.S. citizens. The department has demanded that officials set those ballots aside on Election Day, a demand multiple judges have rejected as unconstitutional, and the administration had objected to sharing the list, calling the effort a "fishing expedition."
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press

item.title: New study casts doubt on theory about the role comets played in kick-starting life on Earth
item.description: Computer simulations published in Scientific Reports suggest comets striking the early Earth were moving too fast to deliver intact hydrogen cyanide, a key prebiotic ingredient, undercutting a theory dating to at least 1961 that they seeded the building blocks of life. Across 100,000 runs, lead author Richard Anslow found that on average there were "no successful impacts," and rare fluke hits would have needed to land where liquid water and other necessary chemicals were already present, though slower impacts on ancient Mars may have preserved more of the compound. Outside scientists Queenie Chan and Nicolle Zellner weren't ready to rule comets out, with Chan noting the chemical may have formed sturdier compounds before the comets ever reached Earth.
item.dc:creator: Jacopo Prisco, CNN

item.title: From salmonberry harvests to traditional tattoos, Native American culture is November spotlight
item.description: For Native American Heritage Month, an AP collection of short profiles highlights joy in Indigenous communities, opening with Las Vegas Paiute artist Fawn Douglas, whose new Wai Gallery shows Indigenous art meant to dismantle the stereotype that Native people are a monolith. Other vignettes follow a Kipnuk, Alaska, family back to pick salmonberries a year after Typhoon Halong, Pascua Yaqui foster mother Rosa Soto Alvarez's advocacy for the Indian Child Welfare Act, and the NAIWA Daughters, Indigenous girls whose resolution led the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians to recognize a river system's rights.
