The collection also visits a Minneapolis Ojibwe and Dakota language program's sugarbush outing, a Tulsa effort to replace a lost Indian youth center, and tattoo artist Hodokii Johnson's work restoring ancestral markings.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Hill, Associated Press

item.title: 'A bucket-list hike': Summiting Mount Timpanogos beyond peak season
item.description: Utah County hiker Josh Abbott recently summited Mount Timpanogos, nearly 12,000 feet up, in late-fall snow and ice, climbing with experienced guides and carrying spikes, axes and ropes. Juggling a full-time job and full-time school, Abbott said the mountains offer "just a pause" from both, a love of exploring he traces to childhood outings his mother allowed as long as he checked in by two-way radio. He has also climbed Guatemala's Acatenango volcano but says much of the reward lies close to home and in the journey rather than the summit.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Elderly couple loses life savings to scammer posing as FBI agent
item.description: Gail Walsh of Burbank, Illinois, says she and her husband lost $18,400, nearly everything they had, after an Aug. 15 caller posing as an FBI investigator, who already knew her account balances, talked her through withdrawing the cash and handing it to a man in a black SUV outside a second Chase branch. The caller claimed some bills were counterfeit and promised a bank employee would bring out "genuine cash," but no one came, and Walsh said Chase told her it could do nothing. The FBI says such impersonation scams are rising and warns against giving money or personal information to anyone who initiated contact.
item.dc:creator: Megan De Mar, WBBN

item.title: Casa Del Tamal operator puts focus on family, tamales; US official visits Mexican restaurant
item.description: Small Business Administration official Lisa Shimkat traveled from Washington to tour La Casa Del Tamal's Post District location in Salt Lake City, which Mexican immigrant Cristina Olvera opened last year with an SBA-backed loan after two decades of selling homemade tamales. The business took off from a 2019 food court stand at West Valley City's Azteca Swapmeet after daughter Frida's social media push drew local foodies, and Olvera's five children and son-in-law Andres Sanchez, CEO of the parent LCDT Restaurant Group, now run key parts of it. Shimkat said she came to hear from owners directly because "We can't just make decisions in D.C."
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Rising health costs and coverage changes are big concerns for older adults as Election Day nears
item.description: Healthcare costs are a top worry for older voters heading into Tuesday's midterms, with an AARP poll finding 83% of voters over 50 extremely motivated to vote as Medicare enrollees weigh higher Part D caps, expiring premium subsidies and Advantage plan pullbacks taking effect in 2027. Ohio retiree Barbara Weigand, 83, who withdrew $4,000 from retirement savings for cancer care, said she has considered taking medication every other day, and about 1 in 5 people in a KFF survey reported cutting pills or skipping doses over cost. AARP also found family caregivers now spend an average of $11,508 a year, up from $7,242 in 2021, while Social Security's trust funds face a 2034 shortfall.
item.dc:creator: Fatima Hussein, Associated Press

item.title: 'Party at the Polls' brings Utah voters together
item.description: The ACLU of Utah and Ignite! Utah held a Party at the Polls event Friday at Salt Lake City's Northwest Community Center, offering free food, music, resource booths and ballot drop-off as part of a decade-old national push to boost turnout. Ignite! Utah executive director Jenessa Jimoh said the group spent the day reaching out to Generation Z, and 20-year-old second-time voter Mariam Dickerson said she felt "very proud that I've been mobilized."
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Thwarting teen gambling may require more than talking to kids
item.description: As Utah fights prediction market Kalshi in court over what the state calls illegal gambling, Utah marriage and family therapist Gregory Noel says DraftKings CEO Jason Robins' advice to talk with kids about gambling addiction falls short because "the internet is a lawless game." Noel says parents also need to limit teens' access to such content, citing a growing problem: half of 16- and 17-year-old boys surveyed by Common Sense Media bet or gamble online, and another study found nearly two-thirds of college students place bets.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Salt Lake City commission voices concerns with proposed new LDS Hospital design
item.description: Salt Lake City planning commissioners pushed back on Intermountain Health's plan to move LDS Hospital from the Avenues to the former Sears Block near 754 S. State, chiefly because it puts about 190 feet of ground-floor retail in an offsite parking structure instead of the hospital, which several questioned against the development agreement's call for ground-floor activation. HDR Architects' Eric Meub said limiting entrances keeps the secured hospital safe, calling the issue "truly life and death," but commissioner Richard Leverett worried the result could look like a correctional facility, and Landon Kracsek floated retail beside the hospital with no interior connection. Commissioner Aimee Burrows also objected to a requested allowance for EIFS cladding, and elements such as a Main Street skybridge still need City Council approval ahead of a hoped-for groundbreaking by year's end.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Woman sentenced to prison for killing roommate after pleading guilty with mental condition
item.description: Laura Darlene Northrup, 62, was sentenced to 15 years to life for murdering roommate Stephanie Lynn Haskett-Carrasco, 62, who was found under her bed with severe head and neck trauma in May 2024 at a Sandy shelter for medically frail people experiencing homelessness. Northrup had pleaded guilty with a mental condition, and Salt Lake County Attorney Sim Gill said the sentence pairs accountability with mental health treatment, after all five of the victim's children addressed the court.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Keep the candy and some healthy habits — 3 tricks for keeping the treats in check
item.description: Nutritionist Ali Essig tells parents Halloween candy and healthy habits can coexist, and her top tip is "fiber first": fruit, veggies and hummus, a wheat-bread PB&J or a pot of chili before trick-or-treating to blunt the sugar spike. She cautions against labeling candy bad, which can breed guilt and sneaking, and suggests bringing the stash out after dinner instead of letting kids snack on it all day.
item.dc:creator: Lauren Tippetts, KSL

item.title: Utah 5-year-old with Down syndrome walks Messi on the field, scores goals with Beckham
item.description: Five-year-old Huddy Droubay of Syracuse, who has Down syndrome, walked onto the field with Lionel Messi and scored goals with David Beckham at an Inter Miami game after Beckham noticed a viral video of him beaming through a city-league soccer game. The connection grew into signed jerseys and a letter inviting the family to Miami, where Beckham wore a jersey printed with Huddy's affectionate nickname for him. His mom, Melanie Droubay, said she wants him to grow up knowing "he belongs everywhere."
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Online registry highlights Utah's haunted 'real estate'
item.description: Real estate broker Kris Bowen created Utah's Real Haunted Houses: The Registry, which lists 42 locations and their ghost stories, after years of buyers asking whether a home was haunted or someone had died there. He said sellers don't have to disclose stigmatized properties but can't lie if asked, and his team researched entries through state archives, property records and old newspapers. A favorite is the Capitol Theatre, where staff say a 17-year-old usher who died fighting a 1949 basement fire still controls the lights.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Utah to start enforcing its law requiring porn sites to verify ages of users
item.description: Utah's Department of Commerce will begin enforcing its age-verification law for adult websites on Monday, saying a court order that paused SB73's provision targeting VPN workarounds still leaves it free to investigate sites and fine them up to $2,500 per violation. The law, sponsored by Sen. Calvin Musselman, also taxes adult sites to fund enforcement and youth mental health, and commerce director Margaret Busse said the state is using "advanced technology" to check compliance and is not after fine revenue. Aylo, the Pornhub owner suing over the VPN provision, said enforcement "changes nothing about our operations" and argued age checks belong on the device.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Halloween through the years: A look back at Utah's spooky season traditions
item.description: KSL dug through its archives for a look at decades of Utah Halloweens, from a 1990 couple who married dressed as Frankenstein and his bride to 1988 yards turned into mock graveyards and a cemetery worried about vandalism in 1991. Safety advice recurs, with 1983 warnings about unsealed candy and a Holladay bank asking customers to skip costumes that resembled robbers, while Operation Desert Storm costumes turned up in 1991. Even complaints about stores pushing Christmas before Halloween date back to a 1995 report.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Red Cross urges Utahns to check smoke alarms as daylight saving time ends
item.description: With daylight saving time ending Sunday, the American Red Cross is urging Utahns to test smoke alarms, since home fires rise about 20% nationwide in November and December as cooking and heating increase, said Jeremiah Lafranca of the Greater Salt Lake Chapter. Red Cross volunteers have answered about 140 Utah home fires so far this year. The group recommends monthly tests and replacing alarms after 10 years, and offers free installation of up to three alarms per home, including bed shakers for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Pamela Atkinson remembered: 'A living embodiment' of Christlike love
item.description: Hundreds of Utahns of many faiths gathered at First Presbyterian Church to remember Pamela Atkinson, the homeless and refugee advocate known as "Utah's Mother Teresa," who died Oct. 10 at 93. The Rev. Jamie White said Psalm 23 was the last thing he heard her say, and eulogists including Gov. Spencer Cox, Sharon Eubank and Elder Patrick Kearon tied her work founding clinics, advising officials and organizing aid to her faith, with Cox recalling her final message: "Just follow Jesus." White also delivered a message she had asked him to share, encouraging people to reach out and help others.
item.dc:creator: Emily Walker, Deseret News

item.title: Utah single mom turns birthday party hobby into thriving events business with reality TV clients
item.description: Single mom Kenzie Bates went from throwing family birthday parties while working several jobs to running an events business whose clients include a luxury handbag store's grand opening and stars of Real Housewives of Salt Lake City and Secret Lives of Mormon Wives. She landed early high-profile clients partly by discounting events in exchange for photos she could share on social media. Bates said the work took a lot of sacrifice, and that her goal is for guests to feel a "VIP experience."
item.dc:creator: Tamara Vaifanua, KSL

item.title: FTC orders Walmart, Delta and others to share how they use personal data to set prices and pay
item.description: The Federal Trade Commission has ordered Delta, United, JetBlue, Walmart, Target, Lyft, DoorDash and Instacart to explain whether they use personal data such as loyalty-program activity to vary prices between customers, and whether gig drivers' pay is set using data like their phone usage or ride-acceptance history. Chairman Andrew Ferguson said the agency intends to scrutinize "opaque methodology" in these industries, and it says it can go to federal court if companies don't comply. Several companies denied the practice, with Delta citing "zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing," while the FTC weighs a separate proposal requiring disclosure of personalized pricing, open for comment until Nov. 21.
item.dc:creator: Dee-ann Durbin, Associated Press

item.title: Daybreak Halloween map helps families plan trick-or-treat routes
item.description: Daybreak families can plan trick-or-treat routes using an online map at DaybreakHolidays.com and PorchlightVillage.com and the Porchlight app, where more than 160 homes have registered their Halloween displays, up from about 75 when organizer Mallory Curnow started. Some participants hire actors or DJs, and the owner of a Stranger Things-themed house said the map helps visitors find smaller displays between the big ones. Curnow said getting on the map brings more trick-or-treaters to a street.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Las Vegas children's hospital groundbreaking brings hope to southern Utah family
item.description: Intermountain Health broke ground this week in Las Vegas on Nevada's first standalone children's hospital, expected to open in 2030 with pediatric cancer, cardiac and emergency care that Desert Region president Mitch Cloward said will also serve southern Utah kids. For St. George's Stone family, whose son Nash was born at 27 weeks, spent 478 days in NICUs and still depends on a ventilator and feeding tube, trips to Primary Children's in Salt Lake City mean packing what they call "an ICU on wheels." A two-hour drive to Las Vegas, mom Lindee Stone said, would make specialist visits "just a day trip."
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Judge puts off decision in Comey case as prosecutors pursue new indictment
item.description: U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden declined for now to dismiss a placeholder criminal information filed against former FBI Director James Comey over a 2016 leak tied to a New York Times story on a secret Yahoo email-scanning order, giving prosecutors time to seek a grand jury indictment. Comey's lawyers argue the 10-year statute of limitations required an indictment, not an information he never agreed to, and that leaving the case open is "very unfair and unjust." The judge, noting grand juries in Washington have rejected politically delicate cases, quipped that ham sandwiches are harder to indict these days and warned against any "dawn raid" to arrest Comey.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker and Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press

item.title: Fear struck Utah: Retired KSL reporter recalls beginning of Ted Bundy saga
item.description: Retired KSL-TV reporter Lynn Packer recounts how, in October 1974, Midvale's police chief came to the station to report his 17-year-old daughter Melissa Smith missing, unknowingly giving Utah its first local coverage of Ted Bundy's crimes. Drawing on KSL archives and records gathered with researcher Tiffany Jean, the piece traces Bundy's arrival in Salt Lake City that September through the killings of Smith, Laura Aime and Debra Kent, the failed abduction of Carol DaRonch, and his 1975 trips to Colorado and Idaho. "Fear sort of struck the state," Packer said, adding that it was "more by luck" that police finally found a suspect when a trooper stopped Bundy's Volkswagen in Granger in August 1975.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Amendment B fight attracts big money ahead of Election Day
item.description: Utah's Amendment B, which would require tax-raising citizen initiatives to win at least 60% of the vote, has drawn more than $3 million in opposition spending from Utahns Protecting Our Constitution, much of it from out-of-state donors, while supporters have raised far less. Taxpayer Shield PAC's Rusty Cannon said that money shows opponents "want to be able to raise your taxes easily," while opposition spokesperson Scott Cuthbertson argued voters should need only the same simple majority the Legislature does. A Noble Predictive Insights poll found 56% of likely voters opposed and 34% in favor ahead of Tuesday's election.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: AAA offers $10 Lyft credits for Halloween weekend
item.description: AAA Utah is paying for $10 Lyft credits from Friday, Oct. 30, through Sunday, Nov. 1, redeemed by scanning QR codes posted at participating bars and restaurants, in a Halloween-weekend effort with the Utah Department of Public Safety and the Utah Restaurant Association. State crash data show alcohol-related crashes are 15 times more likely to be fatal, and impaired-driver crashes killed 102 people in Utah in 2025. With Halloween on a Saturday, Utah Highway Patrol Lt. Zach Randall said extra troopers will be out looking for impaired drivers.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Tooele residents honored with Heart of Service award
item.description: The Tooele City Council is set to present Heart of Service awards Wednesday to 18 of 31 Tooele Valley residents recognized this year as part of the America250 service initiative, with JustServe volunteers Annalese and Cameron Thorpe helping gather nominations. Among the honorees is a Switchpoint Tooele food pantry volunteer who began serving twice a week after her husband died rather than grieve alone at home. Annalese Thorpe said the stories revealed "so many good people quietly serving," and Tooele has also been named a JustServe City.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Man accused of stealing jewelry then making high-value purchases
item.description: Steven Matthew Sattley, 52, of Washington City has been charged with burglary and theft after an August break-in at an Ivins home where silver bars and diamond jewelry valued at about $125,000 were taken. Police say family members noticed sudden spending on veneers, a vehicle and clothes that he attributed to a Family Dollar promotion, though he had never worked there, and his phone showed searches for silver pawn shops and an AI-drafted email offering $280,000 cash for a house. Investigators say he also tried to give his child one of the stolen diamond rings.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Woman sentenced to probation after driving semitruck recklessly on I-15
item.description: An Illinois woman who pleaded guilty to reduced misdemeanor reckless endangerment after callers reported a semitruck weaving on I-15 near Nephi will serve two years of probation instead of a year in jail, and court records say she is "most likely being deported by ICE." Irune Alonso Heredia, 35, was driving with a disqualified license, and dashcam footage showed her passing on the right shoulder.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Parents arrested after 1-month-old son found with multiple broken bones
item.description: Cedar City parents Jarrid Anthony Stoklosa and Amelia Mae Ramirez, both 21, each face seven first-degree felony counts of aggravated child abuse after X-rays in March showed their 36-day-old son had seven fractures to his ribs, arm and leg in various stages of healing. Police say the parents told them no one else cared for the baby, which undercut Stoklosa's claim that the boy's grandmother caused the injuries, and that the infant tested positive for THC.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Dockworkers worldwide strike against arms shipments and to demand better working conditions
item.description: Dockworkers at more than 100 ports joined a Friday strike called by unions in France, Italy, Greece, Spain, Turkey and Morocco against weapons shipments and the "militarization of ports," as well as for better working conditions. Actions ranged from full-day stoppages at ports such as Le Havre, Marseille and Piraeus to demonstrations in Istanbul and Italian ports alongside a national general strike. Logistics experts expected limited effects on global trade, though perishable goods and already-congested ports like Genoa could see delays.
item.dc:creator: Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press

item.title: Farmington man's 30-year pumpkin carving hobby becomes Halloween tradition
item.description: A Farmington front yard filled entirely with carved pumpkins, rather than the usual ghouls and gravestones, is one of about 15 stops on a city pumpkin tour where visitors vote for favorites. Ken Klinker has built the display over 30 years, carving foam pumpkins he can reuse, and said the best part is seeing neighbors and strangers come by.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Boston researchers discover differences in colon cancer tumor cells in younger patients
item.description: Researchers at Mass General Brigham, Dana-Farber and the Broad Institute analyzed 189 colorectal tumors and more than 850,000 cell nuclei and found that tumors from patients under 50 contain a higher proportion of stromal cells, which can suppress immune response and block drugs, along with gene differences that may drive more aggressive disease. Senior co-author Dr. Ana Anderson said the work doesn't explain why young-onset cases are rising but gives researchers differences to "dig into further." Survivor Kristen Vincent, diagnosed with stage 3 cancer at 37 and now five years clear, urged younger adults not to ignore warning signs.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Parseghian

item.title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft
item.description: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, says hackers took more than $6 billion from its hot wallets in what appears to be the biggest crypto theft on record, and it has set aside $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover users while roughly $3 billion has been frozen. Blockchain firms TRM and Chainalysis attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, the North Korean unit the FBI blamed for last year's $1.5 billion Bybit hack, with TRM saying most of the funds moved out "in about 20 minutes." Co-CEO Richard Teng said attackers used a "self-destruct mechanism" that complicates the investigation, and withdrawals remain suspended.
item.dc:creator: Kaitlyn Huamani and Chan Ho-him, Associated Press

item.title: Wall Street drops to its worst day since June after the sell-off for tech stocks deepens
item.description: The S&P 500 fell 1.8% Friday for its worst day since June, with the Nasdaq down 2.9% and the Dow down 1.1%, as worries that the AI frenzy had pushed tech prices too high deepened. Intel lost almost 29%, its worst day since 1974, after a weak profit forecast, and Amazon slid after disclosing $42.4 billion in negative free cash flow over 12 months on heavy AI-driven spending, a day after Alphabet's record drop on similar concerns. One portfolio manager said the AI trade is moving into the "'show me' phase," while Treasury yields eased and crypto stocks fell after the Binance hack.
item.dc:creator: Stan Choe, Associated Press

item.title: Box Elder County sheriff on leave after crash in Weber County that critically injured a woman
item.description: Box Elder County Sheriff Kevin Potter has taken voluntary administrative leave after Ogden police confirmed he was driving the vehicle that collided Tuesday with a motorcycle near the mouth of Ogden Canyon, critically injuring the 22-year-old rider. Ogden police and the Weber Metro CRASH team say the investigation follows the same steps as any serious-injury crash and may take weeks. KSL also obtained a May censure letter in which county commissioners found Potter, who lost his primary bid this year, broke policy during a January roadside confrontation and admitted keeping a cooler of beer in his county vehicle.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack and Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Ogden man facing charges for allegedly sexually assaulting 2 minors
item.description: Weber County prosecutors have filed six first-degree felony charges, including rape and sodomy, against Hunter Blunt, 22, after two children under 14 reported abuse at the Ogden home he shares with his parents. Charging documents say the children described being given candy and gifts and told to stay quiet, and Blunt is being held without bail.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Christa Pike says she's in constant pain and blames her failed execution on 'incompetence'
item.description: In her first public statement since surviving a Sept. 30 lethal injection, Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike said she is in constant pain, still struggles to speak, and blames the failure on "incompetence." Pike, 50, was sentenced for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer, and her lawyers say two doses of pentobarbital left her arms burned and blistered, with experts suspecting an IV problem. Gov. Bill Lee has ordered an investigation and paused another execution, but said he expects her sentence to stand unless courts decide otherwise.
item.dc:creator: Kim Chandler, Associated Press

item.title: Peptides could soon be easier to get in the United States. Here's what to know
item.description: HHS has posted a draft policy, open for 14 days of comment, under which it would not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies that compound six popular wellness peptides such as BPC-157 and TB-500 for patients with a prescription, even though the substances are not FDA-approved. The department says the move will steer users away from an unregulated gray market of foreign research-use-only products, following a narrow July vote by an FDA compounding advisory committee. Pharmacy compounders and the American Peptide Association welcomed it, while the Partnership for Safe Medicines said the outcome "shreds any sense of credibility and transparency," and one industry figure warned users to expect "a very different bill at the pharmacy counter."
item.dc:creator: Jacqueline Howard, CNN

item.title: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US general election
item.description: The Vatican confirmed that Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV cast a mail-in ballot in Will County, Illinois, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, making him the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election. The press office said he believes in "the right and the duty of citizens" to take part in democratic processes, and records show he requested the ballot Oct. 3, days before lung cancer surgery, and has voted in most general elections since 2000 along with both Democratic and Republican primaries. The vote comes after a public clash with President Trump over Leo's criticism of the Iran war and immigration enforcement.
item.dc:creator: Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

item.title: Netanyahu's party claims election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority
item.description: Final Israeli election results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, against 48 for the main opposition and a historic 19 for Arab-led parties, and his Likud party responded by claiming without evidence that the vote had been "stolen" with possible foreign help. The claims escalated after election committee head Noam Sohlberg asked the Shin Bet to look into unverified reports of interference, though the committee called allegations of systematic violations "baseless" and Qatar denied involvement. Rival Gadi Eisenkot, who has signaled conditional openness to working with Arab-led parties, said Likud was attacking the results because it lost, while Netanyahu stays in charge as coalition talks play out.
item.dc:creator: Cara Anna, Julia Frankel and Koral Saeed, Associated Press

item.title: E. coli warning issued for San Juan River
item.description: Recent flooding may have left unhealthy E. coli levels in the San Juan River, San Juan County Public Health warned Thursday night, telling people to keep children, pets and livestock out of the water and not use it for drinking, cooking or hygiene. Because the bacteria can survive in wet areas for weeks, flood-recovery workers are urged to wear gloves and eye protection and make sure tetanus shots are current.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Russia and US discussing sanctions relief for Moscow's sovereign wealth fund, Kremlin aide says
item.description: Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, according to Russian state news agency TASS, that talks with the U.S. on lifting sanctions against the Russian Direct Investment Fund, imposed by the Biden administration after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, have been "going on for some time," and a U.S. official said the fund's delisting application is being assessed as part of efforts to end the war. The fund's CEO, envoy Kirill Dmitriev, has been pressing American officials on the issue. It would be the latest Trump administration concession to Moscow after this month's waivers on Russian diesel exports and other energy sanctions, moves that drew bipartisan criticism and worry Kyiv and European allies.
item.dc:creator: Helen Regan, CNN

item.title: Utah correctional officers required to work mandatory overtime to compensate for short-staffing
item.description: Utah's Department of Corrections is requiring every correctional officer to work one mandatory overtime shift per pay period while it tries to fill 57 vacancies at its Salt Lake City facilities and 12 at the Central Utah Correctional Facility. Spokesman Richard Piatt said the shortage stems from staffing a newly opened section for a growing prison population, along with officers out on military leave, FMLA or sick calls. He called the overtime a "temporary bridge measure" until three academy classes graduate by year's end and said he hadn't heard of pushback from officers.
item.dc:creator: Heather Peterson, KSL

item.title: Man who testified against brother released after years in jail for his part in fatal WinCo shooting
item.description: Damian Coleman, 32, the only one of four defendants in the 2022 killing of Romeo Charles Stevens outside a South Salt Lake WinCo who didn't flee the state, was released after more than four years in jail when 3rd District Judge Amber Mettler suspended his prison sentences and ordered five years of probation. Coleman pleaded guilty in 2023 under a deal requiring him to testify, and this month took the stand against his brother Stafon Coleman Jr. and half-brother Terrell Jones, whom jurors convicted of murder but acquitted of aggravated robbery. Saying he was "very remorseful," Coleman called the case "a life-altering situation" for both families, and prosecutors said they would support ending his probation after 30 months if he does well.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah State University's new live mascot to bring additional Aggie spirit
item.description: Utah State University has introduced Thistle, a Scottish Highland steer named for the school's fight song, The Scotsman, as its new live mascot, a role actually filled by two identical steers because each does better with a buddy. Thistle will appear at athletic and community events and help with children's education tied to USU's land-grant agricultural roots, under handlers in the new Highland Ambassador Program. USU lecturer Brett Bowman said existing mascot Big Blue isn't going anywhere, and Thistle follows Gus the Bull, the Aggies' live mascot in 1976.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Oscar Mayer Wienermobile makes several stops at southern Utah Halloween celebrations
item.description: The Oscar Mayer Wienermobile, marking 90 years on the road, is spending Halloween week in southern Utah, with stops at Utah Tech University's Tricks & Treats Night, Staheli Family Farm in Washington City, a blood drive and other St. George-area venues. Driver Aiden Jaffe, who goes by All Beef Aiden, said he and copilot Lauren Tripper are urging residents to serve hot dogs to trick-or-treaters and request surprise visits to their parties. The tour wraps up Saturday at the St. George Halloween Festival after a Friday trunk-or-treat at Sandtown Pizza.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Parole decisions made for Utah inmates serving time for homicide, manslaughter
item.description: The Utah Board of Pardons and Parole set future release or parole dates for two men convicted of DUI automobile homicide and denied parole to two others convicted in killings, leaving all four to serve more time. Jonathan Ulises Analco-Cruz, whose 103 mph crash in 2014 killed three teenage passengers, may be released in December 2027 but only to an immigration detainer, while former police officer Samuel Andrew Rockwell, convicted in a 2021 Bangerter Highway crash that killed 23-year-old Emily Worley, won't be paroled until 2031 after the board cited prison rule violations and that he "attempted to cover up (his) criminal behavior." Colton James Beed, part of a 2019 robbery in which Marine veteran Mason Hunt was killed, gets a new hearing in 2028, and Darren Neil Grueber Jr., who killed Don Dorton in 2001, gets one in 2030.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
item.description: Dartmouth College Provost Santiago Schnell resigned after a faculty committee found he used AI to "meaningfully alter his writing" and wasn't forthcoming about it, a review that began when Semafor's AI filter flagged his August Washington Post column on AI cheating as entirely AI-written. The student paper, The Dartmouth, then found heavy AI use in his recent writing but not in work predating ChatGPT's 2022 release, while Schnell maintained he used AI for language and clarity on his own drafts. The departure came as the school, which calls itself the birthplace of AI, opened a 70th anniversary conference on the field, with President Sian Leah Beilock saying leaders must model "transparency and human judgment."
item.dc:creator: Heather Hollingsworth, Associated Press

item.title: What to consider if a company that made AI-related job cuts wants you back
item.description: As companies such as Microsoft, Barclays and Kroger cite AI in job cuts, some employers are rehiring laid-off workers after the technology falls short, a reversal nicknamed the "AI boomerang," with Klarna returning to human customer service reps and Ford hiring or promoting 350 veteran engineers after AI quality-control tools underperformed. Experts told the AP that companies often overlook the undocumented, relationship-building work people do, and Forrester's Betsy Summers said firms expecting AI agents to match humans "are frequently mistaken." For workers asked back, Georgetown's Brooks Holtom suggested pitching a role that pairs AI with their expertise and seeking protections like a one-year renewable contract with a buyout clause, while SHL's Lucy Beaumont said returnees are asking for more money and clarity on future AI staffing.
item.dc:creator: Cathy Bussewitz, Associated Press

item.title: Airbnb pledges $500M for its nonprofit to offer more free emergency stays
item.description: Airbnb will put $500 million over five years into its nonprofit Airbnb.org, funded by 10 cents from every booking with the company covering any shortfall, aiming eventually to provide 1 million free nights a year for disaster survivors and families traveling for medical care. CEO Brian Chesky rejected the idea that the giving offsets criticism of short-term rentals' effect on housing costs, saying, "I don't like this idea that somehow you create a nonprofit to make up for or apologize for your core business." Noah Patton of the National Low Income Housing Coalition said such emergency stays help prevent initial displacement but are "a Band-Aid" without longer-term housing solutions.
item.dc:creator: James Pollard, Associated Press

item.title: Development near Herriman halts blasting due to resident concerns
item.description: Fieldstone, the developer of the new Panorama neighborhood near Herriman, has temporarily halted blasting on a rocky mound at the site after neighbors complained that explosions a few hundred feet from homes were showering roofs and yards with rocks. Resident Joeanne Bolnick said blast notices don't narrow down the timing, and video she shared shows debris raining onto her roof, with some rocks clearing her house entirely. Herriman said such blasting is typically outside its jurisdiction, and Fieldstone had not responded to KSL.
item.dc:creator: Cameron Elliott, KSL

item.title: Ex-Cache County worker faces fraud charge for allegedly misrepresenting her education
item.description: Terryl Lee Warner, 63, a Cache County employee for more than 28 years who led its victims services office, is charged with second-degree felony communications fraud for allegedly claiming a 2022 Ph.D. from Liberty University to keep the higher pay she had drawn as interim director of the county's Children's Justice Center. Officials learned in 2024 that her doctorate came from Breyer State Theology University, an unaccredited Florida institution, and the interim county attorney at the time said he would have moved to fire her had he known. The case, investigated by the Utah County Attorney's Office, was moved from Logan to 2nd District Court in Ogden because of her past ties to the Cache County Attorney's Office, and she is due in court Nov. 12.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: San Juan County flood victims seek help as Utah lieutenant governor tours damage
item.description: Touring San Juan County after the San Juan River flooded homes and businesses in Bluff and Navajo Nation communities including Aneth and Montezuma Creek, Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson said state agencies are sending crews, water pumps and UDOT trucks to build a gravel road to families stranded by a river breach. Navajo community organizer Rebecca Benally said some families are stuck and running low on water and groceries, and that rural families deserve the same help as larger towns. Bluff Mayor Josh Ewing, who ordered evacuations as the river rose up to two feet an hour while a faulty gauge left officials relying on a friend's measurements, called for a warning system built for today's extreme weather rather than "for the 1970s."
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: 'The one that transforms Utah's economy': Inland Port Authority unveils PortSLC
item.description: The Utah Inland Port Authority has rebranded its Northwest Quadrant project area as PortSLC, launching an international campaign to draw aerospace and defense, life sciences and advanced manufacturing companies to the 17,000-acre area near Salt Lake City International Airport, two rail systems and three interstates. Executive director Ben Hart called it "the one that transforms Utah's economy" for the next 30 years and highlighted Delta Air Lines' 60,000-square-foot cargo facility, backed by an $18 million port authority loan and due in 2027, noting that 92% of Utah's air cargo now leaves the state by truck. Hart said the authority has given $7.5 million for Great Salt Lake wetland and shoreline conservation, with another $2.5 million expected in the spring.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Utah County survivor warns about breast cancer risk for men
item.description: Utah County man Jon Hadley learned he had breast cancer when a PET scan ordered after melanoma in his ear showed a hotspot over his left breast and a mammogram confirmed it, a diagnosis he never expected and says was unrelated to the skin cancer. Timpanogos Regional Hospital breast surgical oncologist Dr. Lisa Anderson said about 1 in 1,000 men get breast cancer, compared with 1 in 8 women, and that men should watch for a lump behind the nipple, an inverted nipple or discharge, a sign Hadley, a trail runner, had dismissed as run-related leakage. Caught at Stage 2 and treated with chemotherapy, radiation and a mastectomy, he is sharing his story so other men watch for it, saying, "Catching it early ... that saved my life."
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Report: Most produce from Mexico comes from processing facilities 'rarely inspected' by FDA
item.description: A Washington Post analysis found that the FDA has inspected only about 2% of Mexico's produce processing facilities in the last 17 years, even though foreign facilities supply most of the fresh produce sent to the U.S. This year a cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to Taylor Farms de Mexico lettuce and jalapeños sickened nearly 13,000 people, though an FDA official told the Post that inspection counts don't "tell the whole story."
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Woman falsely claims husband armed with chainsaw was going to cut her up
item.description: A 33-year-old Roosevelt woman faces a second-degree felony charge of emergency reporting abuse after allegedly calling 911 on Oct. 22 to say her husband was in the house with a chainsaw, threatening to cut up her and her son. Officers from multiple agencies were forcing their way in when the husband opened the door, and they found no sign of a fight or a chainsaw; according to the affidavit, the woman, who said she had drunk a half-gallon of vodka, "kept saying 'wait this is real now.'" She was also charged with public intoxication and booked into the Duchesne County Jail.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: The goal of a goal: Special Olympics Unified Soccer unites hundreds of high schoolers
item.description: About 200 students with and without intellectual disabilities on 25 teams played in the sixth annual Special Olympics Unified Sports Soccer State Championships at Sandy's America First Field, cheered on by hundreds of classmates as 12 state champions were crowned. Unified teams must field at least three athletes and two peer partners, and Brighton High partner Sam Beckstead said partners try to set up their athletes rather than score, adding, "They become a family for you real fast." Backed by Real Salt Lake, first lady Abby Cox and Gail Miller, the program now runs in about 80 of Utah's more than 400 high schools, and organizers hope to reach every one.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Have You Seen This? Bureau of Land Management holds bat beauty contest
item.description: The Bureau of Land Management is running a Bat Beauty Contest on its social media pages for International Bat Week, pitting bats named after celebrities and fictional characters, such as Batty White, ChewBATca and Ryan GosWING, against each other in public votes, with the winner announced on Halloween. The agency is using the contest to highlight bats' role in eating insects and pollinating plants, a pitch aimed at drumming up support for their conservation.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Humans accidentally canceled the next ice age — but it's no reason to celebrate, scientists say
item.description: A study in Science argues that Canada's Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, began regrowing about 2,000 years ago in what should count as the start of a new ice age, then abruptly began shrinking around 1960 as human-driven warming raised summer temperatures. Researchers dated mosses entombed by the advancing ice and tested nearby rocks to reconstruct its history, and co-author Nicolás Young called the reversal "a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system." Outside scientists were divided, with Potsdam physicist Andrey Ganopolski saying the evidence doesn't show a glacial cycle had begun, and Young cautioned against reading the study as saying warming has "saved humanity from an ice age."
item.dc:creator: Laura Paddison, CNN

item.title: Utah has received above-normal rain for the past 3½ months. Why is it still in drought?
item.description: Utah's mountains have picked up more than 12 inches of precipitation since July 15, about 4 inches above normal, and the share of the state in severe or worse drought fell from 62% to 51% in a week, yet over 90% of Utah is still in drought. U.S. Drought Monitor author Lindsay Johnson explained that the map weighs conditions against each area's history and tracks long-term impacts like low reservoirs, and that nothing substitutes for snowpack, which she calls a "frozen reservoir." After a 2026 snowpack that was the worst on record despite average precipitation, rain has soaked soils and streams but barely refilled reservoirs, so a strong winter snowpack like 2023's remains the surest way out.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: 'Dixie' map that divided the US into North and South fetches nearly $1M at auction
item.description: The hand-drawn survey of the Mason-Dixon Line, completed in 1768 by Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon to settle a Maryland-Pennsylvania border dispute and later synonymous with the divide between free and slave states, sold at Brunk Auctions in Asheville, North Carolina, for $950,000 to an anonymous buyer. The price, reached after 45 bidders competed for under three minutes, fell short of the $1.2 million high estimate but far exceeded the $360,000 Malcolm Forbes paid in 1982. Auction house vice president Lauren Brunk called it "a very high price for a map."
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: International athletes try adaptive sports at Park City's National Ability Center
item.description: Fifteen young international athletes, with a focus on adaptive athletes, are spending two weeks at Park City's National Ability Center through the Sports Visitor Program, a partnership with the State Department and nonprofit FHI 360 that runs through Sunday. They have tried challenge courses, horseback riding and other activities while learning about accessibility and the Olympic and Paralympic movements, and Ukrainian basketball player Mariia Yevtushenko said she hopes the new network could one day lead to something like a national championship. The center's Meghan Campano said adaptive sports teach participants new ways of doing things "and they get to take those home."
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Utah attorney general received campaign donations from gambling companies, disclosures show
item.description: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, who has been pursuing the prediction market Kalshi as illegal gambling, received at least $80,000 in campaign donations from the gambling industry in 2025 and 2026, including $50,000 from Las Vegas Sands and contributions tied to PrizePicks, DraftKings, Underdog Fantasy and two sweepstakes casino companies. Campaign advisor Matt Lusty said the donations "have no influence on his decision-making." The disclosures come as Brown's office escalates its fight with Kalshi, filing a civil suit last week and felony charges on Wednesday, including 12 counts of online gambling promotion, while the federal government and the CFTC have sued Utah, arguing it can't ban federally regulated derivatives markets.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: September 2027 trial date set for charged White House correspondents' dinner attacker
item.description: Cole Tomas Allen of Torrance, California, faces an attempted assassination charge carrying up to life in prison, accused of storming the White House Correspondents' Association dinner at the Washington Hilton on April 25 with guns and knives and firing a shotgun at a Secret Service officer, who was hit in his bullet-resistant vest. U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden set jury selection for Sept. 7, 2027, later than the May 2027 start prosecutors recommended, after a defense attorney asked for more time to prepare. In writings sent to relatives beforehand, authorities say, Allen railed against Trump administration policies and called himself a "Friendly Federal Assassin."
item.dc:creator: Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ donates $3M to Utah's effort to remove phragmites along Great Salt Lake
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is giving $3 million to Utah's fight against phragmites, an invasive reed up to 15 feet tall that blocks water from flowing across the Great Salt Lake's bed and soaks up more water than native plants. The money expands a project that gets about $800,000 a year in state funds, and officials estimate that turning 40,800 acres of the more than 50,000 acres of phragmites into inland saltgrass could save the lake 82,000 acre-feet of water annually. Gov. Spencer Cox, who announced the gift, said protecting the lake "will take all of us working together," as both of its arms sit more than 8 feet below their minimum healthy level.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: AI agent coming to Salt Lake County non-emergency line
item.description: Starting Dec. 4, callers to the Salt Lake Valley Emergency Communications Center's non-emergency lines will reach an AI agent that answers routine questions, like office hours or how to file a police report, and can text or email information in 30 languages. Routine questions make up about 70% of the roughly 600,000 non-emergency calls the center gets each year, and executive director Ivan Whitaker said 911 callers will still reach a live dispatcher, with the AI set to hand anyone describing an emergency to one right away. Residents can try the agent and help pick its voice at the center's West Valley City office on Nov. 19.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Study projects health impacts from proposed data center; O'Leary's team disputes findings
item.description: A report by EmPower Analytics Group, commissioned by the Natural Resources Defense Council, estimates that emissions from the proposed Stratos AI data center campus in Box Elder County, backed by Kevin O'Leary, could cause between five and 45 premature deaths a year and up to $690 million in annual health costs, with Utah Clean Energy's Logan Mitchell warning the pollution would reach "all of northern Utah" and neighboring states. The study, which is not peer-reviewed, modeled two gas-fired power scenarios because Stratos hasn't said how it will power the site, and EmPower CEO Michael Cork said the newer 7.5-gigawatt plan would cut the estimates by roughly 17%. Stratos spokesperson Paul Palandjian said the project will meet air-quality standards and called it "irresponsible" to present modeled assumptions as confirmed health impacts.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: Here's how humanoid robots could fit into the future of defense, society
item.description: At 47G's Zero Gravity Summit, Utah State University professor Mario Harper showed off Dallas and Dallas II, two humanoid robots the school bought overseas, and argued that a human-shaped machine is better suited than wheeled or four-legged robots to operate in a world built for people. He said in military room-clearing exercises other robots slowed troops or gave away their position, while humanoids can maneuver and even bear soldiers' weight as a step, calling that "a very real, tactical benefit." Harper also sees eventual home-care and cleaning roles, though he said robots still lack the combined physical and reasoning ability that requires.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Group works to collect donations for flood victims in Navajo Nation
item.description: After the San Juan River rose to very high levels and forced evacuations in southeastern Utah, the group Navajo Strong is collecting food, hygiene products, clothing and cleaning supplies along the Wasatch Front for flood victims in the Navajo Nation. Program director Leah Swenson, whose own relatives near Tuba City, Arizona, were also flooded, said many people "lost their homes, their belongings." The items will be taken Monday to USU Blanding for distribution, with drop-offs accepted at a West Valley City Les Schwab and details at NavajoStrong.org.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Alvin K. Hellerstein, a federal judge who handled Trump, Maduro and 9/11 cases, dies at 92
item.description: Alvin K. Hellerstein, a Clinton-appointed Manhattan federal judge who worked until his death at 92, presided over cases involving President Trump, former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and the Sept. 11 attacks. Just weeks ago he entered a not-guilty plea on Maduro's behalf after the former president refused to enter one, and in August he rejected for a third time Trump's bid to move his hush money case to federal court. His legacy was shaped by two decades overseeing dozens of wrongful death, injury and property damage lawsuits after the World Trade Center attack, and in 2020 he freed Michael Cohen from prison, finding the government had retaliated against him.
item.dc:creator: Michael R. Sisak and Larry Neumeister, Associated Press

item.title: Utah leads the nation in dropped homeowners insurance policies. Here's why
item.description: National Association of Insurance Commissioners data shows insurers declined to renew 4.45% of Utah homeowners' policies, about one in 22 and the highest rate in the nation, well ahead of California. Utah Insurance Commissioner Jon Pike called it "kinda a perfect storm," citing bigger wildfires, costlier rebuilding and growth in the wildland urban interface, but said the figure is inflated by three large companies that exited the business entirely. Pike said he knows of no one unable to find replacement coverage, though he acknowledged affordability is the open question, and regulators say the market is starting to stabilize.
item.dc:creator: Matt Gephardt, KSL

item.title: Hayden Panettiere death investigation closed by police in South Carolina
item.description: Greenville, South Carolina, police closed their investigation into the August death of actress Hayden Panettiere, 36, after the county coroner ruled it an accidental overdose involving fentanyl and other drugs. Investigators had been examining whether the Heroes and Nashville star got illicit, possibly counterfeit drugs from a Southern California dealer, and police would not say whether the DEA's inquiry remains open. According to the coroner's report, her boyfriend and his brother found her unresponsive in an Airbnb and gave her two doses of Narcan before calling 911.
item.dc:creator: Cindy Von Quednow and Addie Haney, CNN

item.title: Halloween competition gives students a chance to showcase creativity, career skills
item.description: Hair design and nails students at the Jordan Academy for Technology and Careers in Riverton raced the clock in their annual Halloween fantasy competition, turning classmates into characters like Sally from The Nightmare Before Christmas and the Bride of Frankenstein. Instructor Dacia Peterson Sullivan said the event teaches collaboration across hair, makeup and nails, the way the beauty industry actually works. Students said the program lets them earn professional training hours in high school, which one said spares her from paying for expensive schooling later.
item.dc:creator: Dan Rascon, KSL

item.title: Utah school bus driver arrested for investigation of voyeurism while driving children
item.description: Gabriele Basile, 64, a Jordan School District bus driver who has since been fired, was arrested in Herriman for investigation of voyeurism after police say he used his phone to record a 10-year-old girl seated near him while driving a bus full of children. The 33-second video surfaced on a Google account he shared with his wife, and when he did not report himself as he had promised, his daughter gave it to the district, according to a police affidavit. A search of his phone turned up a second deleted video of the same girl, and family members told police he had said he would flee to Italy if he ever got in trouble.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Charges dismissed against man accused of assaulting another man, setting him on fire
item.description: A judge dismissed all charges against Robert Reins, 53, of Draper, who had been accused of stabbing, sexually assaulting and setting fire to a man walking to work from a TRAX station in October 2024, after prosecutors cited "evidentiary concerns" and little chance of winning at trial. The dismissal is without prejudice, so charges could be refiled if new evidence emerges, and Reins was released after more than a year and a half in jail. Police had tied him to the attack through a resemblance to a sketch and a photo lineup in which the victim said he was 90% sure.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: UN condemns US economic embargo of Cuba though more nations sit out after Trump push
item.description: The U.N. General Assembly condemned the U.S. embargo of Cuba for the 34th straight year, but the 130-17 vote with 25 abstentions showed markedly weaker support after a Trump administration lobbying push, with Germany, Italy and Latvia abstaining and several nations voting no for the first time. Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez called the embargo an economic war and said, "Cuba is not a threat," while U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz cast the vote as a potential propaganda win for a "corrupt, kleptocratic communist regime." The vote followed a shouting match between the two diplomats on the Assembly floor a day earlier.
item.dc:creator: Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press

item.title: 'Choosing forgiveness': Man sentenced for leaving collision that caused 9-year-old's death
item.description: At the request of 9-year-old Dalton Gibbs' family, 4th District Judge Roger Griffin suspended a prison term and gave George Parker Hunter, 81, 75 days in jail and three years of probation for hitting the boy in a Pleasant Grove crosswalk in April 2025 and driving on. Hunter pleaded guilty to leaving the scene of an accident and negligent homicide; his attorney said the veteran and retired teacher was not impaired but may no longer have been capable of driving large vehicles. Dalton's father described an "agonizing void" and recalled his wife saying soon after the crash that they needed to pray for the driver.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Utah State University sets enrollment record as concurrent enrollment grows
item.description: Utah State University enrolled a record 32,286 students this fall, an 8% jump over 2025 that officials credit largely to concurrent enrollment and the school's statewide and online programs, despite missionary-age changes and fewer high school graduates. Associate vice president Katie Jo North said USU is trying to reach students earlier and offer multiple paths since the traditional four-year route is less common. Students who took college classes in high school praised the savings, with one calling the program "a no-brainer."
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Utah's aerospace, defense industry poised to help Team USA bobsled athletes 'go faster'
item.description: Utah aerospace composite makers Albany Engineered Composites, Hexcel and Nammo Composite Solutions will build bobsled parts for USA Bobsled and Skeleton under a partnership brokered by 47G and announced at its Zero Gravity Summit. Albany will fabricate next-generation cowlings for four-man sleds, Nammo carbon-fiber cowlings for two-man sleds and Hexcel the raw materials, aiming for lighter, stronger hulls in a sport decided by hundredths of a second. USA Bobsled CEO Aron McGuire said the work gives athletes "a real competitive edge" as they build toward 2034 on home ice.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Cornell faculty to begin voting on no-confidence measure over handling of sexual assault allegations
item.description: Cornell's Faculty Senate debated a no-confidence resolution in the university administration over its response to a woman who says she was gang raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024, with some senators seeking to delay the vote until an independent investigation is released. A day earlier, 20 female science and engineering professors urged President Michael Kotlikoff to resign, writing that the community needed leadership but "faced a leadership vacuum." The resolution itself stops short of calling for his resignation, and the woman's lawsuit alleges seven fraternity members assaulted or exploited her, which they deny.
item.dc:creator: Leah Willingham, Associated Press

item.title: Kearns man pleads guilty to manslaughter for killing friend who said he could dodge a bullet
item.description: Ashton Mann, 25, pleaded guilty Monday to second-degree felony manslaughter in the February 2025 shooting death of his Kearns housemate Dylan Lee Treichel, 23, under a deal that dropped a restricted-person gun charge. According to charging documents, the two had been playing with guns in the garage after a video game when Treichel claimed he could dodge a bullet, and Mann, who had been dry-firing his 9mm, admitted he "recklessly discharged a firearm." Sentencing is set for Jan. 11.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Goods trade deficit widens as AI-related demand pushes imports to record high
item.description: The U.S. goods trade deficit unexpectedly widened 2.1% to $134.9 billion in September, the largest since March 2025, as imports hit a record $344.1 billion on a 7.5% jump in capital goods tied to the AI infrastructure buildout. Economists estimated trade may have subtracted three to four percentage points from third-quarter GDP growth, though the advance estimate is still expected to show strong growth on AI investment and consumer spending. Santander's Stephen Stanley said much of the hardware tech companies need comes from overseas, "driving a massive widening in the trade gap."
item.dc:creator: Lucia Mutikani, Reuters

item.title: Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu remains far from defeated
item.description: Israel faces possibly weeks of uncertainty after an election in which, with 88% of votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud led with 20.7% but neither his bloc nor that of centrist challenger Gadi Eisenkot appeared able to reach the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority. Arab-led parties made a historic showing of about 15%, prompting Netanyahu to warn against a "dangerous government" that included them and Likud to allege without evidence that the vote was stolen. Turnout of nearly 78% was the highest since 1999, and results reflected anger over draft exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox and unease with Netanyahu's far-right partners.
item.dc:creator: Cara Anna, Areej Hazboun and Audrey Horowitz, Associated Press

item.title: Utah pediatrician urges women not to delay mammograms after cancer diagnosis
item.description: Utah pediatrician Dr. Shellie Ring, who had no family history or major risk factors, kept postponing her mammogram and was seven months overdue when it revealed a nine-millimeter Stage 1 triple-negative breast tumor. That aggressive type accounts for about 15% of cases and doesn't respond to the hormone therapies used for other breast cancers, making early detection especially important. With about 12 weeks of treatment left, Ring is urging women not to delay screenings, saying, "Families are better off with moms in them than without them."
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: The long afterlife of a one-use Halloween costume
item.description: Of the $13.5 billion Americans are expected to spend on Halloween this year, costumes account for $4.4 billion, and 4 in 10 store-bought ones, typically cheap polyester, are worn just once before many end up in landfills, where they can take decades or centuries to break down. Experts cited in the piece note that such costumes are often heat-bonded rather than sewn, shed microplastics in the wash, and carry a large upstream footprint in oil and chemicals; Washington University lecturer Zack Bowersox estimated that about 80% end up in landfills. University of Michigan professor Shelie Miller urges shoppers to remember that every purchase carries "all of the environmental impacts" of its production and to consider reusable or thrifted alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: Popemobile exhibition unveiled at the Vatican featuring the vehicle used since 1930
item.description: The Vatican Museums unveiled an exhibition marking A Century of the Popemobile, featuring eight Mercedes-Benz papal vehicles dating to a silk-upholstered Nürburg 460 given to Pius XI in 1930. Later models on display trace the cars' evolution toward letting popes reach the crowds, from John XXIII's 1960 Landaulet with removable rear windows to the transparent-dome 230 G built for John Paul II's 1980 trip to Germany. Pope Leo XIV, a car enthusiast, met Mercedes executives and said the vehicle has become "an instrument of encounter" with the faithful.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Sportelli and Nicole Winfield, Associated Press

item.title: Defense asks judge to order more DNA testing in 42-year-old Provo murder case
item.description: Attorneys for Douglas Carter, who spent more than four decades on death row for the 1985 Provo killing of Eva Olesen before his conviction was overturned for police and prosecutor misconduct, asked a judge to order the kind of investigative genetic genealogy testing used to crack the Golden State Killer case. The defense wants testing on the knife handle and a blood sample outside Olesen's back door, both believed to carry the killer's DNA, after September tests found none of Carter's DNA on the scene evidence. Attorney Neal Hamilton said that when prosecutors asked why the defense wanted the testing, he answered, "We're trying to identify the killer"; the state has dropped the death penalty but still plans to retry Carter.
item.dc:creator: Amy Donaldson, KSL

item.title: Amazon Flex driver accused of taking more than 100 packages
item.description: Mabel Tarache Sogamoso, 28, of West Valley City, has been charged with mail theft and communications fraud after Amazon loss-prevention staff reported that she kept packages she was supposed to deliver as an Amazon Flex driver. Prosecutors say she would mark a package delivered and photograph a stand-in object, mostly between May and August, and she admitted taking items and returned 122 of them. Police believe as many as 200 items worth more than $9,500 were involved.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Feds sue Utah over attempt to ban Kalshi; AG files criminal charges
item.description: The federal government and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission sued Utah, arguing that Kalshi's event contracts are federally regulated swaps and that "Commodity Exchange Act-regulated transactions are not gambling," a week after Attorney General Derek Brown sued to stop the prediction market from offering sports wagers in the state. Brown's office then escalated, filing criminal charges against KalshiEx and its co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, including a second-degree felony pattern of unlawful activity and 12 counts of online gambling promotion. The charges rest on an undercover agent who says he placed bets on 12 games, including Utah football and hockey, while confirming he was in Utah; the federal suit notes similar actions against nine other states.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Fed leaves rates unchanged as it awaits 'accumulation of more information'
item.description: The Federal Reserve voted 10-2 to hold its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4.00%, putting off any change until after next week's midterm elections while saying inflation "remains elevated" and upgrading its description of the economy to strong. Governor Lisa Cook, whom President Trump is trying to remove, cast her first dissent, joining Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack in favoring a quarter-point hike. With inflation at 3.7% and oil above $100, the statement hinted further increases may come, and investors still expect hikes starting in December.
item.dc:creator: Howard Schneider, Reuters

item.title: Man who attacked strangers during mental health crisis sentenced to prison
item.description: Third District Judge Elizabeth Hruby-Mills sent Garrett Thomas Stewart, 36, to prison for zero to five years for a July 19 aggravated assault on a Salt Lake City mother walking home with her husband and two daughters, rejecting his request for probation. Prosecutors said Stewart was on psilocybin mushrooms when he broke a car window and attacked the family, while his attorney attributed it to a mental health crisis; the judge said her concerns for community safety were "so great." In a statement read by her sister, the victim described a lasting scar and said, "Every time I look in the mirror, I see what happened that night."
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Post Malone, Alesso to headline new Salt Lake City New Year's Eve festival
item.description: Post Malone and Swedish DJ Alesso will headline a new New Year's Eve Festival at the Delta Center following the Dec. 31 NHL Winter Classic between the Utah Mammoth and Colorado Avalanche at Rice-Eccles Stadium. Smith Entertainment Group, which is producing the show with Kygo's Palm Tree Crew, is billing it as part of a four-day "Winter Weekend" that also includes Jazz games against the Knicks and Boston and a Mammoth game against Vancouver. More than 6,000 tickets will be priced under $125, with a presale Thursday and general sales Friday.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Smoke from LA fires exposed millions of people to high levels of toxic heavy metals, study says
item.description: A Caltech study in Science Advances found that at the height of the January 2025 Los Angeles fires, millions of residents were exposed over a 24-hour period to smoke carrying lead at about 80 times typical background levels. Comparing the Eaton Fire plume with wildland smoke, researchers found the urban smoke had far more lead, arsenic and halogens from burning vehicles, building materials and electronics, which author Sally Ng said makes it "very different fundamentally" from wildfire smoke. Outside experts said the hour-by-hour measurements offer rare documentation, and the authors said monitoring and emergency response must adapt as more fires reach cities.
item.dc:creator: Dorany Pineda, Associated Press

item.title: Father accused of attacking son with meat cleaver
item.description: Bhan Thor, 39, of West Valley City, has been charged with first-degree felony aggravated child abuse after prosecutors say he grew angry over his 11-year-old son's trouble at school, told the boy they "were going to die that day," and cut two of his fingers with a meat cleaver. According to the charges, the boy escaped and walked more than 3½ miles barefoot to a store where he knew officers would be. Prosecutors have asked that Thor be held without bail.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Apple expected to show first touchscreen laptops amid product blitz
item.description: Apple was expected to unveil its first touchscreen MacBooks at a Los Angeles event, reversing a long resistance that once had Steve Jobs calling laptop touchscreens "ergonomically terrible," as it wraps up a run of launches that included a folding iPhone and a smart home hub. Analysts said a generation raised on touch now expects it, with Moor Insights' Anshel Sag calling the shift "the long arm of reality setting in." Bloomberg reported the touch models will use existing M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, so they may offer little performance gain over current machines.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Nellis, Reuters

item.title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
item.description: Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede!", died at home at 96, her family said, after remaining active into her 90s speaking on race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women's rights through her Bakersfield-based foundation. A New Mexico-born former schoolteacher drawn to organizing by her students' poverty, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012 from Barack Obama, who joked he had borrowed her slogan. Earlier this year she revealed that farmworker co-founder César Chavez had sexually abused her in the 1960s, a secret she said she kept for decades for fear it would undo the movement's gains.
item.dc:creator: Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press

item.title: Former Rep. Trevor Lee makes first court appearance on fraud charges
item.description: Former Republican state Rep. Trevor Lee made a brief first court appearance on communications fraud, mortgage fraud and forgery charges, with a follow-up hearing set for Nov. 23 before 3rd District Judge Joel Ferre. The Utah Attorney General's Office alleges Lee forged mortgage documents and "misrepresented his employment" to get a loan for a Layton home whose subcontractors said they were still owed $165,000. Lee, who lost his reelection bid in June, resigned from the House after the charges were filed and is represented by attorney Kathy Nester.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko and Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: New pediatric unit to help Davis County families stay close to home
item.description: Holy Cross Hospital in Layton is opening an eight-bed pediatric unit, the first of its kind in Davis County, so children who need only a short stay no longer have to be transferred to Primary Children's or other hospitals outside the county. Chief nursing officer Ashlyn Hall said the goal is to keep kids "here in the community," pointing to rapid growth around Hill Air Force Base and the west side of I-15. The refreshed unit, revived under CommonSpirit Health after sitting unused since the pandemic, is staffed around the clock by pediatric hospitalists and pediatric-trained nurses, and the hospital has also earned a state pediatric readiness certification.
item.dc:creator: Britt Johnson, KSL

item.title: This freight train claims to be the longest ever. Here's how long
item.description: South Africa's state-run Transnet says a 4.7-mile train of 696 empty freight wagons, powered by electric and diesel locomotives spread along its length, completed a two-day, 534-mile test run on Oct. 18 from Saldanha Bay to an inland iron ore mine. The company claims it beat the record held by a 4.5-mile train in Western Australia in 2001, far longer than the half-mile to 1.5-mile length typical of freight trains, and Transnet Freight Rail CEO Russell Baatjies called the run a learning exercise for hauling minerals over long distances.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Brigham City man receives no additional jail time for threatening to 'blow up' girlfriend's house
item.description: Jeremy Ruben Perea, 44, of Brigham City, will serve probation rather than more jail time after pleading guilty to reduced charges in a case where prosecutors say he opened the gas lines at the building he shared with his girlfriend in April and texted her that it was his "last goodbye." While awaiting sentencing on a July misdemeanor reckless endangerment plea, he was arrested in August, accused of violating a protective order by bringing a knife to the same woman's home, grabbing her neck and refusing to let her leave. After he pleaded guilty to reduced misdemeanors in that case on Oct. 19, 1st District Judge Brandon Maynard suspended all jail terms in both cases, credited him with 67 days served and ordered two years of probation with mental health and substance abuse evaluations.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: SK Hynix unveils shareholder return plan worth $75 billion after posting 7-fold jump in Q3 profit
item.description: SK Hynix posted a record third-quarter operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, more than seven times the year-earlier figure and above the 76.7 trillion won LSEG SmartEstimate, as AI infrastructure demand pushed memory prices higher and revenue rose 328%. The Nvidia supplier announced about 100 trillion won ($75.4 billion) in shareholder returns this year through dividends and buybacks, and said it expects demand to outstrip supply through 2030. Long-term agreements with 14 major customers already cover more than half of its 2027 and 2028 production capacity, the company said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: 'We're just stuck': Residents impacted by Provo mall redevelopment plan
item.description: Provo's approval of Brixton Capital's plan to redevelop Provo Towne Centre into roughly 1,300 apartments, 77 townhomes, retail space and open areas means residents of the neighboring Shady Acres mobile home park, which Brixton also owns, will have to move. The developer will give each household 18 months' notice and $10,000, but 79-year-old resident Kay Larsen said the nearest open spot they've found is in Price, where towing would cost $20,000. Councilman Jeff Whitlock called the park's fate the "hardest part" of his vote in favor, arguing the city negotiated better terms than residents would get if the owner simply evicted them.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Jury finds two men guilty of murder in 2022 shooting outside WinCo grocery store
item.description: A jury found Roy men Stafon Coleman Jr., 25, and Terrell Jones, 34, guilty of murder on Friday in the May 9, 2022, killing of Romeo Charles Stevens, 27, outside a South Salt Lake WinCo, rejecting self-defense claims but acquitting them of aggravated robbery after roughly 10 hours of deliberation. The weeklong trial featured testimony from two people who had already pleaded guilty to manslaughter and aggravated robbery in the case: Coleman's brother Damian Coleman, who described a plan to collect a debt from Stevens, and McKennalyn Cummins, who denied knowing of any plan to rob him. Sentencing is set for Jan. 4, and Stafon Coleman's attorney has already sought a new trial, arguing the verdict form's "Not guilty beyond a reasonable doubt" option wrongly shifted the burden of proof to the defense.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Halloween candy sales off to slow start amid high chocolate prices and affordability concerns
item.description: Halloween candy sales fell 6.7% in the month ending Oct. 17 compared with a year earlier, according to NielsenIQ, whose Chris Costagli said consumers squeezed by gas, housing and food costs simply can't afford treats this year, with only small bags growing. Candy and gum prices rose 44% over five years through September, compared with 22.5% for groceries overall, driven largely by cocoa prices that hit a record in January 2025 and began rising again this spring after the Iran war disrupted fertilizer supplies. At Aldi, a 135-piece Mars variety pack now costs almost what a 250-piece pack did five years ago.
item.dc:creator: Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press

item.title: 'First Amendment right': Man plans to fight charge for placing sign identifying license-plate reader
item.description: David Belnap, 59, of West Haven, plans to fight a class C misdemeanor citation for tampering with a traffic-monitoring device after deputies arrested him Sunday in Marriott-Slaterville for attaching "Flock is watching you" signs to the poles of license-plate reader cameras. Belnap, who spent a night in jail, said he placed signs at nine cameras around Weber County without damaging them, calling it "a First Amendment right" to show people where the readers are. His supporters in Ogden Indivisible decried the arrest amid a broader Utah debate over automatic license plate readers, which police use to track suspects and missing people but critics see as an invasion of privacy.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Harvest a deer? Better get it checked for chronic wasting disease
