item.description: The Utah Division of Wildlife Resources is asking successful deer hunters on many hunting units to stop at check stations this fall so their animals can be tested for chronic wasting disease, a fatal nervous-system illness of deer, elk and moose that can't be detected by sight in its early stages. So far 435 mule deer and 11 elk have tested positive in Utah, mostly in the state's northeast and southeast, and the agency especially wants hunters to submit deer that were extremely thin, circling or salivating heavily.
item.dc:creator: Adam Eakle, KSL

item.title: Floodwaters recede near Bluff, but families and businesses face uncertain recovery
item.description: As San Juan River floodwaters recede around Bluff, residents and business owners face damaged homes and a recovery many fear they can't handle alone, while State Route 162 between Bluff and Montezuma Creek stayed closed Tuesday. Larena Benn, whose Navajo Nation home is filled with water and mud, is staying at a Bluff hotel and said her family needs flooring, drywall, firewood and hay for livestock, with Aneth Point Downs collecting donations. Melanie Kranz closed her Bluff Gardens cabin rentals and put employees out of work, calling the damage "devastating" and "almost like starting over, but worse."
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Visa results beat estimates as resilient customers keep up spending
item.description: Visa beat fourth-quarter expectations, earning an adjusted $3.48 a share versus $3.44 expected, as payments volume rose 9% and cross-border volumes excluding intra-Europe jumped 14% on strong travel demand. CFO Chris Suh said Visa "did not see signs of the lower spend consumer weakening," though client incentives climbed 21% to $5.1 billion and are set to grow further in fiscal 2027 as about a quarter of payment volumes come up for renewal. Shares slipped about 1.4% after hours on a fiscal 2027 outlook of low-double-digit to low-teens earnings-per-share growth.
item.dc:creator: Arasu Kannagi Basil and Atharva Singh, Reuters

item.title: Some Weber County voters received duplicate ballots, but clerk says count will remain accurate
item.description: A printer error put two ballots into as many as 167 envelopes mailed to Weber County voters, about 0.1% of the county's ballots, though Clerk/Auditor Ricky Hatch suspects far fewer than 100 voters actually got duplicates. Hatch said thickness-detecting machines, three election workers watching each envelope opened, and reconciliation of ballot counts against vote histories keep any ballot from being counted twice, and none of the five duplicates returned so far was counted. "In every election, problems happen," he said, adding that catching this one early leaves time to fix it.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Fed expected to hold rates steady as Utahns continue to feel economic pressure
item.description: Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute economist Maddy Oritt expects the Federal Reserve to hold rates steady at this week's meeting, though an increase is possible in December. She said average U.S. mortgage rates above 7% for the past month are worsening Utah's already severe housing affordability problem, and that high inflation and uncertainty are keeping credit card and auto loan rates elevated as well, so "people don't feel good." Utah's economy still outperforms the nation's on many measures, including a steadier though slowing labor market, but Oritt warned, "We're not immune."
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Ancient armored bottom-feeder is first seagoing amphibian
item.description: Scientists have identified Gerrothorax maritimus, a roughly 30-inch, disc-shaped armored amphibian found in 237-million-year-old ocean sediments in China's Guizhou Province, as the first known amphibian to live fully in the sea. Because amphibians breathe and take in water through permeable skin that seawater would dehydrate, fewer than 2% of the more than 8,000 living species tolerate salt and none are marine, which makes the find notable, said UC Davis paleobiologist Ryosuke Motani, a study leader. Peking University coauthor Da-yong Jiang described the creature, which lived alongside predatory ichthyosaurs, as "a suction feeder that lived on a muddy to silty seafloor."
item.dc:creator: Will Dunham, Reuters

item.title: More than 2,000 shirts, countless stories: UVU exhibit gives survivors of violence a voice
item.description: Utah Valley University's Center for Social Impact is displaying its Clothesline Project in a campus ballroom for Domestic Violence Awareness Month, hanging hundreds of the roughly 2,000 T-shirts survivors and grieving loved ones have decorated since the university began hosting it in 1998. The shirts range from graphic accounts of abuse and assault to messages of healing, and visitors can make their own for a separate section of the exhibit. Program director Jennie Jasperson said the display shows that "these are local stories" from people in Utah's own community.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: 12-week trial scheduled in 2028 for man accused of killing Tremonton officers
item.description: 1st District Judge Spencer D. Walsh has scheduled a 12-week trial running May 15 to Aug. 4, 2028, for Ryan Michael Bate, 34, who faces the death penalty on two counts of aggravated murder in the Aug. 17, 2025, shooting deaths of Tremonton-Garland officer Eric Estrada and Sgt. Lee Sorensen during a domestic violence call. Bate's attorneys have moved to quash the bind-over on half of the 18 charges, arguing that a recorded interview of his former wife with Weber County investigators was inadmissible because her words are mixed with "the interwoven speech of four people." Prosecutors must respond by Nov. 30, and oral arguments are set for Jan. 22.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Logitech beats profit forecast as sales of gaming, conferencing products rise
item.description: Logitech reported second-quarter non-GAAP operating income of $231 million, beating the $204 million analyst consensus and its own guidance, as sales rose 3% to $1.22 billion on demand for gaming and video conferencing gear. CEO Hanneke Faber said its mice and keyboards grew by mid single digits even as global PC shipments fell 20%, and that video collaboration demand, up 12%, is "not discretionary" as employers bring staff back to offices. The company cut its estimate of lost sales from a semiconductor supplier's factory closure to $70 million to $80 million, from up to $200 million, but forecast lower year-over-year operating income for the December quarter because of higher component and transport costs.
item.dc:creator: John Revill, Reuters

item.title: Exit polls show a rebuke of Netanyahu but no clear winner in Israel's election
item.description: Exit polls from Israel's first national election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack showed voters rebuking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, giving his bloc about 50 seats to 52-53 for the opposition and 17-18 for Arab parties. Rival Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief, cited a "lack of confidence" in Netanyahu, but forming a replacement government may require an alliance with Arab-led parties that could split the opposition, setting up weeks of jockeying or even another election early next year. Turnout topped 74% by 8 p.m., the highest at that hour in decades, in a race seen as a referendum on Netanyahu's nearly unbroken 17-year rule.
item.dc:creator: Tia Goldenberg and Cara Anna, Associated Press

item.title: US and Cuban officials engage in shouting match during UN debate over economic embargo
item.description: Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez walked to the front of the U.N. General Assembly and shouted "You are a liar!" at U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz on Tuesday as Waltz urged members to oppose the annual resolution condemning the decades-old U.S. embargo on Cuba. The clash, which Waltz answered by telling Rodríguez to back up, reflects rising tensions as the Trump administration tightens economic pressure, including tariff threats on any country that supplies Cuba with oil that have effectively cut off fuel and caused widespread blackouts. The resolution has drawn overwhelming support for 34 years, passing 165-7 last year with 12 abstentions.
item.dc:creator: Farnoush Amiri, Associated Press

item.title: Salt Lake City's 12-year airport project is over. What happens next?
item.description: Salt Lake City International Airport finished its $5.1 billion, 12-year buildout this week as the last construction phase opened at Concourse B, bringing the complex to 94 gates and more than 100 concession areas, completed ahead of schedule and under budget according to airport director Bill Wyatt. Planning began in the mid-1990s, but 9/11 and the 2008 financial crisis pushed construction back about 20 years, and the first gates opened in September 2020 during the pandemic. The next phase is already hinted at, including a blocked-off escalator between B41 and B46 that would let airlines, such as a new carrier testing the market, board passengers by bus and stairs without a jet bridge.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Judge hears arguments whether California should count 20,000 ballots disputed by feds
item.description: U.S. District Judge David O. Carter heard arguments Tuesday in the Justice Department's bid to stop California from counting the ballots of about 20,000 people it alleges are likely noncitizens until their citizenship is confirmed, a suit filed in mid-October amid the midterm election. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said the government has "not asked to void any ballots," while state and Los Angeles County lawyers questioned how the list was compiled and its reliance on a third-party Social Security number service. An attorney for the county registrar said separating the ballots by hand could not be done by Tuesday or even the December certification deadline, and a divided 9th Circuit panel had rebuffed the government's emergency request Monday.
item.dc:creator: Safiyah Riddle, Associated Press

item.title: Ted Bundy tied to 1974 Utah cold case homicide
item.description: Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates announced Tuesday, 52 years to the day after hunters found her body, that Ted Bundy has been officially linked to the 1974 killing of 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith, closing a case that was long suspected but never solved. Investigators said DNA evidence gathered for the earlier-confirmed case of Laura Ann Aime, who vanished after a Lehi Halloween party that same year, helped bring the closure, and Summit County attorney Margaret Olsen said the evidence "establishes that Ted Bundy is responsible." Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera said agencies pursue such decades-old cases because "We owe that to the families of these cold cases."
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: AP sources: Federal agents search Beverly Hills mansion in investigation of ex-Rep. Eric Swalwell
item.description: Federal agents searched the Beverly Hills mansion of developer and donor Stephen Cloobeck on Tuesday as part of the investigation into former Rep. Eric Swalwell, who resigned from Congress in April amid sexual misconduct allegations and denies criminal wrongdoing, two people familiar with the probe told the AP. Swalwell had spent time at the home before resigning, and Cloobeck, the Diamond Resorts founder who has given his campaigns more than $23,000 since 2017, later said he had cut ties with him. The search escalates an inquiry in which agents in August seized Swalwell's devices at the San Francisco airport and searched his Washington home.
item.dc:creator: Eric Tucker and Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press

item.title: Man shot by police in West Valley City identified
item.description: West Valley City police on Tuesday identified the man fatally shot by an officer Sunday as Sebastian Cerda-Monti, 40, whose last known address was in South Salt Lake. Employees at a TownePlace Suites hotel had reported finding him in a storage building armed and threatening to shoot them; responding officers said he held a "large metal rod," and witnesses said he ran at them with two large metal objects after an officer used pepper spray. The officer is on administrative leave, and city spokesperson Roxeanne Vainuku said "officers have a responsibility to protect the safety of the people around them."
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake County to hold early voting for the 1st time on a Saturday — Halloween day
item.description: Salt Lake County will offer early in-person voting on a Saturday for the first time this Halloween, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the county government center's South Building, 2001 South State Street, Clerk Lannie Chapman announced. Early in-person voting began Oct. 20 and expanded to seven additional sites Tuesday, while voters can also return by-mail ballots by post or at drop boxes ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The clerk's office asked Saturday voters to bring valid ID and said "costumes that cover the face should be left at home."
item.dc:creator: Katie McKeller, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Iron County approves zoning changes allowing large-scale developments amid tribal opposition
item.description: The Iron County Commission on Monday adopted a zone overlay ordinance that could open the door to large data centers and energy projects, and lifted its moratorium on data center applications nearly a month early, over objections from the Paiute Indian Tribe of Utah. Tribal chairwoman Laurel Yellowhorse said the county stripped language guaranteeing the tribe time to comment and meaningful government-to-government consultation, calling that omission "egregious." Indian Peaks Band council member Tamra Borchardt-Slayton stressed that the tribe is a sovereign government, not "merely another stakeholder," with ancestral ties to the land.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Local AI expert weighs in as Musk offers dim forecast for neocloud companies
item.description: After announcing that SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs, Elon Musk warned on X that tightening debt markets mean the 200-plus neocloud companies building AI data centers face "guppy-level death and consolidation." Kevin Williams, CEO of the AI consulting firm AscendAI, told KSL that soaring AI demand doesn't make data center business models sound and that scarce capital could slow development. In Utah, he said, power may be the bigger constraint, since "the timeline to build a data center is shorter than the timeline to build a power plant."
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Can't find your estrogen patch? Here's why and what you can do
item.description: Estradiol patches have become hard to find at Utah pharmacies, with use among PEHP members up 167% in two years and one pharmacist telling KSL the product had been on back order since May. University of Utah pharmacy officer Erin Fox traces the surge to the FDA's November 2025 removal of the "black box warning" on estrogen products, which made patients and doctors more comfortable with hormone therapy, and says she considers it a shortage even though the FDA has not formally declared one. Davis County patient Hansen, who said the patch made her "feel fantastic," found a refill only after calling around to a third pharmacy.
item.dc:creator: Mindy Dunyon, KSL

item.title: Massive rock fall closes Bridal Veil Falls trail until at least spring
item.description: A rockfall with car-sized boulders crashed down near Bridal Veil Falls on Friday, narrowly missing visitors and damaging pavement on the Provo Canyon Trail, which Utah County has closed until repairs are done, likely in late spring or early summer. Bailee Hamilton, whose video of the slide spread online, said it felt like being in "Jurassic Park" or "Indiana Jones" and insisted the footage was not AI. Utah County Public Works director Richard Nielson said slides that large are rare, the last about 20 years ago, and North Fork Fire Chief Dave Marsella warned rocks, trees and brush are still coming down.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: 18-year-old sentenced to jail for assault with a hammer, but judge said crime was 'worthy of prison'
item.description: 4th District Judge Derek Pullan sentenced 18-year-old Kayden Paul Gauger of American Fork to a full year in jail and three years of probation for hitting Ethan Garcia in the face with a hammer in June, suspending a zero-to-five-year prison term even though he called the attack "a crime worthy of prison." Garcia described lasting disfigurement, constant pain, memory problems and medical bills well over $50,000, and prosecutors sought prison, while the defense called it a crime of passion after Gauger was told Garcia had assaulted his girlfriend, an allegation Garcia denies. The judge warned Gauger he would be on "a very short leash" and urged him to pay restitution quickly.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Wall Street banks, Blackstone line up $63 billion to finance Broadcom AI chips for Anthropic
item.description: Bank of America, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley are arranging first-lien loans of about $43.5 billion and Blackstone is committing second-lien debt in a $63 billion package to buy Broadcom AI accelerators and networking gear for Anthropic, one of the largest debt deals of the AI buildout. A new special purpose vehicle will buy the hardware and lease it to the Claude maker, with deliveries starting in 2027 and Broadcom providing "residual value support" to lenders. The deal landed the same day Anthropic filed for its IPO, and Moody's warned Broadcom's risk would rise if it backs several such financings in quick succession.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Soni, Prakhar Srivastava and Saeed Azhar, Reuters

item.title: Groundbreaking announced for Lehi temple
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will break ground Dec. 5 on the roughly 85,000-square-foot Lehi Utah Temple, with Elder John A. McCune of the Utah Area Presidency presiding. The temple, announced by the late President Russell M. Nelson in April 2024, will share a 22.48-acre site in Lehi's foothills at 3950 North and Center Street with a new meetinghouse. Utah has 24 operating temples and eight more announced, under construction or being renovated, including the Salt Lake Temple, which reopens next year.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: JetBlue seeks to reassure investors as losses deepen
item.description: JetBlue posted an adjusted third-quarter loss of 60 cents a share, wider than analysts expected, as fuel costs rose 57% to about $3.91 a gallon, while insisting it has enough liquidity for at least the next 12 months. Its shares, down 48% this year, rebounded 11% after hours following a near-10% drop on a report that creditors were consulting restructuring advisers amid a selloff that halved the price of its loyalty-backed TrueBlue bonds. The airline raised its seat revenue growth forecast on higher fares and Fort Lauderdale expansion, but its nine-month cash burn of $273 million nearly doubled from a year earlier.
item.dc:creator: Doyinsola Oladipo and Nandan Mandayam, Reuters

item.title: Salt Lake City cracked down on unruly parties a year ago. Here's what happened next
item.description: A year after Salt Lake City replaced a $428 service fee for loud parties with a $1,000 fine on the property owner, the city has sent 156 warning letters, more than half in the East Central neighborhood near the University of Utah, but just 26 properties have been fined for repeat violations. Only one property, a private lounge hosting after-hours parties, was fined twice, and police detective Marie Stewart credited warning letters, education and landlords who added eviction clauses to leases, saying "The warnings have been incredibly effective." City officials are weighing tweaks such as extending the 365-day window, and Councilwoman Jennifer Napier-Pearce said the city is not there yet but getting closer.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: US Marine indicted over alleged murder of woman in Okinawa
item.description: Japanese prosecutors have indicted Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine, on suspicion of strangling 39-year-old Anna Yagi with a phone cord in a Naha hotel and stealing her backpack, according to NHK and other Japanese media. The case has renewed outrage over U.S. troop conduct in Okinawa, home to about 30,000 U.S. troops and their families, with Gov. Genta Koja calling military discipline efforts "completely ineffective" and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi lodging a protest with Washington. U.S. forces imposed a monthlong curfew after Ballard's arrest, and the III Marine Expeditionary Force says it is cooperating with Japanese authorities.
item.dc:creator: Lex Harvey, Yumi Asada, CNN

item.title: Get a taste of Greece at historic Pocatello church's Fall Fest
item.description: Pocatello's Assumption Greek Orthodox Church, built in 1915 and among the oldest Greek Orthodox churches in America, will hold its Greek Gyro & Greek Pastry Fall Fest on Saturday, Nov. 7, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. in its social hall. The scaled-back counterpart to the parish's August Greek Festival offers gyros plus baklava, kourabiethes and koulourakia, with proceeds benefiting local nonprofits. The parish recently marked the 50th anniversary of Father Constantine Zozos' ordination, and he invited the community to "a delicious afternoon of Greek food and fellowship."
item.dc:creator: Rett Nelson, EastIdahoNews

item.title: Shriners of Salt Lake City makes Halloween memorable for kids in wheelchairs
item.description: Shriners Children's Hospital in Salt Lake City held its annual wheelchair Halloween costume clinic, where five volunteer "pit crews" built more than 20 costumes that incorporate kids' wheelchairs, including Zeus, Sourdough Sam and a Savannah Bananas player on a motorcycle. Marketing director Raegan Holbrook said parents reported their kids felt left out of door-to-door trick-or-treating, and the hospital wants to meet patients' emotional and social needs as well as physical ones. Clarisa Johnston, whose 9-year-old son Jackson took home the motorcycle, said the hardest part each year is getting the costume to fit in her car.
item.dc:creator: Paige Zamora, KSL

item.title: Bridge demolition underway on I-215 as UDOT project reaches 60% completion
item.description: UDOT's project to rebuild the west side of I-215 is about 60% complete, with crews demolishing aging bridge decks damaged by water, road salt and freeze-thaw cycles, Commissioner Carlos Braceras said. Bridges will get a new sealant to keep water out, and the old concrete pavement is being broken into rubble for a base and covered with an asphalt mix that can go down in one thick layer, halving paving time. The work is expected to wrap up in summer 2027.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Meta eyes record $95 billion equity raise to fund AI expansion
item.description: Meta Platforms plans to raise up to $95 billion in its largest-ever equity offering, about $35 billion in common and preferred stock now plus an at-the-market program of up to $60 billion after its new nonvoting Class C shares begin trading, to fund its AI infrastructure buildout. Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom have shown interest in buying up to $5 billion of the shares, feeding concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, and Meta posted its first negative free cash flow in over a decade last quarter. William Blair analysts said they expect investors "to continue to question the financing," though they believe Meta will eventually build a profitable AI business.
item.dc:creator: Jaspreet Singh, Reuters

item.title: Utah mom launches gratitude campaign with goal of 10,000 thank-you cards
item.description: Park City mountaineer and two-time Guinness World Records holder Jenn Drummond is aiming for 10,000 thank-you cards by the end of November, inviting Utahns to write notes to coaches, teachers and friends and log them through her Somedays app. The mother of seven said she was inspired by the death of her climbing mentor Todd Passey in a ski accident before she could thank him, and that if they reach the goal, "Todd is going to be able to feel it up in heaven." Card-writing parties in Salt Lake City and Park City produced close to 700 cards by midday Monday.
item.dc:creator: Allison Lyons, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake County clerk reminds voters of key deadlines as early voting begins
item.description: With early voting underway, Salt Lake County Clerk Lannie Chapman reminded voters that Tuesday is the last day to request a mailed replacement ballot and that Utah is no longer a postmark state, so mail ballots must reach the clerk by 8 p.m. on election night. She urged voters still holding ballots to use drop boxes and sent anyone missing a ballot to an early voting center, noting her office has handled 60 new voting laws since 2020. Calling voting "our superpower," Chapman stressed local races, which she said can be decided "by less than five votes."
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Man, woman who helped suspected immigrant escape authorities face 4 days in jail
item.description: George Sanchez-Juarez, 22, and Kelzie Ryann Luna, 21, each pleaded guilty to a federal misdemeanor and will serve four days in jail, pay $600 fines and split $28 in restitution for helping a handcuffed man flee a Customs and Border Protection operation at a Salt Lake City Home Depot in October 2025 and then cutting off his cuffs with bolt cutters. Prosecutor Todd Christopher Bouton argued the couple, who had no criminal records and expressed regret, should face jail because they "bragged about their crime online" and the case is about the line between protest and interfering with federal agents. Bouton said the man they helped likely remains at large, and the pair also face six months of supervised release.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Man sentenced to 59 years for murder of his Utah wife in Alaska
item.description: An Alaska judge sentenced former Army soldier Zarrius Hildabrand to 59 years in prison for the August 2023 second-degree murder of his wife, Saria Hildabrand, a fellow soldier originally from Mt. Pleasant, and for hiding her body in a storm drain. Testimony showed he bought cleaning supplies, moved her body in a trash can and then joined the search for her; prosecutors said phone evidence suggested she had confronted him about infidelity after celebrating his 21st birthday. Judge Peter Ramgren cited the "abhorrent nature" of his conduct after the killing and found for sentencing purposes that he acted intentionally.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Microsoft offers a quarter of its global workforce voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
item.description: Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees in the U.S., Canada, India and the U.K., about 27% of its roughly 223,000-person workforce, as it pours money into artificial intelligence. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman wrote that the offer "is new for us" and the company will learn from it, while continuing to help workers build skills and move into new roles. The move follows 4,800 job cuts in July and comes days before Microsoft's quarterly results, as data center spending likely tops $700 billion industry-wide this year.
item.dc:creator: Michelle Chapman, Associated Press

item.title: Trump administration's firing of prosecutor Maurene Comey was unlawful, judge rules
item.description: U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman ruled that the Trump administration unlawfully fired Maurene Comey, the Manhattan federal prosecutor and daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, who had alleged she was dismissed in July 2025 because of who her father is. Rejecting the Justice Department's argument that such prosecutors can be removed without cause, Furman wrote that accepting it "would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this nation's constitutional system," and ordered her retroactively reinstated through December 2025 for back pay and retirement benefits. The department said it will appeal once Furman rules on a remaining claim; Comey, who prosecuted Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean Combs, joined Patterson Belknap Webb & Tyler in February.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen, Reuters

item.title: Iran hosts Saudi Arabia and regional powers as fears grow of return to war
item.description: Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani military chief Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin met Iranian leaders including President Masoud Pezeshkian in Tehran on Monday, the first high-level Saudi-Iranian contact since Houthi attacks on Saudi targets escalated last month. The talks come amid speculation that President Donald Trump could order new strikes on Iran after the midterms, and Saudi Arabia said it hoped to keep negotiation channels open and support Qatari and Pakistani mediation. International Crisis Group analyst Hamidreza Azizi said the meeting looks more like "a last-minute attempt to prevent the resumption of war than the beginning of a new diplomatic process."
item.dc:creator: Mostafa Salem, CNN

item.title: Final exhibit to mark end of an era for Utah Museum of Contemporary Art
item.description: The Utah Museum of Contemporary Art is preparing to leave the downtown Salt Lake City building it has used since 1979, with demolition set for July 2027 and a new, above-ground home due in 2031 as part of the city's downtown overhaul. Executive director Laura Allred Hurtado said the current building's 1970s sunken design "really made the building invisible," while the new one will have natural light and a more recognizable profile. The museum is taking submissions for a final exhibit, "So Long," from local artists and anyone with ties to the old building, and the work will be buried in the rubble.
item.dc:creator: Cameron Elliott, KSL

item.title: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Peltola asks judge to toss lawsuit over certification
item.description: Lawyers for Democrat Mary Peltola's Alaska Senate campaign asked a federal judge to dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Nov. 3 results if Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses. The suit claims a second Republican candidate with a near-identical name, Dan J. Sullivan Jr., could confuse voters, which Peltola's lawyers called "wholly baseless" federal interference in an election process the Constitution leaves to states. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Trump is not trying to take over a state election, while election law experts said the suit lacks merit.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen, Reuters

item.title: Weber County man arrested after allegedly placing signage identifying license plate readers
item.description: Weber County deputies arrested David Belnap of West Haven after a resident reported him on a ladder hanging a "Flock is watching you" sign on a license plate reader in Marriott-Slaterville, booking him on suspicion of tampering with a traffic-monitoring device before releasing him Monday. Peggy Kluthe of Indivisible Ogden, whose web address was on the signs, argued surveillance camera locations should be public and organized a protest, while Sheriff Ryan Arbon said the readers' locations are already public. The arrest adds to Utah's debate over automatic license plate readers, which police credit with finding suspects and missing people and critics call an invasion of privacy.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Serbia's political veteran Vucic outplayed all opponents. Then came the students
item.description: Aleksandar Vucic, who dominated Serbian politics for 14 years, conceded Sunday that his Serbian Progressive Party lost a parliamentary election to a university student movement that had protested for nearly two years after a 2024 train station canopy collapse killed 16 people. Having resigned the presidency to seek the premiership and campaigning with cash handouts and favorable state media coverage, Vucic blamed foreign interference, including what he called "the deep American state." The AP traces his arc from 1990s ultranationalist to a leader balancing the EU, Russia and Trump, whom Belgrade political scientist Dejan Pavlovic described as running a "textbook regime" of autocracy.
item.dc:creator: Jovana Gec, Associated Press

item.title: Pending U.S. home sales hit a new low, fewer homes under contract in Utah
item.description: Redfin reports U.S. pending home sales hit their lowest level since it began tracking in 2021, at 281,749 for the four weeks ending Oct. 18, down 14.4% from a year earlier. Utah followed suit: Salt Lake Board of Realtors data showed 719 Salt Lake County homes under contract, down 16%, and 3,191 statewide, down 18%. National Association of Realtors chief economist Lawrence Yun blamed "fast-rising mortgage rates," which have climbed since the war with Iran began, with Freddie Mac's 30-year average at 7.32%.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Utahns should watch out for deer on the roads as nights grow longer, DWR says
item.description: Utah's Division of Wildlife Resources is warning drivers that deer collisions peak in November, when migration and mating season put more animals on roads just as daylight saving time ends Nov. 1. Migration initiative coordinator Makeda Hanson urged drivers to use high beams, scan for eyeshine and slow down without swerving, and asked Utahns to report roadkill through an app to help place wildlife crossings. More than 3,700 animals have been hit and removed from Utah roads this year as of Oct. 8, and the state has built more than 60 wildlife crossings.
item.dc:creator: Annie Knox, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Empty desks: Headcounts are down at several Utah colleges — but what about K-12 schools?
item.description: Utah public K-12 enrollment fell 2.4% to 640,471 students for 2026-27, the steepest one-year drop since at least 2014, according to Utah State Board of Education data, a trend that pressures school funding tied to headcounts. Charter schools bucked the decline, growing 2.3% to 87,161 students, while 12th-grade enrollment fell for the first time in that span, as falling birth rates and growth in homeschooling and private schooling, aided by the Utah Fits All Scholarship Program, shrink district rolls. Higher education headcounts rose 0.8% overall, with Utah State University up 8.2%, Utah Valley University dipping and technical colleges such as Tooele Technical College posting gains.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: New market space, restaurant part of plan for new history-themed Salt Lake City trail
item.description: Pioneer Trail Foundation board chairman Ryan Beck told a Utah Legislature appropriations subcommittee that the $15 million first phase of the history-themed Pioneer Trail, now under construction on State Street below the Capitol, also aims to bring new life to historic buildings along the route. Plans include a ground-floor restaurant at Council Hall from Arlo chef-owner Milo Carrier, an upstairs debate hall and history bookstore, and a vendor market plaza for summer and Christmas markets, with the bulk of work targeted before the Salt Lake Temple reopens. Modeled on Boston's Freedom Trail, the route will eventually begin at Abravanel Hall and run past Temple Square, backed by $10 million in state money and $5 million in "catalytic funding" from the This is the Place Foundation.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Evacuation notice lifted for Bluff residents in San Juan County
item.description: San Juan County lifted Bluff's evacuation order at 5 a.m. Monday, letting residents return after rising San Juan River floodwaters forced evacuations there and in the Navajo Nation communities of Montezuma Creek and Aneth over the weekend. The county said several properties on Bluff's east side remained flooded and warned that river water may be contaminated with sewage. It urged donations to the Bluff Community Foundation Relief Fund to help flood-affected residents.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Where Salt Lake City, Delta Center and Jazz Bear rank among NBA fans
item.description: USA Today's 2026 Sports Readers Choice Awards put the Utah Jazz in the NBA top 10 in four of five fan-voted categories: arena, arena food, city and mascot. The publication praised the Delta Center's upgrades for Jazz and Mammoth fans, concession options like Proper Burger and J Dawgs, and Jazz Bear, a five-time NBA Mascot of the Year since debuting in 1994. Oklahoma City dominated the rankings, placing first for city, arena and mascot and second for food.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: SpaceX enters $40 billion deal with Apollo for AI chip financing
item.description: SpaceX said an Apollo Global Management affiliate will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the company in a deal with total principal payments of about $40 billion, with leases running a little over five years. The leases are expected to begin in the first half of 2027 once chips arrive, and Elon Musk said on X the financing would not be "a major factor this quarter." The deal underscores SpaceX's heavy spending to tap demand for computing power, with CFO Bret Johnsen still projecting $35 billion to $40 billion in fourth-quarter capital expenditure.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Antelope Island bison roundup brings together family tradition and herd health
item.description: Hundreds of riders on horseback joined Saturday's annual bison roundup at Antelope Island State Park, a tradition volunteers like John Parke say they enjoy passing on to their children. Utah State Parks spokesperson Ally O'Rullian called it "a tool to help ensure the health of the herd and the island at large," since corralled bison get vaccinations and pregnancy checks, and the island can support only about 500 to 550 animals. The public can watch the "Working of the Bison" Oct. 27-29, ahead of a Nov. 3 auction that keeps the herd in balance with the habitat.
item.dc:creator: Alex Cabrero, KSL

item.title: Thousands gather for Dragonsteel's first in-person Light Day Market
item.description: Thousands of Brandon Sanderson fans turned out in Pleasant Grove on Saturday for Dragonsteel's first in-person Light Day Market, the company's discount event created as a Black Friday alternative so employees can spend more holiday time with family. Visitors shopped markdowns and took 20-minute tours of the warehouse and creative department, which operations vice president Matt Hatch said let them "see where the magic happens." First-in-line fan David Finley, there since 7:30 a.m., was after illustrated leather-bound editions and the new Mistborn jacket.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: Some US transit systems weigh whether to run trains without a human at the controls
item.description: Washington's Metro has backed a nearly $1 billion Red Line upgrade that could run trains with no one in the cab as early as 2033, and Los Angeles is studying a fully automated subway under the Santa Monica Mountains, joining Honolulu's driverless Skyline. The Reason Foundation's Baruch Feigenbaum says U.S. transit is "where innovation goes to die," while Transport Workers Union president John Samuelsen calls automation "a catastrophe waiting to happen." Metro CEO Randy Clarke acknowledged the deadly 2009 Fort Totten crash, blamed on signaling maintenance, stalled automation for years, though Honolulu reports no automation-related crash or injury.
item.dc:creator: Jeff Mcmurray, Associated Press

item.title: For Dallas Jenkins, the end of 'The Chosen' brings relief and gratitude
item.description: Dallas Jenkins told viewers in a Sunday livestream that wrapping "The Chosen" in late September, after 527 days of filming over seven seasons, brought relief and "immense gratitude." The final season, shot over 90 days in Utah and Texas, was the series' longest and hottest, and Jenkins credited donations to Come and See with financing the show. Editing on Season 7 is underway, and spinoffs including "Joseph of Egypt" and "Book of Moses" are planned for a franchise now translated into 125 languages.
item.dc:creator: Margaret Darby, Deseret News

item.title: How to catch the Hunter's Moon this weekend — and maybe Saturn, too
item.description: October's full moon, the Hunter's Moon, rises early this weekend and peaks at 12:12 a.m. ET on Monday, Oct. 26, with Saturn sitting a few degrees south of it on Sunday night, though the bright moon may wash out the planet. NASA's Noah Petro, a project scientist for Artemis III, said color differences on the moon's face reveal its "geological history," and that viewers need only "clear eyes and clear skies." From Monday to Wednesday the moon will pass in front of the Pleiades, and 2026's last two full moons will be supermoons.
item.dc:creator: Dharma Niles, CNN

item.title: Utah business, government leaders deepen connections in Ireland
item.description: Gov. Spencer Cox led a World Trade Center Utah and Governor's Office of Economic Development trade mission to Ireland this week, meeting Prime Minister Micheál Martin and U.S. Ambassador Edward Walsh alongside tech, life sciences, energy and quantum firms. Cox argued that with wars and trade wars straining U.S.-Europe ties, "subnational relationships matter more than they maybe ever have," a view echoed by World Trade Center Utah chairman Jeff Flake. Utah companies already operating there, such as Merit Medical with more than a thousand employees since its first Irish plant opened in 1993, describe the country as their gateway to Europe.
item.dc:creator: Suzanne Bates, Deseret News

item.title: International Pez Museum of Erda celebrates 30 years of collecting
item.description: Brent Beazer's International Pez Museum in Erda, more than 3,000 dispensers housed in a building his family designed into its 2021 home, has marked 30 years since a young man in his Arizona ward gave him a Sylvester the Cat dispenser. "Once you have three of anything, you have a collection," Beazer said, recalling the matching set his wife gave him on Valentine's Day. Beazer, who traces Pez to a 1927 Austrian peppermint marketed as an alternative to smoking, offers free tours and calls the hobby fun rather than his "sole focus."
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Navajo Nation communities ordered to evacuate due to potential flooding
item.description: The Navajo Nation Department of Emergency Management issued a late-Saturday evacuation notice for Bluff, Montezuma Creek and Aneth as the rising San Juan River threatened major flooding, with about 150 people from Montezuma Creek and Aneth expected to leave overnight. The National Weather Service expects major flooding Sunday into Monday in those communities as well as Mexican Hat, Halchita and Tselakai Dezza. Shelters opened at Aneth Community School and San Juan High School in Blanding, and Navajo police, who asked people to keep drones away, warned evacuees: "Be prepared to be away from your home for multiple days."
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Almost all coral reef ecosystems face risk of collapse in 50 years, study warns
item.description: The International Union for Conservation of Nature's first global Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems finds 96% of shallow-water reef systems critically endangered and at risk of collapse by 2075, chiefly from ocean warming. Famous systems including the Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle and the Red Sea reefs carry the highest threat level, and a collapsed reef loses its hard corals to algae, rubble and sponges. Scientific lead Mishal Gudka called the findings "a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," citing reefs' ability to recover from bleaching.
item.dc:creator: Michael Casey, Associated Press

item.title: Second oldest congregation in Utah continues to serve Salt Lake City
item.description: Salt Lake City's First Congregational Church, founded in 1865 as Utah's first congregation outside The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, has outlived three homes: Independence Hall on Main Street, a sandstone building nicknamed the Stone Church, and a 1965 building on Foothill Drive. The congregation sold the Foothill building to Crossroads Urban Center for $500,000 in 2022 and now rents space from All Saints Episcopal Church, while its "Road to Emmaus" stained-glass window went to the Church of Jesus Christ for a temple. Rev. Doug Gray said the church "could have folded" like many others, but members decided they were "not done with the adventure that God called us to."
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Man dies after being shot by police outside of West Valley City hotel, police say
item.description: A man died Sunday morning after a West Valley City police officer shot him outside the TownePlace Suites hotel on High Market Drive, where employees had reported a man in a storage building threatening to shoot them. Officers said the man held a "large metal rod," and city deputy communications director Roxeanne Vainuku said the officer used pepper spray moments before shots were fired, with witnesses saying the man ran at officers with two large metal objects. West Jordan police are investigating, and the officer is on administrative leave.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: A First Nation community in Canada is using a data center to preserve its heritage
item.description: The Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory on Ontario's Manitoulin Island has installed a garage-sized data center, believed to be the only one on Indigenous territory in Canada, to hold everything from recordings of Anishinaabe language speakers to health records, moving its data off a Microsoft facility in Toronto. Chief Tim Ominika framed the project as "ownership, access, control and possession of our information," and a 2022 flood that wiped out some scattered digital records added urgency. The data center also underpins 700 surveillance cameras and a fleet of DJI drones, which drew some privacy pushback from residents.
item.dc:creator: Kelvin Chan, Associated Press

item.title: Trump announces Audi will build $4B factory in Georgia
item.description: President Donald Trump announced at a rally in Perry, Georgia, that Audi will build its first U.S. assembly plant there, a $4 billion factory expected to produce 200,000 SUVs a year and about 4,500 jobs, with production starting in the early 2030s. The Volkswagen brand, which imports all its U.S. vehicles from Europe or Mexico, took a $1.4 billion hit from Trump's tariffs last year, and its U.S. sales are down 16% this year. Trump is touting the deal ahead of competitive Nov. 3 Senate and governor races in Georgia, while critics say his auto tariffs have pushed up vehicle prices.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson and David Shepardson, Reuters

item.title: In Europe, budget airlines thrive. Why not the US?
item.description: CNN examines why low-cost carriers such as Ryanair, which flew more than 200 million passengers last year, dominate short-haul flying in Europe while Frontier, the largest U.S. budget airline, flew just 33 million. Former Wizz Air executive Garth Lund and consultant Mike Arnot point to European airlines' relentless cost control, 25- to 30-minute turnarounds, plentiful secondary airports and looser crew-hour limits, along with an American stigma toward no-frills flying. With Spirit Airlines collapsing this year and legacy carriers fending off rivals through basic economy fares, five U.S. low-cost airlines remain.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Skores, CNN

item.title: Pope's lung cancer is a reminder that nonsmokers can be at risk. What to know
item.description: Intermountain Health thoracic surgeon Dr. John Stringham used Pope Leo XIV's early-stage lung adenocarcinoma, removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung, to stress that 15% to 20% of lung cancers occur in people who never smoked. Beyond smoking, he pointed to radon in basements, secondhand smoke, workplace dust and solvents, and Wasatch Front pollution as risks, and noted the disease is often "quite asymptomatic" until it is advanced. Annual low-dose CT screening is recommended only for adults 50-80 with a "20 pack-year" smoking history, while cancers caught early carry an estimated 80% to 90% five-year cancer-specific survival rate.
item.dc:creator: Lois M. Collins, Deseret News

item.title: Salt Lake City International Airport celebrates end of construction
item.description: Salt Lake City International Airport's 12-year, $5.1 billion rebuild is finished, with leaders celebrating Saturday ahead of a Tuesday ribbon-cutting for the last section of Concourse B, which adds 132,000 square feet and seven gates mostly for United Airlines. Officials stressed the project, which broke ground in July 2014 and opened its new terminal during the pandemic, was paid for with federal grants and user fees rather than local taxes. Mayor Erin Mendenhall called the airport "our gateway to the world," and officials tied the completion to next year's Salt Lake Temple open house and the 2034 Winter Olympics.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake City Christmas tradition ends after 30 years as owner faces health challenges
item.description: Forrest Nunley, whose hillside Christmas light display in Salt Lake City's Avenues drew families for more than 30 years, is ending the tradition after a Parkinson's diagnosis five years ago and a cancer fight left him unable to put it up. Nunley, who now lives on a farm in Moab, sold more than 300 decorations at a Saturday yard sale while keeping about 100 for family. "It was probably the hardest thing I had to do," he said, adding that buyers will now "take a little piece of us with them."
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Friends remember Park City pilot Ryan Cutter
item.description: Friends and co-workers gathered in Park City on Saturday, with bagpipes and helicopters overhead, to remember Ryan Cutter, the 46-year-old helicopter pilot killed in late September when his aircraft went down fighting the Dome Fire in Yosemite National Park. Speakers described a backcountry skier and base jumper who never put his crew at risk, and his friend Adam called him "the most loyal person I've ever met in my life." Co-worker Chad Walker said the one thing Cutter did better than flying was being his friend, always checking in on him.
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: 'We need help': Homeless cleanup nonprofit furloughs employees, faces full shutdown
item.description: Advantage Services, a Salt Lake City nonprofit that since 1992 has employed people experiencing homelessness or leaving jail and prison to clean encampments, pick up trash and shuttle shelter residents, furloughed 110 of its roughly 125 workers on Oct. 12 after missing payroll. CEO Rob Ferris says it needs about $750,000 by Nov. 1 or will shut down or merge, after its largest Salt Lake City contract was cut roughly in half. Utah Homeless Services Board chair Randy Shumway warned "we're going to pay for it in spades," and Shelter the Homeless said losing the nonprofit's vans and drivers would threaten transportation to and from shelters.
item.dc:creator: Katie McKellar, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: NTSB reveals what caused 2025 fatal helicopter crash near Ririe Reservoir in Idaho
item.description: The NTSB's final report on the Feb. 20, 2025, helicopter crash near Idaho's Ririe Reservoir that killed ATL Technology founder and CEO Bradford Brown of Alpine blames "the pilot's inadequate preflight planning" and low-altitude flying that brought the Bell 505 into power lines. Surviving passenger Steve Houghton told investigators the pair, out to film an elk herd, didn't see the poorly marked lower wires, about 160 feet up and lacking the orange marker balls on the higher lines, until they were directly ahead. The report says a sectional aeronautical chart showed the lines, though investigators couldn't determine whether Brown reviewed it.
item.dc:creator: Daniel V. Ramirez, East Idaho News

item.title: Utah's annual Reading Marathon begins with kickoff event to promote childhood literacy
item.description: More than 33,000 children logged 26 million minutes in last year's PBS Utah Reading Marathon, and the 34th edition, launched Saturday at the Salt Lake City Public Library, again asks kids to read or be read to for 600 minutes during November. The program is part of Gov. Spencer Cox's Utah Reads campaign, and PBS Utah education manager Annie Frazier said "the foundation of literacy and reading starts right at birth." Families at the kickoff met Daniel Tiger and Carl the Collector, and Frazier made a pitch for library cards as tools for empathy and school success.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Earnshaw, KSL

item.title: Nuclear power could more than triple by 2060, UN agency says
item.description: IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi told the U.N. General Assembly that nuclear power use could more than triple by 2060, driven by electrification, AI data centers and "technology companies' appetite for reliable, carbon-free power." He noted that more than 60 reactors are under construction and that the world's 400-plus operating reactors supplied 10% of global electricity in 2025. Grossi also urged a return to talks with Iran so inspectors can go back, said Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia plant remains "in a precarious position," and reported progress in resolving questions about Syria's past nuclear work.
item.dc:creator: Edith M. Lederer, Associated Press

item.title: Lula, Bolsonaro rally supporters on final day before Brazil presidential runoff
item.description: On the last day before Sunday's runoff, 80-year-old President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva marched on Copacabana beach and Sao Paulo's Paulista Avenue, while Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro rode with a motorcycle caravan in Minas Gerais and then campaigned in Rio de Janeiro. A CNT/MDA poll gave Bolsonaro a 1.3-point lead, and he led by about 5 points in first-round voting in Minas Gerais, a state no candidate has lost and still won the presidency since Brazil's return to democracy. Lula said voters "want to move forward," while Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, told supporters the vote would shape the country "for the next 30 or 40 years."
item.dc:creator: Fernando Cardoso, Sebastian Rocandio and Lais Morais, Reuters

item.title: A fire devastates the Eagle's Nest retreat built for Hitler in Germany. A suspect is detained
item.description: A fire Friday night badly damaged the Kehlsteinhaus, the Eagle's Nest retreat built for Hitler on a cliff above Berchtesgaden in the Bavarian Alps, and police arrested a 33-year-old German man on a motorcycle coming down the mountain road on suspicion of arson. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and was sent to a psychiatric facility but will also look at a possible political motive. Snow and wind forced firefighters to withdraw overnight, and Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann, whose state owns the building, which has operated as a cafe since 1952, pledged: "We're not going to leave a ruin there."
item.dc:creator: Geir Moulson, Associated Press

item.title: New maps reveal who could see more snow during this year's super El Niño
item.description: A CNN Weather analysis of January-March snowfall from 1959 to 2026 found that past El Niño winters usually brought above-average snow to a band from the Southwest and southern Rockies to the southern Plains, southern Appalachians and Mid-Atlantic, and less to the Pacific Northwest, northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes. NOAA forecaster Jon Gottschalck said this year's El Niño, likely one of the strongest on record, makes those patterns more likely but not necessarily bigger, and he described El Niño nor'easters as "very strong, energetic and they're very wet." The analysts caution that the maps describe historical tendencies, not a forecast, and a single storm can still swing a season, as the January 2016 blizzard did in New York during a warm winter.
item.dc:creator: Tyler Ory and Sam Hart, CNN

item.title: Houthis say they targeted Saudi oil sites; attacks reported in Aden
item.description: Yemen's Houthis said Saturday they attacked Saudi oil infrastructure, including an Aramco site in Yanbu, the Rabigh refinery and the East-West Pipeline, as well as airports in Riyadh and Dammam. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two missiles aimed at Yanbu and Taif, and Saudi Civil Defense reported missile debris falling in the Mecca and Medina regions, which the Houthis denied targeting. Yemen's government said Houthi missiles also hit coast guard sites in Aden, as fighting tied to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran breaks the 2022 U.N.-brokered truce.
item.dc:creator: Yasmine Ghania, Eman Abouhassira, Ahmed Tolba and Enas Alashery, Reuters

item.title: More than 400,000 protest across France, challenging Macron as Paris clashes erupt
item.description: The Interior Ministry counted about 410,000 people across France on Saturday, while the CGT union estimated nearly 800,000, in more than a month of protests that began over staffing at one high school and grew to cover school funding and the cost of living. Clashes broke out at the end of the Paris march and in other cities, and police made nearly 1,000 arrests, even as 70,000 officers prevented a repeat of the previous weekend's looting. The unrest is testing President Emmanuel Macron before May's election; student groups want 250,000 more university places and an end to the Parcoursup admissions system, and Marine Le Pen's National Rally is urging voters to channel their anger into votes for her.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Adamson, John Leicester and Tom Nouvian, Associated Press

item.title: Musk says he was behind Starlink speed restriction after service in Ukraine restored
item.description: After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield speeds had been restored after more than a week of disruptions to front-line drone and logistics operations, Elon Musk acknowledged that SpaceX throttled Starlink in Ukraine. Musk said Ukraine's military had broken the terms of service by using the civilian network for offensive drone strikes and that "loophole was closed," while saying the U.S. government controls changes to the military Starshield system. Administration officials have given conflicting accounts of any role, and the restoration comes as Russia agreed to resume three-way talks next month.
item.dc:creator: Susie Blann and Elise Morton, Associated Press

item.title: 'The most complicated launch campaign ever': NASA lays out mad dash to test lunar landers
item.description: NASA laid out the schedule for Artemis III, a roughly 14-day mission in low-Earth orbit next year in which Orion will practice docking with lunar landers from both SpaceX and Blue Origin, which Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons called "likely the most complicated launch campaign ever undertaken." SpaceX still has to show that Starship can transfer propellant in orbit, with a first demonstration expected in early 2027, while Blue Origin has to return New Glenn to flight after a May explosion and fly its Blue Moon Mark 1. Administrator Jared Isaacman said NASA staff will step in when vendors miss schedules, and the agency will decide which lander flies Artemis IV, now set for early 2028, based on which is ready first as it races China.
item.dc:creator: Jackie Wattles, CNN

item.title: 'Worst on record': Brutal summer heat wave killed more than 50,000 in Europe's cities
item.description: Two peer-reviewed papers in Nature Health estimate that this summer's heat waves killed 50,391 people across 854 cities in 30 European countries, the deadliest toll in 26 years and well above the heat waves of 2003 and 2022. The researchers attribute about two-thirds of the deaths to climate change, compared with roughly 40% earlier in the century, and Imperial College London's Clair Barnes called 2026 "likely to have been the worst on record" for heat deaths in much of Europe. EuroMOMO's Lasse Vestergaard cautioned that the modeled figures carry uncertainties but said they are broadly consistent with the network's own summer counts.
item.dc:creator: Laura Paddison, CNN

item.title: What are Tony Finau's favorite kinds of books?
item.description: At a Utah Chamber golf outing with Tony Finau, Salt Lake Chamber CEO Derek Miller pressed the private sector to help get every Utah third grader reading proficiently by 2030. Miller said the goal was raised from 90% to 100% after philanthropist Hope Eccles asked who would be left behind, and Christine Ivory of the Ivory Foundation noted that over the past decade more than half of Utah's roughly 183,000 K-3 students have fallen short of proficiency. Finau, who said reading helped him make up for never earning a college degree, named Phil Knight's "Shoe Dog" as his pick for sports fans and said literacy at his West Valley foundation center has risen 19% in two years.
item.dc:creator: Hayden Madson, Deseret News

item.title: BYU student tackles immigration and practical effects in short film
item.description: BYU engineering doctoral student James Cutler's short film "Can I Put You On Hold?" screens Oct. 26 at FilmQuest at Provo's Velour, drawing on the years his twin brother Matthew and Matthew's wife, Dangmo Kanyawee, spent stuck in visa bureaucracy, during which they lived in Thailand for about three years before she could join him. A $5,000 Davey Foundation grant helped fund it, and its gravity-defying scenes were shot without green screens or CGI, using harnesses, fishing line and a wooden rig on a moving trailer. Cutler said immigration rules created "walls of bureaucracy" that kept the couple apart.
item.dc:creator: Diana Jones and Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: French artist installs imaginative, spiraling wooden sculpture in Ogden plaza
item.description: A French artist known as elparo, a former graffiti artist with a physics degree who has built large public installations in more than 15 countries, is making his first U.S. piece at Ogden's Dumke Arts Plaza: an entry in his spiraling wooden "La Vrille" series, open Oct. 29 through April 9. Gallery director Andrea Ferber said he was chosen partly because his design takes up the whole two-story plaza, which ran its first international call for proposals this year. Elparo usually builds from reclaimed wood but used new lumber because of time limits, and he described public art as something that "comes to you" rather than requiring a gallery visit.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: These airports offer easy access to ski areas
item.description: OnTheSnow's list of 12 U.S. airports with easy ski-resort access puts Salt Lake City International near the top, noting that 10 resorts, including Park City, Deer Valley, Snowbird and Alta, are within an hour's drive and that the airport has hundreds of daily nonstop flights. Romboy calls the airport one of the biggest assets for Utah's $2.5 billion ski industry, and the remodeled terminal that opened in 2020 includes a baggage system designed for skis and oversized luggage. Most of the other airports on the list are in the West.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Romboy, Deseret News

item.title: More than cameras and a crowd: Inside ESPN's 'College GameDay'
item.description: This behind-the-scenes look at ESPN's "College GameDay" stop at BYU, its first in Provo in 17 years, reports that the show takes more than 200 people on the road each week, and the host site is usually picked just six days before the broadcast. ESPN scouts possible campuses before the season, crews start arriving around Wednesday, and colorful broadcast clocks keep the live three-hour show on schedule, which an ESPN spokesperson called "a well-oiled machine." The show heads to Salt Lake City next for No. 10 Utah against No. 14 Houston, giving the state consecutive visits.
item.dc:creator: Na'Andre Emerson, Deseret News

item.title: Woman gets probation for lying to police after fatal shooting at Salt Lake party
item.description: Tommi Tiara Jude Gallegos, 26, received 12 months of probation and a suspended one-year jail term for obstruction of justice after lying to police about who attended her January 2024 birthday party at a Salt Lake City Airbnb, where 18-year-old Gabriel Isidore Vigil was killed by what charges call "friendly fire" as his group fired at least 18 rounds while running away. Her felony charge was reduced to a class A misdemeanor in a plea deal, the last case tied to the shooting to be resolved. Co-defendant Maricio Amar Reyes Valdez was sentenced to five years to life, while Isidore Junior Barrera received probation.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Make-A-Wish Utah brings Halloween magic to children with critical illnesses
item.description: Make-A-Wish Utah turned the Kahlert Foundation Wishing Place in Murray into a Disney-themed trick-or-treat stop Friday for children with critical illnesses and their families, with help from local businesses and volunteers. About 300 Utah children are still waiting for wishes, according to the organization, and volunteer services director Jenny Hortin described the experience as "part of their healing journey" for many families. Lizzie Hansen, whose son Clark's wish was a family trip to Florida to see a rocket launch, said the event connects families who understand what they're going through.
item.dc:creator: Garna Mejia, KSL

item.title: Summit County's children justice center receives national accreditation
item.description: The National Children's Alliance has accredited the Summit County Children's Justice Center, making it the first Utah center in more than 20 years to seek and earn the national credential. The county attorney's office described the review of its child maltreatment teams and interagency practices as "long and arduous," and director Ted Walker said the center, founded in 2012, has grown from a part-time satellite into a flagship facility with a full-time forensic interviewer and family advocate. County Attorney Margaret Olson praised the team, and the office credited social work graduate student Nicole Johansen with pushing the effort to completion.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Utah fans camp out as 'College GameDay' returns for second straight week
item.description: With "College GameDay" in Salt Lake City for No. 10 Utah's game against No. 14 Houston, University of Utah students camped out for days to get a place near the set and a shot at a million-dollar kick. That kick follows the previous week's broadcast in Provo, where a BYU student's make turned into $3 million after Utah Jazz owner Ryan Smith and partner Ryan Sweeney each matched Pat McAfee's $1 million. Junior Hunter Perrero said he'd hit it on the first try, and senior Nick Tripp said winnings would go to student loans "off rip."
item.dc:creator: Tyrese Boone, KSL

item.title: Family of Utah murder victim asks parole board to release man convicted in case
item.description: At a parole hearing Tuesday, the mother and daughter of Jay Wolfinjer, who was beaten to death over a gang-related drug debt, asked the board to release Fonua Kimoana, sentenced in 2010 to 15 years to life for his role. After visiting him in prison, mother Linda Dobbins, who once called him "the monster that beat my son," now believes he loaded her son into a vehicle on his uncle's orders but did not beat him, and daughter Autumn Wolfinjer said he must keep earning his freedom. Their support does not extend to the others involved, and Dobbins said she will oppose the uncle's release at his 2028 hearing.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: CVS is trying out pharmacists in chronic health management
item.description: CVS Health is running a five-store pilot in Michigan in which pharmacists measure customers' blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar, part of a push to give its roughly 9,000 retail pharmacists a larger role in managing chronic disease. Chief Medical Officer Dr. Amy Compton-Phillips, speaking at the Reuters Total Health conference in Nashville, said the company is also talking with Medicare about how pharmacists could expand lower-cost care. She also called for cheaper access to GLP-1 drugs and predicted that once Ozempic goes generic in the U.S. in 2032, doctors will prescribe it "like water."
item.dc:creator: Caroline Humer, Reuters
